teile.einleitung: The first cosmic velocity is the speed a body needs to circle the Earth in an orbit just above the Earth's surface. It is about 7.9 kilometres per second, roughly 28,000 km/h. Anything flying this fast is constantly falling towards the Earth, but keeps missing it.
wichtigste: Just above the Earth's surface, the first cosmic velocity is about 7.9 km/s.
It can be calculated in a simplified way with v = √(g·R).
Newton's cannonball is a thought experiment that explains why a satellite falls around the Earth.
One orbit just above the Earth's surface would take about 84 minutes without air resistance.
The higher the orbit, the lower the orbital speed needed.
Rockets usually launch towards the east to make use of the Earth's speed of rotation.
The Moon moves around the Earth at about 1 km/s.

abschnitte.text: The **first cosmic velocity** is the lowest speed at which a body can circle the Earth in a circular orbit. For an orbit just above the Earth's surface it is about 7.9 km/s. That is about 28,000 km/h, much faster than any aeroplane. It is also called the **circular orbital speed**. The second cosmic velocity, about 11.2 km/s, is needed to leave the Earth completely.

The English physicist **Isaac Newton** explained orbits with a thought experiment. He imagined a cannon on a very high mountain. The faster a ball is fired, the further it flies before it hits the ground. If it is fast enough, the Earth's surface curves away beneath it exactly as much as the ball falls. Then it falls around the Earth for ever, like a **satellite**.

In a circular orbit, gravity must supply exactly the force that keeps the body on its curved path. This gives the simplified formula v = √(g·R). Here g is the **acceleration due to gravity** of about 9.81 m/s² and R is the Earth's radius of about 6370 km. If you put in these values, you get about 7.9 km/s. At this height one orbit would take about 84 minutes without air resistance.

The higher an orbit is, the weaker gravity acts and the lower the speed needed. The **International Space Station ISS** flies at a height of about 400 km at about 7.7 km/s and needs about 90 minutes for one lap. The distant Moon moves around the Earth at only about 1 km/s. At a height of about 150 km there is still some **remaining air**. It brakes a satellite so strongly that it comes down after only a short time and burns up.

The Earth turns from west to east, at about 1670 km/h at the equator. That is why rockets usually launch towards the **east**, so that they take this boost with them. Launch sites near the equator are especially favourable, such as Kourou in French Guiana, from which the European Ariane rockets launch. The first artificial satellite, **Sputnik 1**, reached the necessary speed in 1957. Since then thousands of satellites have been circling the Earth.

begriffe.erklaerung: A body that circles a planet in an orbit.
The path along which a body circles another again and again.
The speed needed for a circular orbit at a particular height.
The distance from the centre of the Earth to its surface, about 6370 kilometres.

gewusst: Astronauts on the ISS experience about 16 sunrises a day.
At the first cosmic velocity you would get from Geneva to Zurich in about half a minute.
People in the space station do not float because there is no gravity, but because they are constantly falling together with the station.

teile.einleitung: District heating is heat that is not produced in your own house, but in a large plant, and then flows through pipes to many buildings. Hot water carries the heat under the street to the cellars. In this way a whole neighbourhood can stay warm without its own boilers.
wichtigste: District heating is produced centrally and distributed through pipes.
In many Swiss towns, waste incineration plants supply district heating.
The Beznau nuclear power station supplies heat to the lower Aare valley through the Refuna network.
The pipes are well insulated so that little heat is lost on the way.
In the house, a heat exchanger transfers the heat to the heating system.
A house with district heating needs no boiler of its own.
Reykjavík in Iceland is heated almost entirely with district heating from geothermal energy.

abschnitte.text: In **district heating**, heat is produced in a central plant, for example in a heating plant or a waste incineration plant. From there hot water flows through a network of pipes under the streets to homes, schools and hospitals. The heat is used for heating and for hot water. The cooled water flows back in a second pipe and is heated again.

In Switzerland district heating is supplied mainly by **waste incineration plants**, because burning rubbish produces a lot of heat. Other sources are wood-fired power plants, waste heat from factories, geothermal heat and lake water with heat pumps. The Beznau nuclear power station supplies several municipalities in the lower Aare valley through the **Refuna** network. Plants that produce electricity and usable heat at the same time are called combined heat and power plants.

The pipes are thickly wrapped in **insulation** so that little heat is lost along the way. Depending on the network, the water is often about 70 to over 100 degrees. In the cellar of the house there is a **heat exchanger**, which transfers the heat from the district heating water to the building's heating circuit. The water of the two circuits does not mix. A meter measures how much heat the house has used.

A house with district heating needs no boiler of its own, no oil tank and no chimney. Large plants can work more cleanly and efficiently than many small heating systems. If the heat comes from rubbish, wood or waste heat, this saves heating oil and natural gas. But building the pipes is expensive and is worthwhile mainly where many houses stand close together.

Many Swiss towns such as Zurich, Basel, Bern and Lausanne are greatly expanding their district heating networks. The aim is to replace oil and gas heating and so give off less **CO2**. Smaller networks in villages are often called heating groups, and they are frequently run on wood chips. Some towns by lakes use the heat of the lake water with large heat pumps.

Iceland lies on volcanically active ground and has a great deal of **geothermal heat**. The capital, Reykjavík, is heated almost entirely with district heating from hot water from deep underground. Some pavements and car parks there are even kept free of ice in winter with leftover heat. Denmark and Sweden also heat a large part of their houses with district heating.

begriffe.erklaerung: A device that transfers heat from one liquid to another without them mixing.
A plant in which rubbish is burned.
Producing electricity and usable heat at the same time.
A protective layer that stops heat from escaping.

gewusst: Through waste incineration, a bag of rubbish from Switzerland can end up helping to heat a flat.
In Reykjavík some streets and pavements are kept free of snow and ice with warm water from the district heating.
District heating pipes often lie only about a metre below the street and yet can hardly be felt, because they are so well insulated.

teile.einleitung: The foehn is a warm, dry downslope wind that blows over the Alps. In northern Switzerland it often brings clear views and high temperatures, while it rains on the southern side of the Alps. Behind the foehn there is exciting physics: air warms up when it sinks.
wichtigste: The foehn is a warm, dry wind on the lee side of a mountain range.
In northern Switzerland the south foehn blows, coming over the Alps.
On the windward side the air rises, cools down and drops its rain.
As it sinks, the dry air warms by about 1 °C per 100 metres.
Well-known foehn valleys are the Reuss valley in Uri, the Hasli valley and the Rhine valley.
The foehn blows especially often in spring and autumn.
During the foehn the danger of fire is great, and snow melts quickly.

abschnitte.text: The foehn is a **downslope wind**, that is a wind that blows down from a mountain range into the valley. Typical of it are warm air, strong gusts and very low **humidity**. In Switzerland it usually comes from the south over the Alps and is then called the **south foehn**. If it blows the other way, from the north into Ticino, it is called the north foehn.

The air is pushed against the Alps and has to rise on the **windward side**. As it does so, it cools down, clouds form and there is often heavy rain or snow. Inside the cloud the air cools by only about 0.5 °C per 100 metres. On the other side, the **lee side**, the now dry air sinks down and warms by about 1 °C per 100 metres. That is why it is warmer at the bottom than it was before at the same height.

Dry foehn air on a pass at a height of 2500 metres has a temperature of 5 °C. It sinks to 500 metres, that is by 2000 metres. For every 100 metres it gets about 1 °C warmer, so about 20 °C in total. Down in the valley it is then about **25 °C** warm, even in the middle of spring.

Above the main ridge of the Alps you often see a mighty wall of cloud during the foehn, the **foehn wall**. On the northern side, on the other hand, the sky clears; this is called the **foehn window**. The view is then so clear that the mountains seem close enough to touch. Sometimes lens-shaped clouds also appear that look like UFOs.

Because the foehn is warm and dry and blows strongly, a **fire** can spread at terrifying speed. In 1861, for example, a fire fanned by the foehn destroyed large parts of the town of **Glarus**. That is why fires are often banned in foehn valleys when the foehn is strong. The foehn also makes snow melt quickly, which can increase the danger of avalanches and floods. Some people get headaches or feel tired during the foehn.

Well-known foehn valleys are the **Reuss valley** with Altdorf, the Hasli valley, the canton of Glarus and the St Gallen Rhine valley. In these valleys there are sometimes spring-like temperatures in winter during the foehn. In spring the foehn helps to melt the snow off meadows and fields. Weather services such as MeteoSwiss issue warnings when the foehn is strong.

begriffe.erklaerung: The side of a mountain that the wind blows against.
The side of a mountain facing away from the wind.
A wall of cloud above the main ridge of the Alps during the foehn.
How much water vapour the air contains compared with the most it could hold.

gewusst: In German a hairdryer is also called a Föhn, because it blows warm, dry air like the wind.
When the foehn is strong, the relative humidity in an Alpine valley can fall below 30 per cent.
The word foehn comes from the Latin word “favonius”, the name of a mild west wind.

teile.einleitung: The watering can is a container with a handle and a long spout that is used to water plants. You can discover a lot of physics in it, such as communicating vessels and gravity. With a rose fitted on the end, the water falls gently onto the soil like rain.
wichtigste: A watering can is used to water plants.
For water to flow out, you have to tip the can forwards.
The spout reaches as high up as the can, otherwise the water runs out of the front when filling.
The rose spreads the water gently like rain.
Limescale from the water can block the small holes of the rose.
If you tip a full can too far, the water also runs out of the filling opening at the top.
In summer it is best to water in the morning or in the evening.

abschnitte.titel: How a watering can is built
abschnitte.text: A **watering can** consists of a container, a handle, a filling opening and a long tube, the **spout**. At the front you can fit a rose, a cap with many small holes. Watering cans are made of plastic, galvanised sheet metal or copper. Normal garden cans hold about 5 to 10 litres of water.

The can and the spout are connected at the bottom. In such **communicating vessels** the water stands at the same height everywhere. That is why the spout must reach at least as high as the can itself. If it were shorter, the water would run out of the front while filling, before the can was full.

For water to come out, you tip the can forwards until the water level is higher than the opening of the spout. Then **gravity** pulls the water out. If you tip a full can too far, the water also runs out of the filling opening at the top. While you are watering, air flows in through this opening so that the water can flow evenly.

The **rose** splits the jet of water into many fine streams. In this way the water falls gently like rain and does not wash away soil or small seeds. Over time, **limescale** from tap water can block the small holes. If you leave the rose in vinegar and water for a while, the limescale dissolves again.

In summer it is best to water in the morning or in the evening, because then less water evaporates in the heat. It is better to water rarely and thoroughly, directly at the roots, than often and a little over the leaves. Wet leaves overnight can encourage fungal diseases. **Rainwater** from a water butt is ideal, because it is soft and contains hardly any lime.

A litre of water weighs about a kilogram. A full 10-litre can therefore weighs about 10 kilograms, as much as a small dog. That is why it is more comfortable to carry two half-full cans, one on the left and one on the right, than one full can on one side. In this way the body stays balanced.

begriffe.erklaerung: Containers connected at the bottom, in which liquid stands at the same height everywhere.
An attachment with many small holes that spreads the jet of water finely.
A mineral dissolved in tap water that settles as a white crust.
Water turns into invisible water vapour and goes into the air.

gewusst: Many Swiss cemeteries provide watering cans for everyone to use to water the graves.
A coffee pot and a teapot also work on the principle of communicating vessels.
A full watering can with 10 litres is about as heavy as ten one-kilogram bags of flour.

teile.einleitung: The bicycle helmet, usually called a velo helmet in Switzerland, protects your head in a fall. It consists of a hard shell and a core of foam that absorbs the impact. In Switzerland it is not compulsory for normal bikes, but it is strongly recommended.
wichtigste: A bike helmet protects your head in falls and accidents.
Inside there is hard foam that cushions the force of an impact.
The helmet must sit straight and firmly on your head.
The chin strap holds the helmet in place under your chin.
After a bad fall the helmet must be replaced.
The holes in the helmet let air through and cool your head.
In Switzerland a helmet is not compulsory for normal bikes, but it is recommended.

abschnitte.text: On the outside a bike helmet has a thin, smooth **shell** made of plastic. Underneath is a core of hard foam, usually **EPS**, which is expanded polystyrene. This foam is squashed on impact and so absorbs a large part of the energy. Inside, soft pads make it comfortable to wear, and ventilation holes let air through.

In a fall, your head would otherwise hit the road or the kerb directly. The helmet spreads the impact over a larger area and slows the head down more gently. This greatly reduces the risk of serious head injuries. Once the foam has been squashed, it no longer protects properly, which is why you replace the helmet after a bad **fall**, even if you cannot see any damage.

The helmet must sit straight and firmly on your head and must not slip backwards. It should cover your forehead, about two finger widths above your eyebrows. The **chin strap** is fastened so tightly that just one finger fits between it and your chin. With a little dial at the back you can adjust the size to fit your head.

For normal bikes and slow e-bikes there is no **compulsory helmet law** in Switzerland. The Swiss Council for Accident Prevention (BFU) nevertheless recommends a helmet for everyone, especially children. Anyone riding a fast e-bike that gives assistance up to 45 km/h must wear a helmet. Many parents and schools make sure that children wear a helmet on the way to school.

A helmet in bright yellow or orange is seen especially well in traffic. Reflective strips also help at dusk. Sun, heat and age make the material brittle over time, so a helmet should be replaced after a few years. Good helmets carry a test mark according to the European **standard** EN 1078.

begriffe.erklaerung: A hard, light foam that absorbs impacts.
A strap under the chin that holds the helmet in place.
A law that requires people to wear a helmet.
The Swiss Council for Accident Prevention.

gewusst: In the playground children should take off their bike helmet, because otherwise they could get caught on equipment by the strap.
A bike helmet often weighs only about 200 to 400 grams, about as much as two to four bars of chocolate.
Since 2003 the riders in the Tour de France have also had to wear a helmet on all stages.

teile.einleitung: Voltage is the push that makes electric current flow. You can imagine it like the pressure in a water pipe. It is measured in volts, and a Swiss household socket supplies 230 volts.
wichtigste: Voltage drives electric current.
Voltage is measured in volts.
One volt is one joule per coulomb.
A single-phase household socket in Switzerland supplies 230 volts.
A voltmeter is connected in parallel with the component.
Kirchhoff’s loop rule says: the sum of all the voltages in a closed loop is zero.
High voltages are life-threatening.

abschnitte.text: **Voltage** tells you how strongly the electrons in a circuit are driven. It is often compared with water pressure: the greater the pressure, the more strongly the water flows. Voltage arises when positive and negative charges are separated, for example in a battery. Without voltage no current flows.

Voltage is measured in **volts**, named after the Italian Alessandro Volta. One volt is one joule per coulomb, that is the energy each unit of charge is given. If a charge of 2 coulombs takes up 24 joules of energy in a source, the voltage is 24 divided by 2, that is 12 volts. An AA battery has 1.5 volts, a car battery 12 volts.

An ordinary single-phase household socket in Switzerland supplies 230 volts of alternating voltage. Cookers and large machines often use **three-phase current** at 400 volts. The SBB trains run with 15,000 volts in the overhead line. Overhead power lines carry electricity at up to 380,000 volts, because less energy is lost that way.

Voltage is measured with a **voltmeter**, which is connected in parallel with the component. In this way it compares the two ends of the component. A real battery has a small **internal resistance**, at which part of the voltage is lost. If a battery with 9 volts and an internal resistance of 1 ohm supplies current to a resistor of 8 ohms, 1 ampere flows, and you measure a terminal voltage of 8 volts at the terminals.

In 1845 the German physicist Gustav Kirchhoff set out important rules for circuits. The **loop rule** says that the sum of all the voltages in a closed loop is zero. So whatever voltage the source supplies is dropped again across the components. In a series circuit of two identical lamps on 230 volts, each therefore gets 115 volts.

Even alternating voltages from about 50 volts can be dangerous for people. That is why you must never tinker with sockets or cables. Railway overhead lines are also life-threatening; you do not even have to touch them, because the voltage can jump across a short distance. For experiments at school, harmless **extra-low voltage** from batteries or power supply units is used.

begriffe.erklaerung: The unit of voltage.
A measuring instrument for voltage.
The resistance inside a battery or power source.
A closed path in a circuit.
A voltage that constantly changes direction, in Europe 50 times a second.

gewusst: An electric eel can produce electric shocks with a voltage of several hundred volts.
Lightning occurs at voltages of many millions of volts.

teile.einleitung: A Fata Morgana is a mirage in which you see things in a place where they are not. It forms when light is bent by layers of air at different temperatures. It is not imagination, because you can even photograph it.
wichtigste: A Fata Morgana is caused by the refraction of light in layers of air at different temperatures.
Warm air has a lower density and therefore a slightly lower refractive index than cold air.
The apparent puddle on hot roads is reflected sky.
The Fata Morgana is named after the fairy Morgana.
In the Strait of Messina in Italy, mirages were described early on as “Fata Morgana”.
A mirage is not imagination; you can photograph it.
Over a cold sea under warmer air, ships sometimes seem to float above the horizon.

abschnitte.text: A **Fata Morgana** is a **mirage**. You see images of objects that appear shifted, doubled or upside down. Best known is the apparent lake in the desert that thirsty travellers searched for in vain. If you walk towards it, it seems to move back, because you can never reach it. Even so, the Fata Morgana is not imagination, but a real optical phenomenon.

Light is bent when it passes from one substance into another; this is called **refraction**. Layers of air at different temperatures also bend light to different degrees. Warm air has a lower **density** and therefore a slightly lower **refractive index** than cold air. Rays of light that pass at a slant through such layers are therefore curved. Our eyes assume that light comes in a straight line, and so they see the image in the wrong place.

On hot summer days a **puddle of water** seems to lie on the road in the distance. Directly above the hot tarmac the air is much warmer than further up. Light from the sky is bent upwards in this layer and so reaches our eyes. So we see reflected sky that shines like water. This is an **inferior mirage**, just like the apparent lake in the desert.

Over a cold sea it can be the other way round: cold air lies below, with warmer air above. Then the light is bent downwards, and ships or coasts seem to float above the horizon. This is called a **superior mirage**. Sometimes you can even see things that are actually hidden behind the horizon. Such mirages are also seen again and again over **Lake Constance**.

The name comes from Italian and means “fairy Morgana”. The **fairy Morgana** is a magical figure from the legends of King Arthur. It was said that she made castles appear in the air to deceive sailors. In the **Strait of Messina**, between Sicily and the Italian mainland, such mirages were described in this way early on. From there the name spread into many languages.

begriffe.erklaerung: An image that appears in the wrong place because of light bent in layers of air.
The bending of light when it passes into another substance.
A number that shows how strongly a substance bends light.
How much mass there is in a particular space.

gewusst: You can see a Fata Morgana not only in the desert, but also on Swiss roads on hot days.
Some sailors' tales of ghost ships probably go back to mirages.
In a superior mirage an image can also appear upside down above the real object.

teile.einleitung: Gliding means moving across a surface or through the air without any driving movement of your own. A skater glides over the ice, a glider glides through the air. For gliding to work well, the braking friction must be as small as possible.
wichtigste: With skates you glide on ice.
A glider is an aeroplane without an engine that glides through the air.
The flying squirrel glides from tree to tree with its gliding membrane spread out.
The albatross glides over the sea for hours, almost without flapping its wings.
In curling, heavy stones glide over the ice towards a target.
On a water slide you slide fast because the water makes the slide smooth.
Penguins sometimes slide quickly on their bellies over ice and snow.

abschnitte.text: On **ice** the friction is very small, which is why skates, sledges and skis glide so well. Under the blade a wafer-thin, watery layer forms that acts like a lubricant. In ice hockey the hard rubber puck glides over the ice into the goal. Penguins use this too: they lie on their bellies and slide forward faster than they could waddle.

In **curling**, granite stones weighing about 20 kilograms are slid over the ice towards a target circle. The players sweep the ice in front of the stone with brooms. This warms the ice slightly and makes it smoother, and the stone glides further and straighter. Curling is popular in Switzerland, and Swiss teams have already won many medals at world championships and Olympic Games.

On a water slide at the swimming pool, the water makes the slide especially smooth. Between the body and the slide there is a thin **film of water**, which greatly reduces the friction. A surfboard glides over the waves in a similar way. Lubricating oil in machines also makes sure that parts slide past each other easily.

In **gliding flight** a body sinks slowly while flying forwards. The albatross has wings with a span of up to more than three metres and makes clever use of the wind over the sea. The flying squirrel stretches a gliding membrane between its front and back legs and so sails from tree to tree. Flying fish can also glide some way over the water with their large pectoral fins.

A **glider** has no engine and is brought up into the air by a winch or a towing aeroplane. Good gliders can glide 40 kilometres or more from a height of one kilometre. With warm rising air, the **thermals**, they gain height again and fly for hours. Paragliders are also very popular in the Swiss Alps, for example near Interlaken.

begriffe.erklaerung: A force that brakes when two surfaces rub against each other.
Flying without a drive, in which you sink slowly while moving forwards.
Rising warm air that carries birds and gliders upwards.
A stretchy fold of skin with which some animals sail through the air.

gewusst: An albatross can travel thousands of kilometres over the sea while hardly flapping its wings.
Curling stones are made from a special granite that comes mainly from a small Scottish island.
A flying fish can glide several dozen metres over the water.

teile.einleitung: A gear system, or transmission, is a device that transfers a movement and changes it in the process. It can make a turning movement faster or slower, change its direction or turn a rotation into a straight movement. Gears are found in bikes, cars, clocks, mixers and even guitars.
wichtigste: A gear system transfers movements and forces from one part to another.
Many gear systems are made of toothed wheels, others of belts or chains.
With bevel gears a turning movement is redirected by 90 degrees.
The tuning mechanism of a guitar contains a worm gear.
A toothed wheel with a rack turns a rotation into a movement in a straight line.
The differential lets the driving wheels of a car turn at different speeds on bends.
An automatic gearbox chooses the right gear by itself.

abschnitte.text: A gear system connects a **drive**, for example an engine or the pedals, with the part that is to move. If a small toothed wheel meshes with a large one, the large one turns more slowly, but with more force. The ratio of the teeth is called the **gear ratio**. So you can trade speed for force and the other way round.

**Spur gears** with straight teeth transfer rotations between parallel axles. **Bevel gears** redirect the rotation by 90 degrees, for example in a hand drill. In a **worm gear** a screw drives a toothed wheel, which then turns very slowly and powerfully. In a planetary gear, small planet wheels circle around a sun wheel in the middle.

An engine only runs well within a certain range of speeds. That is why a car has different **gears**. In first gear it has a lot of torque at low speed, ideal for starting off. An automatic gearbox chooses the gear itself, and the **differential** makes sure that the outer wheel can turn faster than the inner one on a bend.

On a **rack railway**, a toothed wheel on the locomotive meshes with a toothed rack between the rails. In this way the rotation is turned into a straight movement uphill. The Vitznau-Rigi railway of 1871 was the first mountain railway of this kind in Europe. With a gradient of up to 48 per cent, the Pilatus railway is considered the steepest rack railway in the world.

On a **bike**, a chain transfers the force from the pedals to the back wheel, and the gears change the ratio. Two pulleys connected with a simple belt turn in the same direction, whereas two toothed wheels meshing together turn in opposite directions. In mechanical **clocks**, tiny toothed wheels make sure that the second, minute and hour hands turn at the right speed. On the guitar, the worm gear makes it possible to tune the strings finely.

begriffe.erklaerung: A wheel with teeth on its edge that meshes with another toothed wheel.
The ratio of how fast the driven wheel turns compared with the driving wheel.
The turning effect of a force.
A straight bar with teeth into which a toothed wheel meshes.
The toothed wheel in the middle of a planetary gear.

gewusst: Even in ancient Greece people built a geared device, the Antikythera mechanism, with which the movements of the heavens could be calculated.
A worm gear can usually only be turned from the worm, which is why a guitar string does not go out of tune by itself.
Swiss watchmakers make toothed wheels that are smaller than a grain of rice.

teile.einleitung: Electric current tells you how much electric charge flows through a wire in a certain time. You can compare it with the amount of water that flows through a garden hose per second. It is measured in amperes, abbreviated A.
wichtigste: Current tells you how much charge flows through a cross-section of a conductor per second.
Its unit is the ampere (A), named after the Frenchman André-Marie Ampère.
At 1 A, about 6.24 · 10^18 elementary charges flow through the conductor per second.
Charge equals current times time, that is Q = I · t.
Current is measured with an ammeter, which is built into the circuit.
In metals the electrons move opposite to the conventional direction of current, that is from the negative to the positive terminal.
At a junction, the sum of the currents flowing in equals the sum of the currents flowing out.

abschnitte.text: Electric **current** is the movement of electric charges, for example of electrons in a copper wire. The **current** with the symbol I tells you how much charge flows past a point in the wire per second. If a charge of 1 coulomb flows in one second, the current is 1 ampere. That corresponds to about 6.24 · 10^18 elementary charges, that is more than six quintillion electrons per second.

The charge Q is calculated with the formula **Q = I · t**. If, for example, 0.5 A flows for 2 minutes, that is 120 seconds, then 0.5 A times 120 s equals 60 coulombs. So the unit **coulomb** (C) is the same as the ampere second. Batteries often show the charge in milliampere hours (mAh), for example 4000 mAh for a mobile phone.

At a branch in a circuit, a so-called **junction**, no charge is lost. Whatever flows in must also flow out again. This rule is called the **junction rule** or Kirchhoff’s first law, after the German physicist Gustav Robert Kirchhoff. If, say, 3 A and 2 A flow into a junction and 4 A flow out, a further current of 1 A must flow away.

Current is measured with an **ammeter**, which is often a multimeter. It is connected in series, so the current has to flow through the measuring instrument. An ideal ammeter has an **internal resistance** as close to zero as possible, so that it does not change the current. If you held it directly to a socket, there would be a dangerous short circuit.

It was decided long ago that current flows from the positive terminal to the negative terminal; this is the **conventional direction of current**. Later it was found that the electrons in metals travel exactly the other way, from the negative to the positive terminal. And they are astonishingly slow: their **drift velocity** in a copper wire is only a fraction of a millimetre per second. Even so, the lamp lights up at once, because the electric field spreads through the wire at almost the speed of light.

An LED lamp needs only a few hundredths of an ampere. A kettle at the socket draws about 10 A. In Swiss homes the circuits are usually protected by **fuses** of 10 A or 13 A. Even about 0.05 A flowing through the body can be life-threatening for a person.

begriffe.erklaerung: The unit of current, named after André-Marie Ampère.
The unit of electric charge; 1 C is 1 ampere times 1 second.
The smallest free charge, as carried by an electron.
A measuring instrument for current that is built into the circuit.
The average speed at which electrons travel forward in a wire.

gewusst: An electron in a copper wire is often slower than a crawling snail.
The ampere is one of the seven base units of the International System of Units.
A lightning bolt can briefly reach a current of more than 10,000 amperes.

teile.einleitung: A damped oscillation is an oscillation that gets weaker and weaker over time until it stops completely. The cause is friction, which gradually takes energy away from the oscillating object. Every swing that you stop pushing shows this behaviour.
wichtigste: In a damped oscillation the amplitude, that is the greatest swing, decreases over time.
The energy of the oscillation is usually converted into heat by friction.
If the friction force is proportional to the speed, the amplitude decreases exponentially.
If a constant sliding friction is braking, the amplitude decreases linearly.
Depending on the strength of the damping, a distinction is made between underdamping, critical damping and overdamping.
A weakly damped oscillation has a slightly lower frequency than the undamped one.
A high quality factor means that an oscillator is only weakly damped.

abschnitte.text: Without friction a pendulum or a spring would keep oscillating for ever. In reality **air resistance**, friction in bearings or internal friction in the material slow down the movement. The energy of the oscillation is not lost, but is converted into **heat**. This process is called **damping**.

If the braking force depends on the speed, as with air or oil, the amplitude shrinks by the same fraction with every oscillation. This is called an **exponential decrease**. If, for example, the amplitude falls to 80 per cent per period, only about 33 per cent remains after five periods. If, on the other hand, a constant **sliding friction** is braking, the amplitude becomes smaller by the same amount with every oscillation, that is linearly.

With weak damping the system still swings back and forth several times; this is **underdamping**. With **critical damping** the system returns to its rest position fastest, without shooting past it. If the damping is even stronger, it is called **overdamping**: the system creeps back slowly to its rest position without oscillating.

The **logarithmic decrement** is the logarithm of the ratio of two successive amplitudes. It shows how quickly an oscillation dies away. The **quality factor** describes the same thing from the other side: a high quality factor means little damping. A tuning fork or a quartz crystal in a watch has a high quality factor and rings on for a very long time.

In a car, **shock absorbers** make sure that the car does not keep bouncing for long after a bump. They are set roughly to critical damping. The pointers of old measuring instruments and scales are also damped so that they quickly come to rest. In the Taipei 101 skyscraper in Taiwan, a huge steel ball hangs as a **vibration damper**, reducing the swaying in wind and earthquakes.

begriffe.erklaerung: The greatest swing of an oscillation, that is how far it swings out at most.
The point where a pendulum or a spring comes to hang still.
The damping at which a system comes to rest fastest without overshooting.
A number that shows how weakly an oscillator is damped.
A decrease in which the same share disappears in equal times.

gewusst: A bell rings on for several seconds because it is only very weakly damped.
If you hold a ringing bell with your hand, you damp it so strongly that the sound stops almost at once.
Good shock absorbers are an important part of road safety, because otherwise the wheels could lose contact with the ground.

teile.einleitung: A Faraday cage is a closed shell of metal or a metal mesh that shields the inside from electric fields. It is named after the English natural scientist Michael Faraday. That is why, for example, you are well protected from lightning in a car during a thunderstorm.
wichtigste: Inside a closed Faraday cage, an external static electric field is zero.
The excess charge of a charged hollow metal body sits on its outer surface.
In 1836 Michael Faraday showed with a metal-lined room that the inside stays free of fields.
An ordinary cage made of thin metal does not protect against static magnetic fields.
A convertible with a fabric roof offers hardly any protection in a thunderstorm, because it lacks a closed metal shell.
The perforated mesh in a microwave oven door holds the microwaves back, because the holes are much smaller than the wavelength.
In a metal lift car a mobile phone often has poor reception.

abschnitte.text: A **Faraday cage** is a shell made of conducting material, usually metal, that is closed all round. It can also be a mesh or net, as long as the holes are small enough. Inside you are protected from external **electric fields**. Even if high voltages occur outside, the inside remains almost unaffected. That is why such cages are used to protect people and sensitive devices.

In metal there are many freely moving **electrons**. If an electric field acts from outside, these charges shift within the shell. They arrange themselves so that their own field exactly cancels out the external field inside. That is why the field strength inside is zero for a static field. Additional charge on a hollow metal body also always sits on the **outer surface**.

The English natural scientist **Michael Faraday** lived from 1791 to 1867 and made many important discoveries about electricity. In 1836 he built a room whose walls were lined with metal. Outside he produced strong electric charges and sparks. With a measuring device inside he showed that no field could be detected there. The unit of electrical capacitance, the **farad**, is also named after him.

A car with a metal body acts like a Faraday cage. If lightning strikes, the current flows over the outer skin into the ground, and the people inside stay protected. **Aeroplanes** are also struck by lightning quite often without anything happening to the passengers. A **convertible** with a fabric roof, on the other hand, offers hardly any protection, because the closed metal shell is missing. In a thunderstorm it is therefore safer to stay in the car than to stand outside.

A perforated metal mesh is built into the door of a **microwave oven**. The holes are much smaller than the wavelength of the microwaves, about 12 centimetres, so the waves cannot get out. In a **coaxial cable**, the outer shield of wire mesh acts as a cage for the signal. In a closed metal lift car a mobile phone often has poor reception, because the radio waves are shielded. Against static magnetic fields, for example from a magnet, a thin metal cage does not help.

begriffe.erklaerung: A closed metal shell that protects the inside from electric fields.
The area around electric charges in which forces act on other charges.
Protection from fields or waves by means of a shell.
The distance from one wave crest to the next.
A cable with an inner conductor and a sheath of wire mesh, for example for aerials.

gewusst: On average a passenger aircraft is struck by lightning about once a year.
At physics shows people sometimes sit in a metal cage while sparks metres long strike the outside.
Rooms for examinations with an MRI scanner are shielded so that no radio waves from outside disturb the images.

teile.einleitung: Galileo's falling experiments are famous experiments by the Italian scientist Galileo Galilei on how bodies fall. He found out that without air resistance all bodies fall equally fast and keep getting faster. In this way he disproved a teaching that had been accepted for almost 2000 years.
wichtigste: The ancient scholar Aristotle had claimed that heavy bodies fall faster than light ones.
Galileo showed that without air resistance all bodies fall equally fast.
To slow down the falling movement, he let balls roll down a slope.
He measured the time with a water clock.
The distance fallen grows with the square of the time.
In the 1st, 2nd and 3rd seconds a falling body covers distances in the ratio 1 : 3 : 5.
He published his results in 1638 in a book known as the Discorsi for short.
In 1971 the astronaut David Scott dropped a hammer and a feather at the same time on the Moon.

abschnitte.text: **Galileo Galilei** lived in Italy from 1564 to 1642. He was a mathematician, physicist and astronomer and is considered one of the founders of modern science. What was new was that he answered questions not only by thinking, but through **experiments** and measurements. He taught at the universities of Pisa and Padua, where he studied accelerated motion around 1604.

In the 4th century BC the Greek scholar **Aristotle** had taught that heavy bodies fall faster than light ones. This seems to be true in everyday life, because a stone falls faster than a feather. But Galileo realised that the difference comes from **air resistance**. Without air, all bodies would fall equally fast.

Free fall happens so quickly that Galileo could not measure it accurately with the clocks of his time. So he let balls roll down a **slope**, a long, gently sloping groove. In this way the same kind of movement happened more slowly. He measured the time with a **water clock**: he weighed the water that flowed out during the rolling. He found that the distance covered grows with the square of the time.

According to Galileo, a falling body gets faster at an even rate; it is **uniformly accelerated**. In twice the time it covers four times the distance, in three times the time nine times the distance. The distances in the 1st, 2nd and 3rd seconds are therefore in the ratio 1 : 3 : 5, like the odd numbers. Near the Earth's surface the speed increases by about 9.81 metres per second every second.

It is often said that Galileo dropped balls from the **Leaning Tower of Pisa**. Whether he really did is disputed among historians, because he does not describe it himself. What is certain is that he published his results in 1638 in the book known for short as the **Discorsi**. He wrote it in the last years of his life, when he was under house arrest after a trial by the Church.

In 1971, during the Apollo 15 mission, the astronaut **David Scott** repeated Galileo's idea on the Moon. In front of a running camera he dropped a hammer and a feather at the same time. Because there is no air on the Moon, both landed at exactly the same time. Today Galileo's laws of falling are a firm part of physics lessons, in Switzerland too.

begriffe.erklaerung: A rule for how a falling body moves over time.
The slowing force of the air on moving bodies.
A sloping surface on which things roll more slowly than in free fall.
How quickly the speed of a body changes.

gewusst: Galileo measured time by weighing water as it flowed out.
In a vacuum tube without air, a feather and a coin fall equally fast.
Whether Galileo really dropped balls from the Leaning Tower of Pisa is still not known for certain.

teile.einleitung: Saving energy means using less electricity, heat or fuel for the same things. This protects the environment and saves money. Even with small everyday habits, everyone can make a big difference.
wichtigste: Saving energy protects the environment and saves money.
When cooking, a lid on the pan saves a lot of energy.
A short shower needs less energy for hot water than a bath.
Televisions and other appliances should be switched off completely instead of being left on standby.
The fridge door should be closed again quickly.
Walking or cycling is the most energy-saving way to get to school.
On the energy label, the letter A shows a particularly economical appliance.

abschnitte.text: Electricity, heat for heating and fuel must first be produced, and this often harms the **environment**. Burning oil, gas or coal produces **carbon dioxide**, which makes climate change worse. Hydroelectric power stations and solar panels also need space and materials. So anyone who uses less energy protects nature and the climate. In addition, the bills for electricity, heating oil or petrol go down.

When cooking, a **lid** on the pan saves a lot of energy, because the heat does not escape. A short shower needs much less hot water than a full bath. The **fridge door** should be closed again quickly so that not too much cold air falls out. Televisions, games consoles and computers should be switched off completely after use instead of being left on **standby**. Anyone who switches off the light when leaving a room also saves electricity.

A large part of the energy in Swiss households is used for **heating**. That is why it is worth not heating rooms too much in winter. A rule of thumb says that every degree less saves about six per cent of heating energy. Instead of leaving a window tilted open for hours, it is better to open it wide for a short, strong **burst of airing**. Well-insulated walls and windows keep the heat in the house.

Walking or cycling to school uses no fuel and keeps you fit. For longer distances, trains, trams and buses are much more economical than a car with only one person in it. Switzerland has a particularly dense **public transport** network. If a car is really needed, it helps to share lifts. Air travel also uses a very large amount of energy.

When buying fridges, washing machines or lamps, the **energy label** helps. It uses letters and colours to show how much energy an appliance needs. The letter **A** with a dark green bar stands for a particularly economical appliance, the letter G for a very wasteful one. In Switzerland the label is required for many appliances. LED lamps, for example, need much less electricity than old light bulbs.

begriffe.erklaerung: A ready mode in which an appliance seems to be off but still uses electricity.
A sticker with the letters A to G that shows how economical an appliance is.
Opening windows wide for a few minutes to change the air quickly.
A gas that is produced when things burn and warms the climate, abbreviated CO2.

gewusst: Boiling water with a lid on is not only more economical but also faster.
An LED lamp can use up to five times less electricity than a light bulb for the same brightness.
A fridge works more economically if it does not stand next to the oven or the radiator.

teile.einleitung: A combined cycle gas turbine power station, CCGT for short, produces electricity with two turbines one after the other. First hot combustion gas drives a gas turbine, then a steam turbine uses the leftover heat of the exhaust gases. In this way more energy is got out of the fuel than in almost any other thermal power station.
wichtigste: A CCGT power station combines a gas turbine and a steam turbine.
The hot exhaust gases of the gas turbine turn water into steam in the heat recovery steam generator.
It combines the Joule cycle of the gas turbine with the Clausius-Rankine cycle of the steam turbine.
Modern plants reach an efficiency of about 60 per cent.
Per kilowatt-hour, a CCGT power station gives off about half as much CO2 as a hard coal power station.
It can start quickly and change its output rapidly.
Natural gas is usually used as the fuel.

abschnitte.text: In the first part of the power station a compressor sucks in air and squeezes it strongly. In the combustion chamber **natural gas** is added and burned, producing very hot gas. This gas flows through the **gas turbine** and makes it turn, rather like an aircraft engine. The turbine drives a generator, which produces electricity. Experts call this process the **Joule cycle**.

The exhaust gases still leave the gas turbine at about 600 degrees Celsius. Instead of simply blowing this heat into the air, it is led into the **heat recovery steam generator**. There the exhaust gases heat water in pipes until it turns into steam. The steam drives a second turbine, the **steam turbine**, and with it a further generator. After that the steam is cooled in the condenser, so that it turns back into water and starts again.

A gas turbine on its own uses about 38 per cent of the energy in the fuel. If the steam turbine then uses another 35 per cent of the remaining energy, the total is about 60 per cent **efficiency**. A simple coal power station, on the other hand, usually reaches much less. Even so, energy is lost here too as **waste heat**: with a fuel input of 1000 megawatts and 60 per cent efficiency, that is 400 megawatts. Part of this heat can be used for district heating.

Because natural gas contains a lot of hydrogen and the power station works so efficiently, about half as much **carbon dioxide** is produced per kilowatt-hour as in a hard coal power station. But a CCGT power station running on natural gas is not climate-neutral, because natural gas is a fossil fuel. In addition, methane can escape when natural gas is extracted and transported, and this also warms the climate. For the future, researchers are looking into running such power stations on **hydrogen** or biogas.

CCGT power stations can start within a short time and change their output quickly. That is much more flexible than a **nuclear power station**, which works best running steadily. That is why CCGT power stations often step in when there is little wind or little sunshine. In many European countries, such as Germany, Italy and Britain, they supply a large part of the electricity. In Switzerland, on the other hand, most electricity comes from hydropower and nuclear power, and gas power stations have so far played only a small part.

begriffe.erklaerung: A wheel with blades that is turned by flowing gas, steam or water.
A machine that converts turning movement into electric current.
A large boiler in which hot exhaust gases turn water into steam.
Heat that is left over from a process and is usually lost without being used.
The part in which steam is cooled and turns back into water.

gewusst: The gas turbine of a CCGT power station works in a similar way to the engine of a passenger aircraft.
Some of the best CCGT power stations in the world reach an efficiency of more than 60 per cent.
If the waste heat is also used to heat flats, more than 80 per cent of the fuel's energy can be used.

teile.einleitung: The bicycle, usually called a velo in Switzerland, is a vehicle with two wheels that you power with your own muscles. It is quiet, environmentally friendly and healthy. Since it was invented a good 200 years ago, it has developed from a wooden running machine into the modern e-bike.
wichtigste: A normal bicycle has two wheels, one behind the other.
You sit on the saddle, steer with the handlebars and drive the bike with the pedals.
In 1817 Karl Drais invented the running machine, a balance bike without pedals.
The penny-farthing had a huge front wheel.
A moving bike does not fall over as easily as a stationary one, because it is moving.
In Switzerland children aged 6 and over may ride alone on main roads.
A bicycle bell is not compulsory in Switzerland, but it is useful.

abschnitte.text: A bike consists of a **frame**, two wheels, handlebars, a saddle and a drive. With your feet you push the **pedals**, which drive the back wheel through the crank and the chain. With the handlebars you turn the front wheel and decide the direction. You can fasten a bag to the carrier. Brakes, lights and reflectors make it safe.

In 1817 **Karl Drais** from Mannheim presented his **running machine**, a wooden vehicle without pedals that you pushed along with your feet on the ground. In the 1860s pedals were added to the front wheel. To go faster, people built bigger and bigger front wheels, and so the **penny-farthing** was born, on which you sat very high up and in danger. From about 1885 the safety bicycle, with wheels of equal size and a chain drive, won out. With the pneumatic tyre, riding soon became much more comfortable.

abschnitte.titel: Why you do not fall over
abschnitte.text: A stationary bike tips over immediately, but a moving one stays amazingly stable. This is due to the movement: when the bike starts to tip, you steer a little in that direction and bring the wheels back under your body. The shape of the **fork** also helps, because it makes the front wheel steer a little by itself. That is why riding slowly is harder than riding fast. Today children often learn balance first on a balance bike.

In Switzerland children aged 6 and over may ride a bike alone on main roads. Up to the age of 12 they may ride on the **pavement** if there is no cycle path or cycle lane, and they must be considerate towards pedestrians. A bike needs working brakes, reflectors and lights at night. A bell is not compulsory, but it is useful. A **cycle helmet** is not compulsory for normal bikes, but it is strongly recommended.

The bike is one of the most environmentally friendly means of transport, because it needs no fuel and makes no noise. Many people ride to school or work, and cycling keeps you fit. **E-bikes** with an electric motor help on hills and long distances. In Switzerland there is a large network of signposted **cycle routes**, for example from SwitzerlandMobility. In many schools a cycling test is part of road safety lessons.

begriffe.erklaerung: The supporting structure of the bike, to which all the other parts are fixed.
Karl Drais's first balance bike from 1817, without pedals.
An old bicycle with a huge front wheel and a small back wheel.
A rack above the back wheel on which you fasten bags.
A bike with an electric motor that helps when you pedal.

gewusst: In Switzerland people usually say velo; the word comes from the French vélocipède.
Karl Drais is said to have invented the running machine partly because horses were scarce and expensive at the time.
On a bike you get about three to four times as far as on foot with the same effort.

teile.einleitung: A camera is a device with which you capture pictures. Light falls through a lens onto a light-sensitive sensor or a film. Today there is also a camera in almost every smartphone.
wichtigste: The lens focuses the light and creates a sharp image on the sensor.
The aperture controls how large the opening for the light is.
A larger f-number such as 16 instead of 4 means a smaller opening and less light.
The shutter decides how long light falls on the sensor.
For fast ski racers you need a very short exposure time, such as 1/2000 of a second.
A higher ISO value makes the sensor more sensitive, but the picture grainier.
A sensor with 24 megapixels has 24 million picture points.
In a single-lens reflex camera a mirror directs the image into the viewfinder.

abschnitte.text: A **camera** is basically a dark box with an opening through which light falls in. At the front sits the **lens** with its glass elements, at the back the sensor or, in older cameras, a film. The lens forms a smaller, upside-down image of the surroundings. In digital cameras an image processor turns the light into an image file.

For a picture to be sharp, the distance between the lens and the sensor must be right. For a nearby object the lens is moved further away from the sensor, and for distant things closer to it. Modern cameras do this themselves with **autofocus**, often in a fraction of a second. Incidentally, the eye works the same way, except that it changes the shape of its lens to do so.

Three things decide how bright a photo will be. The **aperture** is an adjustable opening: the larger the f-number, the smaller the opening. The **shutter** opens for a certain time, for example 1/2000 of a second for a fast ski racer or several seconds for stars at night. The ISO value shows how sensitive the sensor is; high values make the picture brighter, but also grainier.

The **image sensor** consists of millions of tiny light-sensitive points, the **pixels**. A sensor with 24 megapixels has 24 million such points. Each point measures how much light falls on it, and coloured filters make sure that colours are recorded. More pixels mean more detail, but a larger sensor is often more important for good pictures in low light.

In a **single-lens reflex camera** a mirror directs the image into the viewfinder, and it flips up when you take the picture. Mirrorless system cameras, on the other hand, show the image directly on a small screen. Compact cameras are small and have a built-in lens. Smartphones have tiny cameras and improve the pictures with a lot of computing power.

Even in ancient times people knew the **camera obscura**, a dark room in which a small hole projects an image onto the wall. Around 1826 the Frenchman Nicéphore Niépce made the oldest surviving photograph, which needed an exposure of many hours. In 1839 the daguerreotype was presented, which made photography well known. From about 2000 digital cameras won out and largely replaced film.

begriffe.erklaerung: The part with glass elements that focuses the light and creates an image.
An adjustable opening that controls the amount of light.
The length of time during which light falls on the sensor.
The smallest picture point of a digital image.
A number for the light sensitivity of the sensor or film.

gewusst: The world's first surviving photograph had to be exposed for many hours.
A photo with an exposure time of 1/2000 of a second can freeze a drop of water in the air.
The word photography comes from Greek and means something like “drawing with light”.

teile.einleitung: Geothermal energy is energy obtained from the heat inside the Earth. The deeper you drill into the Earth, the warmer it gets. This heat from the Earth can be used to heat houses or to produce electricity.
wichtigste: Geothermal energy is energy obtained from the heat inside the Earth.
On average it gets about 3 degrees Celsius warmer for every 100 metres of depth.
In the Earth's core there are temperatures of about 5000 degrees Celsius or more.
Geothermal heat counts as renewable energy because it is practically inexhaustible.
In Switzerland a great many houses use ground probes with heat pumps.
Iceland obtains a large part of its heat and electricity from geothermal energy.
Deep drilling can trigger small earthquakes, as in Basel in 2006.

abschnitte.text: The word **geothermal** comes from Greek: geo means earth and thermos means warm. Inside the Earth it is very hot; in the Earth's core there are temperatures of about 5000 degrees Celsius or more. The heat comes partly from when the Earth was formed and partly from the decay of **radioactive** substances in the rock. In the Earth's crust the temperature rises on average by about 3 degrees for every 100 metres of depth.

Just a few metres below the surface the ground has roughly the same temperature all year round. With **ground probes** that reach 100 to 300 metres into the ground, this heat is brought up. A **heat pump** raises it to a temperature at which houses can be heated and hot water prepared. Switzerland is one of the countries with the most ground probes per area.

For electricity you need very hot water or steam from several kilometres down. The steam drives a **turbine** and a generator. The world's first geothermal power station was built in 1904 in **Larderello** in Italy. Geothermal energy is especially favourable in volcanic areas such as Iceland, New Zealand or Kenya.

In **Iceland** the hot earth lies close to the surface, and there are geysers and hot springs. Almost all houses there are heated with geothermal heat. A considerable part of the electricity comes from geothermal power stations, and the rest mainly from hydropower. Also well known is the Blue Lagoon, a bathing spot with warm water from a geothermal power station.

Geothermal energy supplies energy day and night, regardless of weather and season. It gives off hardly any **greenhouse gases** and needs little space. But deep drilling is expensive, and it is not certain whether enough hot water will be found. In **Basel** a deep geothermal project triggered noticeable earthquakes in 2006, and something similar happened in St Gallen in 2013, so both projects were stopped.

begriffe.erklaerung: A pipe in the ground with which heat is brought up from deep down.
A device that raises heat from the surroundings to a higher temperature.
A hot spring that shoots water up into the air at intervals.
Using heat from several kilometres down in the Earth.

gewusst: In theory, the heat flowing out from inside the Earth would cover humanity's energy needs many times over.
The word geyser comes from a hot spring in Iceland called Geysir.
Even the ancient Romans used warm springs for their baths, for example in Baden in the canton of Aargau.

teile.einleitung: There is a lot of physics in football: force, air pressure, friction and spin decide how the ball flies. If you know how a ball reacts to a kick, you can pass more accurately and shoot at goal more dangerously. A football is a ball filled with air that weighs about 430 grams for adults.
wichtigste: The harder you strike the ball, the faster it flies.
You play an accurate pass with the inside of the foot.
You shoot especially hard with the instep.
If you strike the ball low down, it flies high into the air.
A football is filled with air and bounces badly if there is too little air in it.
A ball struck with spin flies in a curve because it is spinning.
The air slows down a kicked ball.

abschnitte.text: A football for adults has a circumference of about 68 to 70 cm and weighs about 430 grams. Inside there is a **bladder** filled with air at above atmospheric pressure. Today the cover is usually made of plastic panels that are stitched or glued together. If the ball has too little air, it is deformed a lot on impact and bounces badly.

The more **force** you transfer to the ball, the faster it flies. With the inside of the foot you strike the ball with a large, flat surface, which is why passes made this way are especially accurate. With the **instep**, that is the top of the foot, the leg swings through with full force, which gives hard shots. Where you strike the ball decides its direction: if you strike it low down, it rises high into the air.

If you strike the ball off-centre, it spins in flight. The air then flows past the ball faster on one side than on the other, and a sideways force is produced. This phenomenon is called the **Magnus effect**. This is how free kicks curve around the defensive wall; fans call it a banana kick.

A ball kicked high is slowed down by the air; this is **air resistance**. It grows strongly with speed, which is why a hard shot quickly loses pace. At the same time gravity pulls the ball down, so it flies in an arc. In matches at stadiums high up, where the air is thinner, the ball flies a little further.

When the ball rolls over the grass, **friction** slows it down. On wet, closely cut grass it rolls faster, which is why the pitch is often watered before matches. Football boots have studs so that players do not slip when they sprint off. Goalkeeper gloves also use friction so that the ball does not slip through the fingers.

begriffe.erklaerung: A sideways force on a spinning ball in the air.
The turning of a ball around itself.
The upper part of the foot, used for hard shots.
The slowing force of the air on a moving body.
A force that arises between two surfaces and slows down movement.

gewusst: A famous example of the Magnus effect is a free kick by the Brazilian Roberto Carlos in 1997, which flew into the goal in a huge curve.
Professionals kick the ball at over 100 km/h, faster than a car is allowed to drive on the motorway.
The rules lay down exactly how big and heavy a match ball must be and how hard it must be pumped up.

teile.einleitung: Energy degradation means that energy is converted into a form that can hardly be used any more. The energy does not disappear, but it usually becomes weak heat that spreads out into the surroundings. This happens all the time: when braking on a bike, rubbing your hands or when a mobile phone gets warm.
wichtigste: Energy is never lost; it is only converted.
Energy degradation usually produces low-temperature heat that can hardly be used.
Friction turns kinetic energy into heat, for example when rubbing your hands or braking.
Laptops and mobile phones get warm because part of the electrical energy becomes heat.
The heat an appliance gives off without being used is called waste heat.
Lukewarm water can hardly be used, because the temperature difference to the surroundings is too small.
Many Swiss waste incineration plants use their heat for district heating.

abschnitte.text: According to the **law of conservation of energy**, energy can be neither created nor destroyed. It only changes its form, for example from electrical energy to light or from kinetic energy to heat. Even so, in everyday life we say energy is “lost”. What is meant is that it passes into a form with which we can no longer do anything useful. This process is called **energy degradation**.

When you rub your hands together, they get warm, because **friction** turns kinetic energy into heat. When you brake on a bike, the brake pads rub against the rim or the disc. The kinetic energy is not lost; it becomes heat that spreads into the air. This heat can hardly be recovered. That is why ski racers go faster with well-waxed skis, because less energy is degraded by friction.

Almost all appliances give off part of their energy as **waste heat**. Laptops and mobile phones get warm because electric current flows in the chips and produces heat. An old light bulb turned most of the electricity into heat and only a little into light. Car engines also get very hot and therefore need cooling. The less waste heat an appliance has, the higher its **efficiency**.

Heat can only be used well when there is a large **temperature difference**. Hot steam at several hundred degrees can drive a turbine. Lukewarm bath water, on the other hand, is hardly warmer than its surroundings, so it can drive almost nothing. Physicists describe this degradation with the term **entropy**. By itself, heat only ever flows from warm to cold, never the other way round.

Energy degradation cannot be prevented, but waste heat can often be used once more. Many Swiss **waste incineration plants** supply their heat through pipes as **district heating** to flats and schools. The waste heat of data centres or factories is also sometimes used for heating. In sewers, heat pumps recover heat from the warm water. In this way energy is used better before it is finally degraded.

begriffe.erklaerung: The conversion of energy into a form that can hardly be used any more.
Heat that an appliance gives off to its surroundings without it being used.
A force that arises when two surfaces rub against each other and slows down movement.
The share of energy that is really used for the desired task.
Heat for heating that comes through pipes from a central plant into houses.

gewusst: By the end of the day, the energy from your breakfast has almost completely become body heat, which you give off to the air.
Modern electric cars can feed part of the kinetic energy back into the battery when braking, instead of turning it into heat.
At rest, a person gives off about as much heat as a 100-watt light bulb.

teile.einleitung: Gamma radiation is very high-energy, invisible electromagnetic radiation. It is produced inside atomic nuclei, for example in radioactive substances. It can penetrate deep into matter and is dangerous, but it is also used deliberately in medicine for healing and examinations.
wichtigste: Gamma radiation is very high-energy electromagnetic radiation.
It is produced in the atomic nucleus, often after alpha or beta decay.
When gamma radiation is given off, the nucleus does not turn into another element.
It has an even shorter wavelength than X-rays.
It is best shielded with thick layers of lead or concrete.
In medicine it is used to sterilise syringes and instruments.
With the Gamma Knife, tumours in the brain are targeted with radiation.

abschnitte.text: Like light, radio waves and X-rays, gamma radiation belongs to **electromagnetic radiation**. But it has an extremely short wavelength and therefore a great deal of energy. A gamma photon with an energy of 1 MeV has a wavelength of only about 1.24 picometres, much smaller than an atom. Our eyes cannot see gamma radiation; it is measured with devices such as the Geiger counter.

After alpha or **beta decay**, the new atomic nucleus often still has too much energy. It gives this off as gamma radiation. The numbers of protons and neutrons stay the same, so the nucleus does not turn into another element. A well-known example: caesium-137 decays into an excited barium-137m, which then gives off gamma radiation at 662 keV.

Gamma rays and X-rays are very similar. The basic difference lies in how they are produced: **gamma radiation** comes from the atomic nucleus, X-rays from the electron shell. Gamma radiation usually has the shorter wavelength and more energy. It was discovered in 1900 by the Frenchman Paul Villard, and Ernest Rutherford later gave it its name.

Gamma radiation passes through paper, skin and even thin metal plates. As it passes through matter, its strength decreases **exponentially** with the thickness of the layer; it never disappears completely. That is why thick layers of **lead** or concrete are used. Very high-energy gamma photons of 1.022 MeV and more can even create an electron and a positron in matter; this is called pair production.

In radiotherapy, tumours are destroyed with gamma radiation; a well-known source for this is cobalt-60. The **Gamma Knife** focuses many beams precisely on a tumour in the brain. In scintigraphy, patients are given a small amount of technetium-99m, and a camera shows how organs are working. Gamma radiation is also used to sterilise syringes, dressings and instruments.

Strong gamma radiation damages cells and genetic material and can cause illnesses such as cancer. That is why radiation at nuclear power stations and hospitals is strictly monitored in Switzerland. In space, exploding stars produce enormous gamma-ray bursts. The Earth's atmosphere protects us from them, which is why they are observed with satellites.

begriffe.erklaerung: Energy that spreads out as a wave, like light or radio waves.
A single tiny packet of energy of gamma radiation.
Atomic nuclei that decay by themselves and give off radiation in the process.
The thickness of a substance that weakens the radiation to half.

gewusst: Gamma-ray bursts from space are among the brightest events in the whole universe.
The name comes from the Greek letter γ (gamma), because this radiation was discovered as the third type of radiation after alpha and beta.

teile.einleitung: An experiment is a planned test with which you want to find something out or check an idea. You change something on purpose and watch carefully what happens. Experiments are the most important tool of the natural sciences, and even children can make exciting discoveries with them.
wichtigste: An experiment is a test to find something out.
Researchers do many experiments as their job.
In a fair comparison experiment you change only one thing at a time.
An experiment is often repeated several times to check whether it always turns out the same.
In a record you write down how an experiment went.
In experiments with liquids, safety goggles protect your eyes.
In experiments with fire an adult must always be present.

abschnitte.text: An **experiment** is a test in which you ask nature a question. At the start there is often an idea, called a **hypothesis**. For example: “Plants grow better with light than in the dark.” Then you plan a test with which you can check this idea. The result shows whether the idea is right or whether you need to think again.

A good experiment usually follows fixed steps: question, hypothesis, planning, carrying out, observation and evaluation. Everything is written down carefully in a **record**, including measurements and drawings. In a fair comparison you change only one thing at a time, which is called a **variable**. Everything else stays the same, so that you know what caused the difference. Because chance can play a part, an experiment is often repeated several times.

In experiments you must take good care of yourself and others. With liquids such as vinegar or cleaning products you wear **safety goggles**. In experiments with fire, electricity or hot objects an **adult** must always be present. You never taste unknown substances and you do not eat anything in the experiment area. After the experiment you tidy up and wash your hands.

For a long time scholars tried to explain nature mainly by thinking about it. Around 1600 the Italian **Galileo Galilei** made the experiment the foundation of physics. He let balls roll down slopes and measured exactly how fast they became. Since then the rule has been: a theory must prove itself in an experiment. This way of working is called the **scientific method**.

In Geneva there is **CERN**, one of the largest research centres in the world. There researchers make tiny particles collide in a ring 27 kilometres long. Experiments are also carried out every day at ETH Zurich, EPFL in Lausanne and at many universities. Young people can present their own research projects in the **Swiss Youth in Science** competition. Many museums, such as the Technorama in Winterthur, invite you to experiment for yourself.

begriffe.erklaerung: An idea that you want to check with an experiment.
A text in which you write down how an experiment went and what the results were.
A quantity that you deliberately change or measure in an experiment.
Looking carefully and noting down what happens.

gewusst: Even a failed experiment is valuable, because it shows that an idea is wrong.
Some famous discoveries, such as penicillin, came about by chance during an experiment.
In 2012 the long-sought Higgs particle was detected at CERN.

teile.einleitung: A geostationary satellite circles above the equator in such a way that, seen from the Earth, it always stands at the same point in the sky. That is why a satellite dish can stay pointed at it permanently. Such satellites bring us television pictures, weather images and radio links.
wichtigste: A geostationary satellite orbits the Earth exactly once per sidereal day, that is in about 23 hours and 56 minutes.
It flies at a height of about 35,786 kilometres directly above the equator.
On its orbit it travels at about 3.1 kilometres per second.
Seen from the Earth, it seems to stand still in the sky.
In Switzerland satellite dishes therefore point roughly south.
The idea of worldwide radio links with such satellites came from the writer Arthur C. Clarke in 1945.
Geostationary satellites cannot cover the polar regions.

abschnitte.text: A geostationary satellite is an artificial object that circles the Earth in a very special orbit. It takes exactly as long for one lap as the Earth takes to turn once around itself, namely a **sidereal day** of about 23 hours and 56 minutes. Because it turns along with the Earth, it always stays above the same point on the equator. This orbit is called the **geostationary orbit**, or also the Clarke orbit.

Only above the equator does the satellite's orbital plane lie in the same plane as the Earth's rotation. An orbit with a period of one sidereal day that is tilted against the equator is called a **geosynchronous orbit**. A satellite on it moves up and down in the sky every day in a kind of figure of eight. For the orbit to take exactly one sidereal day, the satellite must circle at a height of about 35,786 kilometres, almost three times the Earth's diameter.

Most television satellites, for example the Astra satellites, are geostationary. A **satellite dish** on the balcony therefore only has to be lined up once and can then stay fixed. A radio signal takes about 0.24 seconds to go from the ground to the satellite and back, because the path is so long. You sometimes notice this small delay in live television links.

Weather satellites are also often geostationary above the equator. The European **Meteosat** satellites are operated by the organisation EUMETSAT, of which Switzerland is also a member. They constantly photograph almost a whole half of the Earth and show how clouds and storms move. MeteoSwiss uses these images for weather forecasts.

In 1945 the British writer **Arthur C. Clarke** suggested in a magazine article that three such satellites could provide the whole Earth with radio. At that time there were no satellites at all. In 1964 Syncom 3 was one of the first satellites to reach this orbit, and it transmitted pictures of the Olympic Games in Tokyo. Today hundreds of geostationary satellites circle the Earth in a narrow ring.

From the polar regions the satellite lies below the horizon, so it cannot be received there. Space on the orbit is limited, which is why the positions are allocated internationally. Satellites that are no longer in use are usually pushed a few hundred kilometres higher into a **graveyard orbit**. In this way they make room for new satellites.

begriffe.erklaerung: The time in which the Earth turns once completely around itself, measured against the distant stars: about 23 hours and 56 minutes.
The path of a satellite or body in space.
The imaginary line that divides the Earth into a northern and a southern half.
A curved dish that collects radio signals and directs them onto a receiver.
A European organisation that operates weather satellites, with its headquarters in Darmstadt.

gewusst: A geostationary satellite races through space at over 11,000 kilometres per hour, yet to us it stands still.
Just three geostationary satellites evenly spaced are enough to reach almost the whole Earth except the poles.
The idea for communication satellites came from a science fiction writer, almost 20 years before it became reality.

teile.einleitung: The violin, also called the fiddle, is a string instrument with four strings that is made to sound with a bow. It is the highest instrument of the string family and plays the main melody in many orchestras. How a vibrating string becomes a full sound is an exciting piece of physics.
wichtigste: Another name for the violin is the fiddle.
It belongs to the string instruments, together with the viola, cello and double bass.
It has four strings, tuned to the notes G, D, A and E.
The hairs of the violin bow are usually horsehair.
So that the hairs grip the strings better, they are rubbed with rosin.
The hollow wooden body amplifies the vibrations of the strings.
Famous violins come from Antonio Stradivari of Cremona.

abschnitte.text: The violin has a hollow wooden **sound box**, usually with a top made of spruce and a back made of maple. On the top there are two curved openings, the **f-holes**. The four strings run from the tailpiece over a small bridge to the pegs on the head, with which they are tuned. Inside there is a small wooden rod, the sound post, which connects the top and the back.
