The **bow** consists of a slightly curved wooden stick and a band of many hairs, usually **horsehair**. So that the hairs do not just slide over the string, they are rubbed with **rosin**, a resin. When bowing, the string sticks briefly to the hairs and then snaps back. This happens very many times a second, and so the string starts to vibrate evenly.

A vibrating string on its own is very quiet, because it hardly moves any air. The **vibration** is passed through the bridge to the wooden body, which then vibrates along with it. This vibrating along is called **resonance** and makes the note much louder. How high a note sounds depends on the frequency, that is how often the string vibrates per second. If you press a string onto the fingerboard with your finger, the vibrating part becomes shorter and the note higher.

Besides the violin, the **string instruments** include the slightly larger viola, the cello and the double bass. When playing, the cello is placed between the knees, and the double bass is usually played standing up. The larger the instrument, the lower it sounds. For children there are smaller violins, for example in half or three-quarter size.

The violin was developed in the 16th century in northern Italy. In the town of **Cremona**, violin makers such as Andrea Amati and later **Antonio Stradivari** built instruments that are still considered the best today. A Stradivarius can cost millions of francs today. In Switzerland you can learn violin making at the violin-making school in Brienz in the Bernese Oberland. Violins are heard in classical music as well as in folk music, jazz and pop music.

begriffe.erklaerung: A body vibrating along with something, which amplifies a note.
A resin that is rubbed onto the bow hairs so that they grip the string.
The number of vibrations per second; it decides the pitch.
A small wooden piece over which the strings run and which passes on the vibration.
The long wooden board onto which you press the strings with your fingers.

gewusst: You can also pluck the strings of the violin with your fingers; this is called pizzicato.
A violin bow is strung with many dozens of individual horsehairs.
Most violin strings today are no longer made of gut, but of synthetic material or steel.

teile.einleitung: Whispering is a very quiet way of speaking in which the voice does not sound. You whisper when someone is asleep, when you want to tell a secret or when there should be silence. Whispering is interesting in terms of physics, because it produces a quite different sound from normal speaking.
wichtigste: When you whisper, the vocal folds in the larynx do not vibrate.
Whispering is much quieter than normal speaking.
You can only hear a whisper from close by, not from a great distance.
Hissing sounds such as “sh” or “s” can be heard especially well when whispering.
People often cup a hand around their mouth when whispering so that only one person hears.
In the game Chinese whispers, a word is passed on by whispering.
A “shh” usually means that someone is asking for quiet.

abschnitte.text: When **whispering** you speak without the sound of your voice. You form words quite normally with your mouth, tongue and lips, but only a breathy sound is produced. That is why everyone sounds similar when whispering, and voices are harder to recognise. Whispering is a good way to communicate quietly without disturbing others.

In the **larynx** lie the **vocal folds**, two small folds of muscle. When you speak normally, they vibrate quickly back and forth and produce a tone. When you whisper, they stay slightly open and do not vibrate. The air flows past them and is swirled about, which produces a rushing noise. Your mouth and throat then shape the sounds from this noise.

Loudness is measured in **decibels**. A soft whisper is about 30 decibels, a normal conversation about 60 decibels. Because sound spreads out in all directions, it quickly gets quieter with distance. That is why you can only understand a whisper from close by. Hissing sounds such as “s” and “sh” can be heard well even when whispered, because they are made without the voice anyway.

In some round rooms you can hear a whisper amazingly far away. This is called a **whispering gallery**. The curved walls guide the sound along the wall, so that it hardly gets quieter. A famous example is the dome of St Paul's Cathedral in London, where you can whisper against the wall and be heard at the other end of the gallery.

People whisper in libraries, at the cinema, at the theatre or when a baby is asleep. Teachers often say “shh” to ask for quiet. In the game **Chinese whispers**, a word is whispered from ear to ear, and at the end something quite different often comes out. This shows how hard it is to understand whispered words exactly. By the way, anyone who is hoarse should not whisper much, because that strains the voice too.

begriffe.erklaerung: Two folds of muscle in the larynx that vibrate when you speak.
The part of the throat where the voice is produced.
The unit of measurement for loudness.
A sound such as “s” or “sh” that is made by air rubbing.

gewusst: When whispering, almost everyone sounds the same, which is why it is hard to tell who is whispering.
In a whispering gallery you can hear a whisper over many metres.
Whispering can also strain the voice, which is why many experts recommend rest and silence when you are hoarse.

teile.einleitung: The equivalent resistance is a single imaginary resistor that has exactly the same effect in a circuit as several resistors connected together. With it you can simplify complicated circuits and easily calculate how much current flows. What matters is whether the resistors are connected one after the other or side by side.
wichtigste: In a series circuit you simply add up the resistances.
47 Ω, 33 Ω and 20 Ω in series give 100 Ω.
In a parallel circuit you add up the reciprocals of the resistances.
60 Ω and 30 Ω in parallel give 20 Ω.
The equivalent resistance of a parallel circuit is always smaller than the smallest single resistance.
Two equal resistors in parallel give half the value of one.
Mixed circuits are calculated step by step from the inside out.

abschnitte.text: An electrical **resistor** slows down the current, rather like a narrow point in a water pipe. It is measured in ohms, abbreviated with the Greek letter Ω. The unit is named after the German physicist Georg Simon Ohm. His **Ohm's law** says: voltage equals resistance times current.

In a **series circuit** the current flows through all the resistors one after the other. So the current has to overcome every brake, which is why you add all the resistances together. 47 Ω, 33 Ω and 20 Ω give 100 Ω. Two equal resistors that give 40 Ω in series each have 20 Ω. If one component breaks, the whole circuit is broken.

In a **parallel circuit** the current splits up into several paths. Because it has more paths, more current gets through overall, and the equivalent resistance becomes smaller. You calculate: 1 divided by R equals 1 divided by R1 plus 1 divided by R2. For 60 Ω and 30 Ω this gives 20 Ω; three resistors of 12 Ω each give 4 Ω. If you want to turn 120 Ω into an equivalent resistance of 40 Ω, you connect 60 Ω in parallel with it.

Many circuits are mixed. Then you first replace one group by its equivalent resistance and carry on calculating from there. A 10 Ω resistor in series with 30 Ω in parallel with 60 Ω gives 10 plus 20, that is 30 Ω. If 25 Ω and 35 Ω are in series, that makes 60 Ω, and in parallel with 40 Ω that gives 24 Ω. Likewise, 2 Ω, then 6 Ω in parallel with 3 Ω, and 4 Ω in series together give 8 Ω.

The sockets in a flat are connected in parallel so that each appliance gets the full voltage. That is why the total resistance falls when you plug in many appliances, and the current rises. A **fuse** then protects the wires from overheating. In some older **fairy lights** the little bulbs are connected in series, which is why in the past the whole string went out when one bulb was faulty.

begriffe.erklaerung: The unit of electrical resistance.
Components lie one after the other, and the current flows through all of them in turn.
Components lie side by side, and the current splits up.
One divided by a number; for example, the reciprocal of 4 is a quarter.
A single resistor that has the same effect as a whole group.

gewusst: If you connect any number of resistors in parallel, the equivalent resistance keeps getting smaller, but never reaches zero.
Gustav Robert Kirchhoff set out the rules for current and voltage in branched circuits while he was still a student.
On small resistors, coloured bands show how many ohms they have.

teile.einleitung: Electricity is the general term for everything to do with electric charges, their forces and their movement. It shows itself in lightning, in the crackling of a jumper and in the current from a socket. Without electricity there would be no electric light, no computers and no SBB trains.
wichtigste: Electricity is based on electric charges, which can be positive or negative.
Like charges repel each other, unlike charges attract.
Voltage is measured in volts, current in amperes.
In a metal wire, electrons move when current flows.
Normal sockets in Switzerland have a mains voltage of 230 V.
Electrical power is calculated as voltage times current.
A large part of Swiss electricity comes from hydropower.

abschnitte.text: All substances are made of atoms with positively charged **protons** and negatively charged **electrons**. Two bodies with the same charge, for example two negative ones, **repel each other**. A positive and a negative body, on the other hand, attract each other. Charges at rest are studied in electrostatics; moving charges form electric current.

**Voltage** drives the current and is measured in **volts** (V). Current says how much charge flows per second; its unit is the **ampere** (A). Resistance in ohms shows how strongly a material slows down the current. Power in watts is calculated with P = U · I, that is voltage times current.

Normal sockets in Switzerland supply **alternating current** at 230 volts and 50 hertz. Switzerland has its own plugs, type J with three pins. A 2300-watt kettle draws a current of 10 A at 230 V. Consumption is measured by the **electricity meter** in kilowatt-hours, which you pay for.

Electricity is produced in **power stations** with generators that convert movement into electrical energy. In Switzerland about half to just under sixty per cent of electricity comes from **hydropower**, and another large part from nuclear power stations. Solar panels on roofs supply a fast-growing share. Through high-voltage lines the electricity reaches every house.

Even the ancient Greeks knew that rubbed **amber** attracts light things; the Greek word for amber is elektron. Around 1752 Benjamin Franklin showed that lightning is electrical. Around 1800 Alessandro Volta built the first battery. In the 19th century Faraday and Maxwell studied the connection between electricity and magnetism.

Electricity from a socket can be deadly, because it can flow through the body and the heart. That is why you never put your fingers into sockets and never use appliances with wet hands. **Fuses** and residual current circuit breakers switch off the current in case of danger. During a thunderstorm you take shelter in buildings or cars.

begriffe.erklaerung: A tiny, negatively charged particle in the shell of every atom.
The unit of electrical voltage.
The unit of power, that is how much energy is converted per second.
Current that constantly changes direction, 50 times per second in Switzerland.
The amount of energy that a 1000-watt appliance uses in one hour.

gewusst: The word electricity comes from the Greek word for amber.
The Swiss type J plug does not fit any socket in neighbouring countries, but many flat Europlugs do fit Swiss sockets.
Most trains in Switzerland run on electricity, with an overhead line voltage of 15,000 volts.

teile.einleitung: The Earth's magnetic field is an invisible magnetic field that surrounds the whole Earth. It lines up compass needles and protects us from dangerous particles from the Sun. That is why the Earth can be compared to a giant magnet.
wichtigste: The Earth's magnetic field is created in the outer core by currents of liquid metal.
It lines up compass needles roughly in a north-south direction.
The magnetic north pole is not exactly at the geographic North Pole and moves slowly.
In terms of physics, there is a magnetic south pole near the geographic North Pole.
The magnetic field protects the Earth from charged particles from the Sun.
The northern and southern lights form when such particles enter the atmosphere near the poles.
Migratory birds and other animals use the Earth's magnetic field to find their way.

abschnitte.text: The Earth behaves roughly as if there were a giant **bar magnet** inside it. That is why a compass needle always points roughly north. Because unlike poles attract, in terms of physics there is a magnetic south pole near the geographic North Pole. It is still usually called the “magnetic north pole” because it lies in the north. Near the poles the Earth's magnetic field is strongest.

Deep inside the Earth lies the **outer core**, made of liquid iron and nickel. This hot metal is constantly moving and flows in circles. Moving metal that conducts electricity creates electric currents, and these in turn create a magnetic field. This process is called the **geodynamo**. Without it the Earth would have no strong magnetic field, as is the case with Mars today.

The area around the Earth in which the magnetic field acts is called the **magnetosphere**. It deflects the **solar wind**, a stream of charged particles that the Sun hurls into space. Without this protection the particles would gradually strip away the atmosphere. During strong solar storms the magnetic field can be disturbed. Then satellites, radio links and even power grids can have problems.

Near the poles, particles from the Sun can enter the upper atmosphere along the magnetic field lines. There they make oxygen and nitrogen glow, creating green, red or violet **auroras**, the northern and southern lights. They are seen most often in the far north, for example in Norway, Iceland or Canada. During very strong solar storms they can exceptionally be seen in Switzerland too. This was the case, for example, in May 2024.

The magnetic north pole is not exactly at the North Pole on the map, but a little to the side, and it **wanders** slowly. In recent decades it has moved from Canada towards Siberia. If you stand directly above a magnetic pole, a freely moving compass needle points straight down. In the course of the Earth's history, the north and south poles have often swapped places. This **magnetic reversal** can be read from magnetic traces in old rock.

Many **migratory birds** find their way over thousands of kilometres with the help of the Earth's magnetic field. Sea turtles, salmon and some bees probably also use this inner compass. Exactly how the animals sense the magnetic field is still being researched. Humans cannot sense the Earth's magnetic field. We need a compass for that, which was probably first invented in China.

begriffe.erklaerung: The area around a magnet in which it exerts forces on other magnets.
The space around the Earth in which the Earth's magnetic field acts.
A stream of electrically charged particles that the Sun sends into space.
When the Earth's magnetic north and south poles swap places.
The process in the Earth's core that creates the Earth's magnetic field.

gewusst: The last magnetic reversal was about 780,000 years ago.
At the Earth's surface, the Earth's magnetic field is much weaker than a small fridge magnet.
Because the magnetic pole wanders, airports sometimes have to change the numbers of their runways, as these are named after compass directions.

teile.einleitung: Entropy is a quantity in physics that describes how many ways there are to arrange the particles of a system. In simple terms it is often said to measure “disorder”. Entropy explains why heat always flows from warm to cold and why many things in nature do not reverse by themselves.
wichtigste: The unit of entropy is joules per kelvin (J/K).
Rudolf Clausius introduced the term in 1865.
Ludwig Boltzmann explained entropy through the number of microstates; his formula S = k · log W is on his gravestone in Vienna.
In a closed system entropy can never decrease; this is what the second law of thermodynamics says.
When heat flows from warm to cold, the total entropy increases.
When two different gases mix, entropy rises.
When ice melts, entropy increases because the molecules gain more freedom of movement.

abschnitte.text: Imagine a children's bedroom: there are only a few ways for it to be tidy, but a great many ways for it to be untidy. It is similar with particles. A **macrostate** is what we see, such as the temperature and pressure of a gas. Every exact arrangement of all the particles is a **microstate**. The more microstates fit the same macrostate, the greater the entropy.

The German physicist **Rudolf Clausius** introduced the word entropy in 1865; it comes from the Greek word for transformation. He defined the change in entropy as the heat supplied divided by the temperature. The Austrian physicist **Ludwig Boltzmann** later linked entropy with the number of microstates W. His formula S = k · log W is engraved on his gravestone in Vienna's Central Cemetery.

If a system at 300 kelvin reversibly receives 600 joules of heat, its entropy rises by 600 divided by 300, that is by 2 J/K. When 1 kg of ice melts at 0 °C, it needs 334 kJ of heat, and the entropy rises by about 1.22 kJ/K. If 1000 J flow from a body at 400 K to one at 200 K, the warm one loses 2.5 J/K and the cold one gains 5 J/K. So the **total entropy** increases by 2.5 J/K.

The **second law of thermodynamics** says that in a closed system entropy never decreases. That is why heat always flows by itself from warm to cold. A drop of ink in water spreads out, but it never gathers together again by itself. Many researchers see this as the reason why time has a direction.

A hot cup of tea cools down until it reaches the temperature of the room. A sugar cube dissolves in tea, and gases mix by themselves. Fridges can create order inside, but they give off more heat at the back and so increase the entropy of their surroundings. In computer science there is also an **information entropy**, which Claude Shannon described in 1948.

begriffe.erklaerung: A measure of how many arrangements of particles fit the same state.
The exact position and movement of all the individual particles.
What can be measured from outside, such as temperature, pressure and volume.
A unit of temperature that starts at 0 at absolute zero.
The constant of nature k, which links entropy and microstates.

gewusst: Living things build up order in their bodies, but in doing so they increase the entropy of their surroundings, for example through the heat they give off.
If you double the volume of 1 mol of ideal gas at the same temperature, the entropy rises by about 5.76 J/K.
A perfectly pure crystal would have zero entropy at absolute zero; this is what the third law says.

teile.einleitung: Bicycle lights make sure that you can see when cycling in the dark and, above all, that you are seen. At the front a white lamp shines, at the back a red rear light. There are also reflectors, which throw back the light from car headlights.
wichtigste: On a bike a white light shines at the front and a red light at the back.
In Switzerland you must ride with lights at night and when visibility is poor.
In tunnels lights are compulsory even during the day.
Lights are important above all so that others can see you well.
The electricity comes from a dynamo, a battery or a rechargeable battery.
LED lamps are bright and use very little electricity.
Reflectors shine without electricity when light falls on them.

abschnitte.text: When it gets dark, drivers see a bike without lights only very late. That is why **bike lights** are mainly there so that you are seen. The lamp at the front also helps you spot holes and obstacles on the road. Dark clothing makes cyclists almost invisible at night, so light-coloured clothing helps too.

In Switzerland you must switch on your lights from dusk until daylight and when visibility is poor, for example in fog or heavy rain. In a **tunnel** this applies even in the middle of the day. A white light must shine at the front and a red one at the back. A bike must also have **reflectors**, red ones at the back. Anyone who rides without lights risks a fine and, above all, an accident.

In the past many bikes had a **dynamo** that turns against the tyre and produces electricity while you ride. Modern bikes often have a hub dynamo, which is built into the centre of the front wheel. Lamps without a dynamo get their electricity from a battery or a **rechargeable battery**. If a rechargeable light stops shining, you have to charge the battery, for example with a USB cable. On e-bikes the electricity often comes straight from the large main battery.

Today almost all bike lamps shine with **LEDs**, which are light-emitting diodes. They are very bright, use little electricity and hardly ever break. In the past there were small light bulbs that turned a lot of energy into heat instead of light. Many lamps today have a standlight that keeps shining for a few minutes when you stop at traffic lights.

**Reflectors** throw light back exactly to where it came from. So they light up brightly when a car shines its headlights on them. They are found at the back of the bike, on the pedals, in the spokes and on jackets or school bags. They work entirely without electricity, but they do not replace lights.

Before riding in the dark, check that everything at the front and back is shining. Point the front lamp slightly downwards so that it does not dazzle people coming towards you. With rechargeable lamps, take the charging cable with you in winter or charge them regularly. A high-visibility vest or reflective bands make you even easier to see.

begriffe.erklaerung: A small generator that turns the turning of the wheel into electricity.
A device that throws light back.
A light-emitting diode, a very economical and bright source of light.
A battery that can be charged again and again.

gewusst: A reflector can make a bike visible from more than a hundred metres away when a headlight hits it.
A hub dynamo runs almost silently, and you hardly feel when pedalling that it is producing electricity.
Without lights and wearing dark clothing, you are often seen only very late in the dark.

teile.einleitung: The acceleration due to gravity shows how strongly an object keeps getting faster when it falls freely on Earth. At the Earth's surface it is about 9.81 metres per second squared and is abbreviated with the letter g. It is the reason why an apple falls from the tree and why we feel weight.
wichtigste: The acceleration due to gravity at the Earth's surface is about 9.81 m/s².
It is represented by the letter g.
The international standard acceleration of gravity is 9.80665 m/s².
Without air resistance, a falling body gets about 35 km/h faster every second.
On the Moon the acceleration due to gravity is only about a sixth as large as on Earth.
With a simple pendulum you can measure the acceleration due to gravity in the classroom.
On the Jungfraujoch the acceleration due to gravity is slightly smaller than in Zurich.

abschnitte.titel: What is the acceleration due to gravity?
abschnitte.text: The Earth pulls all bodies towards it with its **gravity**. If you let go of something, it does not fall at a steady speed but keeps getting faster. The **acceleration due to gravity** g tells you by how much the speed increases each second. At 9.81 m/s², a body gets faster by 9.81 metres per second every second, which is about 35 km/h. After 2 seconds of free fall it is therefore moving at about 19.6 m/s.

Around 1600 the Italian scholar **Galileo Galilei** found out that all bodies fall equally fast without air. In everyday life a feather falls more slowly than a stone because **air resistance** slows it down. But in a vacuum a feather and a stone fall exactly the same. The astronaut David Scott showed this on the Moon in 1971 with a hammer and a feather. Both landed in the Moon dust at the same time.

The acceleration due to gravity is not exactly the same everywhere. At the poles it is about 9.83 m/s², at the equator only about 9.78 m/s². This is due to the flattening of the Earth and its rotation. At great heights g is also slightly smaller, because you are further from the centre of the Earth. That is why the acceleration due to gravity on the **Jungfraujoch** is slightly smaller than in Zurich. For calculations, the **standard acceleration of gravity** has been fixed internationally at 9.80665 m/s².

With a **simple pendulum** you can determine g in the classroom. You hang a weight on a thread and measure the time for one swing back and forth. The period depends only on the length of the thread and on g, not on the weight. A pendulum about one metre long needs about two seconds for a full swing. From the length and the time, g can be worked out with a formula.

On the **Moon** the acceleration due to gravity is only about 1.6 m/s², roughly a sixth of the Earth's value. That is why the astronauts there could make long jumps in their heavy suits. On Mars it is about 3.7 m/s², while on the giant planet Jupiter it is about 25 m/s². The more mass a body in space has and the smaller its radius, the greater its acceleration due to gravity.

begriffe.erklaerung: How quickly the speed of a body changes.
The force with which the Earth pulls all bodies towards it.
Falling in which only gravity acts, without air slowing things down.
The slowing force of the air on a moving body.
A weight on a thread that swings back and forth.

gewusst: Skydivers do not become infinitely fast, because from about 200 km/h the air resistance is as large as their weight.
Someone who weighs 60 kg on Earth would weigh only about as much as 10 kg on the Moon.
With very precise instruments called gravimeters, differences in g can be measured and used to detect cavities in the ground.

teile.einleitung: St Elmo's fire is a mysterious bluish glow on pointed objects that appears during thunderstorms. In the past, sailors saw it on the tips of their ships' masts and took it as a sign from their patron saint. Today we know that it is an electrical discharge and that nothing burns.
wichtigste: St Elmo's fire is a glow on points that appears during thunderstorms.
It usually glows bluish to violet.
Nothing burns; it is an electrical glow of the air.
It is named after St Erasmus, the patron saint of sailors.
In the past, sailors often saw it on the tips of ships' masts.
Mountaineers can see it on the tip of their ice axe during a thunderstorm.
Today St Elmo's fire is also seen on aeroplanes.

abschnitte.text: **St Elmo's fire** is a glowing electrical discharge on pointed objects. It looks like small bluish flames or tufts, but it is not hot. Experts call this kind of discharge a **corona discharge**. The glow can last a few minutes and is often accompanied by a soft crackling or hissing.

During thunderstorms a very strong **electric field** builds up between the clouds and the ground. On pointed objects the field is especially strong, because the field lines crowd together there. If it becomes strong enough, the air particles around the point are **ionised** and start to glow. The bluish to violet colour comes mainly from the nitrogen and oxygen in the air.

In the past, sailors often saw the glow on the tips of **ships' masts**. They interpreted it as a sign from St **Erasmus**, the patron saint of sailors, who is also called Sant'Elmo in Italy. That is where the name St Elmo's fire comes from. Some saw it as a good sign that the worst of the storm was over; others feared it as a warning.

St Elmo's fire can also be seen in the Alps, for example on summit crosses, aerials or on the tip of an **ice axe**. For mountaineers it is a serious warning sign. It shows that the electric field is very strong and that a **lightning strike** is likely. Anyone who feels their hair standing on end or hears a buzzing from metal parts should leave exposed ridges immediately.

Today St Elmo's fire is often seen by **pilots**. It appears on wing tips, on the nose of the aeroplane or as glowing sparks on the windscreen. It is usually harmless to the aeroplane. Special rods on the wings, called static dischargers, help to release electric charge in a controlled way.

begriffe.erklaerung: A glowing electrical discharge at points, without lightning forming.
When atoms or molecules lose electrons and so become electrically charged.
The area around charges in which electrical forces act.
A saint who, according to Christian belief, protects a particular group of people.

gewusst: Even ancient writers such as Pliny the Elder described the glow on ships' masts.
The seafarer Ferdinand Magellan and his crew reported St Elmo's fire on their voyage around the world.
St Elmo's fire can also be seen on church spires and tall trees.

teile.einleitung: A speed-time graph, or v-t graph for short, shows how fast something is moving at every moment. Time is plotted to the right, speed upwards. From the shape of the line you can read whether a body is moving at a steady speed, accelerating or braking.
wichtigste: In a v-t graph, time t is on the horizontal axis and speed v on the vertical axis.
A horizontal line means that the speed stays the same.
A rising straight line shows uniform acceleration.
A falling straight line means that the body is braking evenly.
The gradient of the line is the acceleration.
The area under the curve corresponds to the distance covered.
In free fall without air resistance, the graph is a straight line through the origin.

abschnitte.text: A **v-t graph** is a diagram that makes a movement visible. The v stands for speed (Latin velocitas) and the t for time (tempus). For every moment you plot how fast the body is going. This produces a line that is like a fingerprint of the movement.

A **horizontal line** means that the speed stays the same, for example with a train travelling at a constant 80 km/h. A rising straight line means that the body is getting faster evenly. A falling straight line shows even braking, for example when a bike stops at a red light. If the line lies on the time axis, the body is standing still.

How steep the line is reveals the **acceleration**. It is calculated as the change in speed divided by the time. If a straight line rises from 0 to 30 m/s in 3 seconds, the acceleration is 10 m/s². The steeper the line, the stronger the acceleration or braking.

The area between the line and the time axis corresponds to the **distance covered**. With a horizontal line this area is a rectangle, that is speed times time. If a straight line rises from 0 to 10 m/s in 5 seconds, the area is a triangle with an area of 5 s times 10 m/s divided by 2, that is 25 metres. In this way you can work out distances without measuring them.

In **free fall** without air, a body gets about 9.81 m/s faster every second, which gives a straight line through the origin. A skydiver, on the other hand, speeds up less and less because of air resistance. Their curve rises and approaches a maximum of roughly 200 km/h. The data from a tachograph in lorries can also be shown as a v-t graph.

Besides the v-t graph there is the **distance-time graph**, which shows where a body is. Its gradient is the speed. In an acceleration-time graph you can see when forces are acting. Physicists and engineers use these graphs to plan vehicles, roller coasters or rocket launches.

begriffe.erklaerung: How much distance a body covers in a certain time, for example in metres per second.
How quickly the speed changes.
How steeply a line in a graph rises or falls.
A fall in which only gravity acts and no air resistance slows it down.

gewusst: A negative speed is also possible in a v-t graph: then the body is moving backwards.
Even in the Middle Ages the area rule could be used to calculate how far a body that speeds up evenly would travel.
A car that accelerates from 0 to 100 km/h in 10 seconds covers just under 140 metres in doing so.

teile.einleitung: With the bicycle brake you bring a bike safely to a stop. Brake blocks or brake pads rub against part of the wheel and turn the movement into heat. There are different types of brake, such as rim brakes, disc brakes and coaster brakes.
wichtigste: On most bikes the brake levers are on the handlebars.
Braking produces heat through friction.
The rim brake presses brake blocks against the edge of the wheel.
The disc brake brakes on a metal disc in the centre of the wheel.
With a coaster brake you pedal backwards.
On a wet road the braking distance is longer.
It is safest to brake with both brakes at the same time.

abschnitte.text: A moving bike has kinetic energy. When braking, this energy is turned into heat by **friction**. That is why brakes get really hot on long descents in the mountains. The harder you pull the brake lever, the harder the pads press and the faster you slow down.

With a **rim brake**, two rubber brake blocks press from both sides against the rim, that is the edge of the wheel. Well-known designs are the V-brake and the side-pull brake on a racing bike. Rim brakes are light and cheap. But in wet and dirty conditions they brake less well, and the rim wears down over time.

With a **disc brake**, a metal disc sits on the hub in the centre of the wheel. A brake calliper presses pads from both sides against this disc. Disc brakes brake reliably and powerfully even in the rain. Many mountain bikes and e-bikes today have hydraulic disc brakes, in which a liquid carries the force from the lever to the brake.

With a **coaster brake** you brake by pedalling backwards. The brake is hidden in the hub of the back wheel. Many children's bikes and Dutch-style bikes have such a brake. You need no lever for it, but you cannot pedal backwards to bring the pedals into a good starting position.

The **braking distance** is the distance a bike still rolls after you start braking. On a wet road, on leaves or gravel it is much longer. Anyone riding twice as fast needs a braking distance about four times as long. The front brake does most of the work, which is why it is safest to brake with both brakes at the same time and with control.

In Switzerland a bike must have two brakes in good working order, one for the front wheel and one for the back wheel. Worn brake blocks or pads should be replaced in good time. Before every ride a quick brake test while standing still is worthwhile. On a cycling course you learn how to brake correctly and with control.

begriffe.erklaerung: A force that arises when two surfaces rub against each other and that slows down movement.
The outer edge of the wheel, on which the tyre sits.
The distance needed from the start of braking to standing still.
A technology in which a liquid passes on force.

gewusst: On long descents from mountain passes, brake discs can get so hot that you must not touch them.
Anyone who brakes very hard with only the front brake can go over the handlebars, because the weight shifts forwards when braking.
Track racing bikes have no brakes at all; riders brake with their legs.

teile.einleitung: A colour filter is a transparent piece of glass or film that lets through only light of a particular colour. It absorbs the other colours. This lets you colour light, make colours disappear or give photos and stages special moods.
wichtigste: A red colour filter lets only red light through from white light.
The colours that a filter does not let through, it absorbs.
Behind a red film, red writing on white paper disappears, because both look equally red.
A green leaf looks dark through a red filter.
If you hold a red filter and a green filter one behind the other, almost no light gets through.
Colourful church windows colour the sunlight.
Old traffic lights with a white light bulb got their red light from a red glass in front.

abschnitte.text: A **colour filter** is made of coloured glass, plastic or gelatine. When **white light** falls on it, it lets through only one particular colour. A red filter, for example, lets only red light through. The other colours are swallowed up in the filter; this is called **absorption**. The absorbed energy becomes a little heat.

Through a filter, objects often look completely different. A green leaf looks dark through a **red filter**, because it reflects no red light. A yellow banana also looks dark through a **blue film**. Red writing on white paper disappears behind a red film, because the writing and the paper then look equally red. This is also how puzzle books with secret writing work, which you can only read with a coloured film.

If you hold several filters one behind the other, each lets only its own part through. A red filter lets no green light through, and a green one no red light. That is why almost no light gets through a red and a green filter together. This principle is called **subtractive colour mixing**, because each filter takes colours away. When painting with watercolours, too, colours get darker in this way.

Even in the Middle Ages, **church windows** made of coloured glass coloured the sunlight and told stories in pictures. Famous in Switzerland are the windows by **Marc Chagall** in the Fraumünster in Zurich, from 1970. Traffic lights also worked with colour filters for a long time. Old traffic lights had a white light bulb with a red, yellow or green glass in front. Today's traffic lights mostly use coloured LEDs, which shine directly in the right colour.

In **photography**, colour filters are used to create moods or strengthen contrasts. In the theatre, filters in front of the spotlights colour the stage lighting. In every digital camera there is a fine pattern of red, green and blue filters in front of the image sensor. Only with this can the camera recognise colours. Screens and projectors also work with tiny colour filters.

begriffe.erklaerung: A transparent material that lets only certain colours of light through.
A substance swallowing up light.
Colour mixing in which colours are taken away and everything gets darker.
Light that contains all the colours of the rainbow.

gewusst: With black-and-white film, photographers often used a red filter to make the blue sky look dramatically dark and the clouds bright.
Red-cyan glasses for 3D pictures work with colour filters that show each eye only one part-image.
Around 1860, one of the first colour photos was made with three colour filters in red, green and blue.

teile.einleitung: The elementary charge is the smallest electric charge found on a free particle. A proton carries exactly one positive elementary charge and an electron exactly one negative one. It is a constant of nature and is abbreviated with the letter e.
wichtigste: The elementary charge e is about 1.602 · 10⁻¹⁹ coulombs.
Since 2019 its numerical value has been fixed exactly in the SI system of units.
Electrons carry the charge -e, protons and positrons the charge +e.
Every freely observed charge is a whole-number multiple of e.
About 6.24 · 10¹⁸ electrons together make a charge of 1 coulomb.
Quarks carry charges of one third, but never occur freely.
Robert Millikan determined the elementary charge at the beginning of the 20th century with the oil drop experiment.

abschnitte.text: The **elementary charge** is the basic portion of electric charge. In nature, charges do not come in any size you like, but only in whole-number multiples of e. That is why charge is said to be **quantised**. A calcium ion Ca²⁺, for example, has given up two electrons and carries the charge 2e, about 3.2 · 10⁻¹⁹ C.

The elementary charge is exactly 1.602176634 · 10⁻¹⁹ **coulombs**. Since the reform of the International System of Units in **2019**, this value has been fixed exactly. Since then the ampere has been defined using the elementary charge. Because e is so small, it takes about 6.24 quintillion electrons to make a single coulomb.

Between 1909 and 1913 the American physicist **Robert Millikan** made tiny oil droplets float between two charged plates. From the voltage needed to keep a droplet floating, he calculated its charge. All the charges were multiples of one smallest portion. For this **oil drop experiment** he received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1923.

Protons and neutrons are made of even smaller particles, the **quarks**. An up quark has the charge +2/3 e, a down quark -1/3 e. Yet free particles with charges of one third are never observed, because quarks only occur bound inside composite particles. Other elementary particles carry exactly one elementary charge: the **muon**, a heavy relative of the electron, has -e, and the positron, the antiparticle of the electron, has +e.

The charge of one mole of electrons is called the **Faraday constant**; it is about 96,500 coulombs. It is used to calculate how much substance is deposited during electrolysis, for example in copper plating or in producing aluminium. In batteries, too, ions with whole-number charges move about. In this way the elementary charge links physics and chemistry.

begriffe.erklaerung: The unit of electric charge.
An atom that has given up or taken in electrons and is therefore charged.
A tiny building block of protons and neutrons with a charge of one third.
The antiparticle of the electron, with a positive charge.
Only present in fixed, smallest portions, not divisible as finely as you like.

gewusst: When a current of 1 ampere flows, more than six quintillion electrons pass through the cable every second.
The charges of the proton and the electron are so exactly equal in size that measurements find no difference.
Murray Gell-Mann put forward the idea of quarks with charges of one third in 1964.

teile.einleitung: An electric circuit connects a power source, wires and devices in such a way that current can flow. The two most important types are the series circuit and the parallel circuit. Whether a string of fairy lights goes out completely or only one lamp is missing depends on the circuit.
wichtigste: Current only flows in a closed circuit.
Every circuit needs a power source, wires and a device that uses the current.
In a series circuit the current flows along only one path.
In a parallel circuit the current flows along several paths.
If one lamp breaks in a series circuit, all the others go out too.
In a house the sockets and lamps are connected in parallel.
Circuit diagrams show components with simple symbols.

abschnitte.text: For a lamp to light up, you need a closed **circuit**. The current flows from the source, for example a battery, through a wire to the lamp and back again. If the circuit is broken anywhere, no current flows. A **switch** opens or closes the circuit and so switches the light off or on.

In a **series circuit** the components are arranged one after the other, and the current flows along only one path. The same current flows through all the lamps, and the voltage is shared between them. If one lamp breaks, the circuit is broken and all the others go out too. Some Christmas fairy lights used to be built like this.

In a **parallel circuit** the components lie side by side, and the current flows along several paths. Each lamp gets the full voltage. If one fails, the others stay lit. That is why all the lamps and sockets in homes are connected in parallel.

Electricians draw circuits as a **circuit diagram**. It uses simple symbols: a circle with a cross for a lamp, two lines for a battery, a rectangle for a resistor. In this way even large circuits can be shown clearly. Computers contain billions of circuits on tiny chips.

A **short circuit** happens when current flows directly from one terminal to the other without passing through a device. The wires then get very hot and a fire can start. That is why fuses and residual current devices protect the circuits in a house. You must never experiment with mains electricity from a socket; for experiments you use batteries.

begriffe.erklaerung: A closed path along which current can flow.
Components one after the other; the current has only one path.
Components side by side; the current has several paths.
A dangerous direct connection between plus and minus without a device in between.

gewusst: In a torch with two batteries, the batteries are usually connected in series so that their voltages add up.
The first computer chip with an integrated circuit was built by Jack Kilby in 1958.

teile.einleitung: A gas turbine is a machine that produces a turning movement from burning gas or oil. It drives electricity generators in power stations and is found as the engine in almost every large aeroplane. The world's first gas turbine power station for generating electricity went into operation in Neuchâtel in 1939.
wichtigste: Air flows through a gas turbine in the order compressor, combustion chamber, turbine.
The gas turbine is based on the Joule cycle.
A large part of the turbine's power is needed to drive the compressor.
The exhaust gases are about 500 to 600 °C hot.
The world's first gas turbine power station went into operation in Neuchâtel in 1939.
Gas turbines can be started up within minutes and are therefore suitable as reserve power stations, for example in Birr in the canton of Aargau.
To increase efficiency, engineers try to raise the temperature at the turbine inlet.
Hydrogen is increasingly being tested as a more climate-friendly fuel.

abschnitte.text: A **gas turbine** is a heat engine that turns continuously. It sucks in air at the front, burns a fuel in it and lets the hot gases flow out at the back through a bladed wheel. This produces a powerful turning movement. Unlike a car engine, it does not work in separate strokes, but in a steady flow.

First the **compressor** squeezes the air that has been sucked in. In the **combustion chamber** natural gas, oil or another fuel is injected and burned, making the gases very hot. Then they flow through the **turbine** and set its blades turning. Through a shared shaft the turbine drives the compressor and also a generator. In physics this process is called the Joule cycle.

The hotter the gases are at the **turbine inlet**, the more work the turbine delivers. Modern plants reach well over 1000 °C there, which is why the blades need special metals and cooling. The exhaust gases leave the turbine at about 500 to 600 °C. In a **combined cycle power station** this heat is used to produce extra steam for a steam turbine, reaching an efficiency of about 60 per cent.

The firm **Brown, Boveri & Cie.** from Baden built the world's first gas turbine power station for generating electricity. It went into operation in **Neuchâtel** in 1939 and served as an emergency power plant for the town. This machine is now considered a technical monument and is today on display in Birr in the canton of Aargau. Birr is also home to a reserve power station with gas turbines that can step in within minutes in an electricity shortage.

The **jet engines** of aeroplanes are also gas turbines. In them the turbine drives only the compressor and a large fan, and the gases flowing out produce the thrust. Helicopters and some ships also use gas turbines. Gas turbines are light and small in relation to their power, which is why they are well suited to aviation.

Gas turbines mostly burn natural gas and give off **carbon dioxide** in doing so. That is why tests are being carried out to run them on hydrogen, which produces mainly water vapour when burned. Because gas turbines start quickly, they complement solar and wind energy when these are supplying little electricity. In Switzerland they are intended mainly as a reserve for emergencies.

begriffe.erklaerung: The part that squeezes the air that has been sucked in.
The space in which the fuel burns with the air.
A wheel with blades that is turned by flowing gas.
The share of the energy put in that is converted into usable energy.
A machine that converts turning movement into electric current.

gewusst: The world's first gas turbine for generating electricity came from Switzerland and ran in Neuchâtel.
A large part of a gas turbine's power is needed just to drive its own compressor.
The blades of modern gas turbines work at temperatures above the melting point of their metal, and for this they are cooled from the inside.

teile.einleitung: Field lines are imaginary lines that make invisible fields visible, such as the magnetic field of a magnet or the electric field of a charge. They show in which direction a force acts and how strong it is. If you sprinkle iron filings around a magnet, they line up exactly along such lines.
wichtigste: Field lines are a model for showing invisible force fields.
Outside a bar magnet, the magnetic field lines run from the north pole to the south pole.
Field lines never cross.
Where field lines are close together, the field is especially strong.
Around a straight wire carrying current, the field lines form concentric circles.
Magnetic field lines are always closed loops; electric ones are not.
The idea of field lines comes from the English physicist Michael Faraday.

abschnitte.text: A **field** is a space in which a force acts, for example on a piece of iron or an electric charge. You cannot see a field. **Field lines** are therefore imaginary lines that show the direction of the force at every place. A small compass placed in a magnetic field always lines up along a field line.

Field lines never cross, because the force can have only one direction at each place. Their density shows the strength of the field: if they are close together, the field is strong; if they are far apart, it is weak. If the lines run parallel and are equally dense, it is called a **uniform field**. Such a field exists, for example, roughly between the arms of a horseshoe magnet.

In a bar magnet the field lines come out at the **north pole** and run on the outside to the **south pole**. Inside the magnet they carry on back to the north pole, which is why magnetic field lines are always closed loops. This is because there are no single magnetic poles; every magnet always has a north and a south pole. The Earth also has a magnetic field, by which every compass lines itself up.

Electric field lines begin at positive charges and end at negative charges. So they are not closed, but have a beginning and an end. Around a single charge they run outwards like the rays of a star. Between two parallel charged plates, as in a **capacitor**, a uniform field is created.

abschnitte.titel: The field around a wire carrying current
abschnitte.text: Electric current also creates a magnetic field, as Hans Christian Ørsted discovered in 1820. Around a long, straight wire the field lines form **concentric circles**. You can find their direction with the **right-hand rule**: if your thumb points in the direction of the current, your curled fingers show the direction of the field lines. If you wind the wire into a coil, a field like that of a bar magnet is created.

In the 19th century the Englishman **Michael Faraday** introduced the idea of lines of force. He had not learned higher mathematics, so he pictured the fields in his mind. The Scot James Clerk Maxwell later turned this into exact equations. Today experts use field line diagrams, for example when building electric motors, loudspeakers and particle accelerators.

begriffe.erklaerung: The area around a magnet in which it exerts forces on iron or other magnets.
A field that is equally strong everywhere and has the same direction.
A memory aid using the right hand to find the direction of the magnetic field around a current.
Tiny pieces of iron that make field lines visible.

gewusst: The northern and southern lights form where the field lines of the Earth's magnetic field lead down to the ground near the poles.
In terms of physics, the Earth's geographic North Pole is a magnetic south pole, which is why the compass needle points there.
Field lines exist only in our imagination, yet you can calculate very precisely with them.

teile.einleitung: The electron is a tiny, negatively charged particle and one of the building blocks of all atoms. Without electrons there would be no electric current, no chemical compounds and no light from lamps. It was discovered in 1897 by the English physicist Joseph John Thomson.
wichtigste: Electrons are found in the shell around the atomic nucleus.
Joseph John Thomson discovered the electron in 1897 in experiments with cathode rays.
Robert Millikan measured the charge of an electron with his oil drop experiment.
The flow of many electrons through a metal wire is electric current.
The innermost shell of an atom can hold at most 2 electrons.
The electrons in the outermost shell are called valence electrons.
The electron microscope uses a beam of electrons instead of light.

abschnitte.text: The electron is an **elementary particle**; according to what we know today, it cannot be split any further. It carries the smallest negative charge, about 1.6 times 10 to the power of minus 19 coulombs. Its mass is tiny, about 1836 times smaller than that of a proton. The name comes from the Greek word for **amber**, because even in ancient times people charged amber electrically by rubbing it.

In the 19th century researchers studied glowing rays in glass tubes with the air removed, the **cathode rays**. In 1897 Joseph John Thomson showed that they consist of tiny, negatively charged particles. He received the Nobel Prize in Physics for this in 1906. A few years later Robert **Millikan** determined the exact charge of the electron using floating oil droplets.

Every atom consists of a nucleus and an **electron shell** full of electrons. In the shell model the innermost shell holds at most 2 electrons and the second at most 8. The electrons in the outermost shell are called **valence electrons**. They determine how an element forms chemical bonds with others.

In metals some electrons can move freely, which is why metals conduct so well. When many electrons flow through a wire, that is **electric current**. Old tube televisions created their picture with an electron beam that swept across the screen. In solar cells, too, light sets electrons in motion.

The **electron microscope** uses an electron beam instead of light and can therefore show much smaller things. In 1931 Ernst Ruska and Max Knoll built a first such device, and Ruska later received the Nobel Prize for it. Today it can be used to see viruses and even individual rows of atoms. In particle accelerators such as the one at CERN near Geneva, electrons and other particles are brought to almost the speed of light.

begriffe.erklaerung: The smallest building block of matter, which is not made of even smaller parts.
The area around the atomic nucleus where the electrons are found.
Electrons in the outermost shell, which are important for chemical bonds.
Rays of electrons in a tube with the air removed.

gewusst: The electron has a twin with a positive charge, the positron, which belongs to antimatter.
When you rub a balloon on your hair, electrons move from your hair onto the balloon.
An electron is so light that you would need about 10 to the power of 30 electrons to make one kilogram.

teile.einleitung: Energy density tells you how much energy is contained in a certain amount of a substance or store. It can be given per kilogram or per litre. It explains, for example, why a car can travel a long way with a small petrol tank, while an electric car needs a heavy battery.
wichtigste: Gravimetric energy density gives the energy per mass, usually in kWh per kilogram.
Volumetric energy density gives the energy per volume, usually in kWh per litre.
Among fuels, hydrogen has the most energy per kilogram.
Per volume, however, hydrogen has a low energy density, so it is strongly compressed in tanks.
Petrol contains about 8.8 kWh per litre, a lithium-ion battery only about 0.15 to 0.25 kWh per kilogram.
The stored energy is calculated as mass times energy density.

abschnitte.text: **Energy density** describes how much energy is stored in an amount of a substance. If it is related to mass, it is called **gravimetric energy density**, for example in kilowatt-hours per kilogram. If it is related to volume, it is called **volumetric energy density**, for example in kilowatt-hours per litre. For aeroplanes, weight matters most; for a car's fuel tank, space matters more.

You get the stored energy by multiplying the mass by the energy density. A **battery** of 500 kg with 0.2 kWh/kg therefore stores 100 kWh. The other way round, you divide the energy by the mass: a battery with 60 kWh and 400 kg has 0.15 kWh/kg. A tank with 40 litres of petrol at 8.8 kWh each contains 352 kWh of chemical energy. A house that needs 20,000 kWh of heat a year would, without losses, use about 5000 kg of wood at 4 kWh/kg.

At about 33 kWh per kilogram, **hydrogen** has the most energy per mass of all fuels. Petrol and diesel supply about 12 kWh per kilogram, dry wood about 4 kWh. But because hydrogen is a very light gas, only a little of it fits into a litre. That is why it is **compressed** to several hundred bar in vehicle tanks. Even then, a litre of hydrogen contains much less energy than a litre of petrol.

Lithium-ion batteries in mobile phones and electric cars store about 0.15 to 0.25 kWh per kilogram. That is roughly fifty times less than petrol. An electric car therefore needs a battery that weighs several hundred kilograms. On the other hand, an **electric motor** uses the energy much better than a petrol engine, which loses a large part as heat. Researchers all over the world are working on batteries with higher energy density.

Water pumped uphill also stores energy, namely as **potential energy**. But the energy density is very small: to store 1 kWh, you have to pump about 734 kg of water up 500 m. That is why a **pumped-storage power station** needs huge reservoirs. In Switzerland there are several such plants in the Alps, for example Nant de Drance in Valais. They store electricity when there is plenty and release it when it is needed.

begriffe.erklaerung: How much energy is contained in a kilogram or a litre of a substance.
A unit of energy, abbreviated kWh, for example on the electricity bill.
Related to mass, that is per kilogram.
Related to space, that is per litre.
To squeeze together so that more gas fits into a container.

gewusst: A bar of chocolate has about half as much energy per kilogram as petrol.
Hydrogen has almost three times as much energy per kilogram as petrol.
Because of the low energy density of batteries, large passenger aircraft still fly on kerosene today.

teile.einleitung: Balance, or equilibrium, means that all the forces acting on something cancel each other out. An object in balance stays still, whether it is standing, hanging or lying. We humans also have to keep our balance all the time, otherwise we would fall over.
wichtigste: In balance, all forces cancel each other out.
A beam balance is level when both sides are equally heavy.
A ruler stays on your finger if you support it exactly in the middle, at its centre of gravity.
A tower that is wide at the bottom and narrow at the top stands especially securely.
A roly-poly toy always stands up again because it is heavy at the bottom.
Tightrope walkers carry a long pole to keep their balance better.
Our organ of balance sits in the inner ear.

abschnitte.text: In a **beam balance** the beam is supported in the middle. If both sides are equally heavy, it is level and the balance is in **equilibrium**. If there are 3 identical cubes on the left and 2 on the right, you have to add 1 more cube on the right. If there are 2 kilograms on the left and 500 grams on the right, 1.5 kilograms are still missing on the right.

Every object has a **centre of gravity**, where you can imagine all its weight concentrated. A ruler has its centre of gravity exactly in the middle, which is why it balances there on your finger. An object falls over when its centre of gravity no longer lies above its **base**. That is why a tower of building blocks that is wide at the bottom and narrow at the top stands most securely.

A ball in a bowl always rolls back; this is **stable** equilibrium. A ball on a hill rolls away at the slightest push; this is **unstable** equilibrium. A ball on a flat table stays wherever it is put; this is called **neutral** equilibrium. A roly-poly toy is stable because its heavy base keeps the centre of gravity low.

A tightrope walker often carries a long **balancing pole**. The pole makes it harder for her to turn quickly, so that the performer has more time to correct small mistakes. Animals use such tricks too: the squirrel helps itself with its long, bushy tail when climbing. Cats also use their tails for balancing.

Our **organ of balance** sits in the inner ear. It consists of three fluid-filled **semicircular canals** and two small sacs. They tell the brain how we are turning and tilting our head. Together with the eyes and the muscles, the brain makes sure that we can stand and walk upright.

begriffe.erklaerung: The point at which an object can be balanced exactly.
The surface on which an object stands.
When an object returns by itself after a small push.
When an object falls over or rolls away at the slightest push.
Three curved, fluid-filled tubes in the inner ear.

gewusst: If you spin round quickly, the fluid in the semicircular canals keeps moving, which is why you feel dizzy afterwards.
If one apple weighs the same as 2 mandarins, then 3 apples weigh the same as 6 mandarins.
A bike falls over when standing still, but when moving it stays balanced almost by itself.

teile.einleitung: The garden hose is a flexible tube made of plastic or rubber that carries water from the tap into the garden. With it you water plants, fill the paddling pool or spray yourself down in summer. At the same time it is a small physics laboratory in which you can observe pressure, flow and recoil.
wichtigste: If you cover the opening with your thumb, the water squirts further.
If someone steps on the hose, less water comes out.
If the hose lies in the sun, the first water is warm.
A nozzle with many small holes produces a fine spray.
A loose hose thrashes about because the water flowing out pushes it back.
With a hose you can empty a pool if the outer end lies lower.
Before winter you should empty the hose so that ice does not damage it.

abschnitte.text: A garden hose is usually made of plastic such as PVC or of rubber. Good hoses have a **fabric layer** built in so that they withstand the water pressure and do not kink so easily. At the end they are attached with click-on connectors to the tap, spray gun or sprinkler. Long hoses are wound onto a **hose reel** on wheels.

A certain amount of water flows through a hose every second. If you make the opening smaller with your thumb, the water must flow out faster through the narrow point and squirts further. This is explained by the **continuity equation** in physics. A nozzle with many small holes, on the other hand, breaks the jet up into a fine spray. If someone steps on the hose, the inside is almost closed off, and less water comes out.

If you let go of a hose while the water is running strongly, it thrashes wildly back and forth. The water flowing out pushes the hose backwards; this is **recoil**. According to Newton's third law, every force has an equal opposite force. Rockets fly on the same principle.

With a hose full of water you can empty a paddling pool over the edge, as long as the outer end lies lower than the water in the pool. This trick is called a **siphon**. A hose full of water with both ends open always shows the same water level at both ends. Builders use this as a **water level** to mark the same height on two walls.

A dark hose lying in the sun heats up a lot, which is why the first water is warm or even hot. Be careful, you can scald yourself with it. In winter the water in the hose turns to ice and expands by about a tenth. This can burst the hose, which is why you empty it in autumn and store it somewhere frost-free.

begriffe.erklaerung: The force with which the water in the pipe pushes.
An opposite force that arises when something is pushed out backwards.
A tube with which you can drain liquid down over an edge.
A water-filled tube with which you find equal heights.
An attachment that shapes the jet of water.

gewusst: Water in a hose that has been lying in the sun can get so warm that bacteria grow better in it, which is why you let it run off first.
The ancient Egyptians already used the principle of the water level with water channels to build flat surfaces.
Fire hoses are flat and only become round with the water pressure.

teile.einleitung: Solidification is the name for the change of a substance from the liquid to the solid state. For water it is usually called freezing. Solidification happens when you make ice cubes, when bells are cast and also when glowing lava turns into rock.
wichtigste: The change from liquid to solid is called solidification.
Most substances shrink in volume when they solidify.
Water is an exception: when it freezes, its volume increases by about 9 per cent.
Freezing water in cracks in rock gradually breaks the rock apart.
When liquid lava solidifies, volcanic rock is formed.
In casting, liquid metal is poured into a mould and solidifies in it.
If water is cooled below 0 °C without freezing, this is called supercooling.

abschnitte.text: In **solidification** a substance changes from the liquid to the solid **state of matter**. Its particles move more slowly and often arrange themselves into a fixed lattice, a **crystal**. The reverse process is called melting. For pure substances, the solidification temperature is the same as the melting temperature. Water solidifies at 0 °C, iron only at about 1538 °C and mercury at about minus 39 °C.

When a substance solidifies, it gives off heat to its surroundings, the **heat of solidification**. Fruit growers use this during frost: they spray their blossoms with water. The freezing water gives off heat and keeps the blossom under the layer of ice at about 0 °C. In this way the blossoms survive even cold spring nights. This is called **frost protection irrigation**.

Most substances contract when they solidify, and their volume decreases. **Water** behaves differently: when it freezes, its volume increases by about 9 per cent. That is why ice floats on water and lakes freeze from the top down. A full glass bottle in the freezer can therefore burst. In the Alps, water gets into **cracks in the rock**, freezes and gradually breaks the rock apart; this is called frost weathering.

Rock can also form through solidification. When liquid **lava** from a volcano cools, it becomes volcanic rock such as basalt. If it cools very quickly, shiny, glass-like obsidian sometimes forms. Deep in the Earth, molten rock solidifies slowly; this is how **granite** forms, for example. In Switzerland granite is found, for example, in the Gotthard and Grimsel areas.

In **casting**, liquid metal is poured into a mould, where it solidifies. This is how bells, statues, engine parts and jewellery are made. Candles and chocolate are also cast and solidify in their moulds. Sometimes water can be cooled below 0 °C without freezing; this is called **supercooling**. If supercooled water then touches something solid, it freezes in a flash, as in dangerous freezing rain.

begriffe.erklaerung: The change of a substance from liquid to solid.
The state of a substance: solid, liquid or gas.
A solid substance whose particles are arranged regularly.
Rock breaking apart because of water freezing in cracks.
A liquid that is colder than its freezing point but has not yet frozen.

gewusst: Salt water only freezes below 0 °C, which is why salt is spread on the roads in winter.
Water droplets in clouds can stay liquid down to well below minus 30 °C.
Because ice expands, water pipes can burst in winter if they are not protected.

teile.einleitung: Electric current is the movement of electric charges, usually of tiny electrons in a wire. It makes lamps shine, motors turn and mobile phones work. Electricity is very useful, but it can also be dangerous.
wichtigste: Electric current is the directed movement of electric charges.
For a lamp to light up, the circuit must be closed.
The inside of a cable is usually made of copper.
Cables are covered in plastic because plastic does not conduct electricity.
A light switch opens and closes the circuit.
Lightning is a giant electric spark.
You must never put your fingers into a socket.

abschnitte.text: Current only flows when there is a **closed circuit**. It consists of a **power source** such as a battery, of wires and of a device such as a lamp. If the circuit is broken anywhere, no current flows and the lamp stays dark. A **switch** opens or closes the circuit, so you can turn the light on and off.

**Voltage** is what drives the current; it is measured in volts. A normal battery has 1.5 volts, a socket in Switzerland 230 volts. **Current strength** says how much current flows; it is measured in amperes. You can compare it with water: voltage is the pressure, current strength is the amount of water.

Inside a cable there is usually **copper**, because this metal conducts electricity very well. On the outside the cable is covered in **plastic**, because plastic does not conduct electricity and so protects us from an electric shock. Water and the human body also conduct electricity. That is why electrical appliances do not belong near a bath or washbasin.

The electricity from a socket is **life-threatening**, so you must never put your fingers or objects into it. In Swiss homes, **fuses** and residual current circuit breakers protect against fires and electric shocks. Damaged cables should no longer be used. You must always keep your distance from high-voltage lines and railway lines, including when flying a kite.

**Lightning** is a giant electric spark between clouds or between a cloud and the ground. It forms when large charges separate in thunderclouds. A **lightning conductor** on the roof leads the lightning safely into the ground and so protects the house. Our nerves also work with tiny electrical signals.

Around 1800 the Italian Alessandro Volta built the first **battery**, the voltaic pile. Around 1880 Thomas Edison improved the light bulb and built one of the first power grids. In Switzerland a large part of the electricity is produced in **hydroelectric power stations** in the Alps. Today almost every household uses electricity every day for light, cooking and appliances.

begriffe.erklaerung: A closed path along which current flows from the source to the device and back.
What drives the current, measured in volts.
A component that cuts off the current when too much flows.
A metal rod with a wire that leads lightning safely into the earth.
When the current flows straight back without passing through a device; this can get dangerously hot.

gewusst: A bird can sit on a power line because it only touches one wire and no current flows through it.
Your heart also beats thanks to small electrical signals.
Electric eels can produce shocks of several hundred volts.

teile.einleitung: The flute is one of the oldest musical instruments in the world. You blow air against an edge, which makes the air in the tube vibrate and produces a note. Many children in Switzerland learn the recorder at school.
wichtigste: The flute belongs to the wind instruments.
In a flute the air in the tube vibrates and produces the note.
If you cover more holes on the recorder, the note gets lower.
Recorders are made of wood or plastic; the soprano recorder is small and sounds high.
The concert flute is usually made of metal, but still counts as a woodwind instrument.
At the Basel carnival many people play the small, very high piccolo.
The oldest known flutes are made of bone and are over 35,000 years old.

abschnitte.text: A **flute** is a tube in which a column of air vibrates. Unlike with the trumpet, it is not the lips that vibrate; instead the stream of air is split at a sharp edge. The air swirls and makes the air in the tube vibrate; this is called an **edge tone**. Flutes exist all over the world in many forms, for example as pan pipes, concert flutes or recorders.

The pitch depends on the length of the vibrating **column of air**. A long column of air vibrates more slowly and sounds lower; a short one vibrates faster and sounds higher. If you cover all the holes, the air vibrates in the whole tube and the note is low. If you open a hole, the column of air becomes shorter and the note higher. If you blow harder, the note jumps to a higher range; this is called **overblowing**.

The **recorder** has a beak at the top with a built-in block that directs the air exactly onto the edge. That is why even beginners quickly manage to make a note. It comes in different sizes: the soprano recorder is small and high, while the alto, tenor and bass recorders are larger and lower. School recorders are often made of plastic; more valuable instruments are made of woods such as maple or pear.

You hold the **concert flute** sideways and blow across a hole in the side of the tube. It has keys with which you close the tone holes. Although today it is usually made of metal, it belongs to the woodwind instruments because it used to be made of wood. The **piccolo** is a small transverse flute and sounds an octave higher; it is the lead voice at the Basel carnival alongside the drums.

The oldest known flutes were found in caves in the Swabian Jura in southern Germany. They are carved from bird bones and mammoth ivory and are over 35,000 years old. This makes them among the oldest musical instruments of humankind. In the Middle Ages and the Baroque period the recorder was very popular; after that the louder concert flute pushed it out of the orchestra.

In many Swiss schools the recorder is the first instrument children learn. Music schools offer lessons for the recorder and the concert flute. Besides the Basel carnival, the piccolo is also important in drum and **fife groups**. In folk music flutes are played less often; there the Schwyzerörgeli accordion and the alphorn are better known.

begriffe.erklaerung: A musical instrument in which you produce a note by blowing.
The air inside a tube, which vibrates when you play.
The interval between two notes in which the higher one vibrates twice as fast.
A small transverse flute with a very high sound.

gewusst: The concert flute counts as a woodwind instrument, even when it is made of silver or even gold.
A bass recorder is so long that you often blow into it through a curved pipe.
More than 35,000 years ago people were already carving flutes from bones.

teile.einleitung: A deep geological repository is a store deep in the rock in which radioactive waste from nuclear power stations, medicine, industry and research is to be safely enclosed for a very long time. Switzerland is planning such a repository in Opalinus Clay, a few hundred metres underground. The planning is the responsibility of Nagra, the National Cooperative for the Disposal of Radioactive Waste.
wichtigste: A deep repository is meant to keep radioactive waste away from people and the environment for hundreds of thousands of years.
Switzerland wants to store its waste in Opalinus Clay.
The repository is to be built a few hundred metres underground.
Nagra is planning a combined repository for high-level and for low- and intermediate-level waste at the same site.
In 2022 Nagra proposed the Nördlich Lägern area in the canton of Zurich as the site.
Until it is built, spent fuel elements are kept at the interim storage facility in Würenlingen.
An optional referendum can be called against Parliament's decision on the general licence.

abschnitte.text: Radioactive waste gives off radiation for a very long time, which is dangerous for living things. **High-level waste** in particular, for example spent fuel elements from nuclear power stations, must be kept safely for hundreds of thousands of years. On the surface, wars, accidents or ice ages could endanger the store. Deep in stable rock, on the other hand, the waste is well protected, even without people having to watch over the repository.

**Opalinus Clay** is a dark, very dense clay rock that formed about 175 million years ago on the floor of a sea. Water can hardly flow through it. When it comes into contact with water, it swells, so that small cracks close up again. In addition, its clay particles hold on to many radioactive substances like a sponge.

In the **Mont Terri rock laboratory** near St-Ursanne in the canton of Jura, Opalinus Clay has been studied for many years. Researchers from many countries carry out experiments there in tunnels inside the mountain. Nagra's **Grimsel rock laboratory**, on the other hand, lies in the granite of the Bernese Alps. There they test, for example, how containers and seals behave in the rock.

abschnitte.titel: The search for a site in Switzerland
abschnitte.text: The search for a site took many years and ran in several stages according to a federal plan. In the end three areas in the cantons of Zurich, Aargau and Thurgau were left. In 2022 Nagra proposed the **Nördlich Lägern** area in the canton of Zurich, because the Opalinus Clay there is particularly suitable. A **combined repository** for all kinds of radioactive waste is planned at this one site.

The repository needs a **general licence**, which is decided first by the Federal Council and then by Parliament. The people can call an **optional referendum** against this decision, and then there would be a popular vote. Until the repository is built, spent fuel elements are kept at the **interim storage facility in Würenlingen** in the canton of Aargau. The deep repository is expected to go into operation only in a few decades' time.

begriffe.erklaerung: The National Cooperative for the Disposal of Radioactive Waste, which is planning the deep repository.
A very dense clay rock about 175 million years old.
Very strongly radioactive waste, mainly spent fuel elements.
A store for different kinds of radioactive waste at the same site.
The right of the people to have a vote on a decision of Parliament.

gewusst: Opalinus Clay gets its name from an ammonite, an extinct sea creature that is often found as a fossil in this rock.
A deep repository must stay safe even if glaciers of a new ice age move across the area in the future.
Hospitals and research facilities also produce radioactive waste, which is to be stored in the deep repository.

teile.einleitung: The law of conservation of energy is one of the most important laws of physics. It states that energy can be neither created nor destroyed, but only converted from one form into another. In a closed system the total energy therefore always stays the same.
wichtigste: Energy can be neither created nor destroyed, only converted.
In a closed system the total energy always stays the same.
When an apple falls from a tree, potential energy is converted into kinetic energy.
A perpetual motion machine that runs for ever without a supply of energy is impossible.
Julius Robert Mayer and Hermann von Helmholtz formulated the law in the 1840s.
