When energy seems to be lost, it has usually been converted into heat.
The law applies throughout physics, from atoms to stars.

abschnitte.text: The **law of conservation of energy** says that the sum of all the energies in a **closed system** always stays the same. So energy cannot come from nothing and cannot simply disappear. But it can change its form, for example from potential energy to kinetic energy or from electrical energy to heat. When we talk about producing energy in everyday life, we actually mean converting energy.

An apple hangs high up on the tree and has **potential energy**, that is energy due to its position. When it comes loose, it gets faster and faster, and its potential energy is converted into **kinetic energy**, that is energy of movement. Just before it hits the ground, almost all the potential energy has become kinetic energy. On impact it becomes deformation, sound and a little heat.

On a **swing**, potential energy at the highest point and kinetic energy at the lowest point keep taking turns. A **roller coaster** is first pulled up to the highest hill; after that it rolls only with the stored potential energy. That is why no later hill can be higher than the first. Through **friction** part of the energy becomes heat, which is why a swing slowly comes to rest without a push.

In 1842 the German doctor **Julius Robert Mayer** was one of the first to describe that heat and movement can be converted into each other. In the 1840s the Englishman James Prescott **Joule** measured exactly how much work gives how much heat. In 1847 Hermann von Helmholtz formulated the general law of the conservation of force, as energy was called at the time. Since then it has been considered a cornerstone of physics.

For centuries inventors have tried to build a **perpetual motion machine**, a machine that runs for ever and does work without being given energy. The law of conservation of energy shows that such a thing is impossible. Every real machine loses energy as heat through friction. That is why many patent offices do not even accept applications for a perpetual motion machine.

begriffe.erklaerung: An area from which no energy escapes and into which none enters.
Energy that a body has because of its position or height.
Energy that a body has because of its movement.
An imaginary machine that is supposed to run for ever without a supply of energy.

gewusst: The brakes of a bike get hot because the kinetic energy is converted into heat.
Julius Robert Mayer got the idea as a ship's doctor, when he noticed that the sailors' blood was brighter in the tropics.
The energy in sunlight also comes from a conversion, namely from nuclear fusion inside the Sun.

teile.einleitung: A liquid thermometer measures temperature with a liquid that rises or falls in a thin glass tube. When it gets warmer, the liquid expands; when it gets colder, it contracts. You read the temperature on a scale next to the tube.
wichtigste: When it gets warmer, the liquid expands and rises in the tube.
The very thin tube is called a capillary.
Many thermometers contain alcohol coloured red or blue.
Mercury thermometers are not suitable below about -39 °C, because mercury then freezes.
Because mercury is poisonous, such thermometers have largely been replaced.
A classic clinical thermometer has a narrowing that holds the highest value.
Around 1600 Galileo Galilei built a thermoscope, a forerunner of the thermometer.

abschnitte.text: A **liquid thermometer** consists of a small reservoir, the bulb, and a very thin glass tube, the **capillary**. Both are filled with a liquid and sealed airtight at the top. Next to the capillary there is a scale, usually in degrees Celsius. Such thermometers are found as outdoor thermometers, room thermometers or in the laboratory.

Almost all substances expand when they get warmer; this is called **thermal expansion**. The liquid in the bulb needs a little more space when warm and moves into the capillary. Because the tube is so thin, it rises clearly visibly even with a small expansion. When it gets colder, the liquid contracts and the thread falls.

In the past **mercury**, a liquid metal that rises very evenly, was often used. But it freezes at about -39 °C and is poisonous if a thermometer breaks. That is why mercury thermometers have largely been replaced; in Europe they have not been allowed to be sold to private individuals for years. Today coloured **alcohol** is often used, which only freezes at very low temperatures and is therefore also suitable for polar regions.

A classic **clinical thermometer** has a narrowing just above the bulb. As it cools, the thread breaks there, so the highest value stays until you shake the thermometer. A **maximum-minimum thermometer** shows with small markers the lowest and highest temperatures since it was last reset. Gardeners use it to see whether there was frost in the night. Today many clinical thermometers are being replaced by digital devices.

Around 1600 **Galileo Galilei** built a thermoscope that showed differences in temperature with air and water, but did not yet have a scale. At the beginning of the 18th century Daniel Gabriel Fahrenheit built precise mercury thermometers and developed his own scale. In 1742 the Swede Anders Celsius proposed a scale with 100 parts between the freezing and boiling points of water. The Celsius scale is used today in Switzerland and almost everywhere in the world.

begriffe.erklaerung: A very thin tube in which the liquid rises.
Substances need more space when they get warmer.
A poisonous metal that is liquid at room temperature.
A division with marks and numbers for reading off values.

gewusst: The thinner the capillary, the more precisely a thermometer can show small differences in temperature.
In the USA temperature is still measured mainly in degrees Fahrenheit; 100 °F is about 38 °C.
An alcohol thermometer can measure temperatures at which a mercury thermometer would long since have frozen.

teile.einleitung: The spring constant shows how stiff or soft a spring is. It says how much force you need to stretch or squeeze the spring by one metre. It is measured in newtons per metre, and it also decides how fast a spring oscillates.
wichtigste: The spring constant is given in the SI unit newtons per metre (N/m).
A large spring constant means that the spring is stiff and hard to stretch.
If you cut a coil spring into two equal halves, each half has twice the spring constant.
More turns, with the spring otherwise the same, make the spring constant smaller.
If you only double the wire diameter, the spring constant becomes 16 times greater.
If you quadruple the spring constant, the period of a spring pendulum is halved.

abschnitte.text: If you pull on a spring, it gets longer, and the force grows evenly with the extension. This law was discovered by the Englishman **Robert Hooke** in the 17th century; it is called **Hooke's law**. It is F = D · s, where F is the force and s is the extension. The number D is the **spring constant**, often also written as k. Its unit is newtons per metre, that is N/m.

A **large** spring constant means that the spring is stiff and can only be stretched with difficulty. A spring with 1000 N/m stretches by only one centimetre with a force of 10 newtons. A soft spring in a ballpoint pen has a small spring constant. The springs of a car or a railway carriage, on the other hand, are very stiff. If a spring is stretched too far, it is permanently deformed and the law no longer applies.

For a **coil spring** the spring constant depends on the material, the wire diameter, the diameter of the turns and the number of turns. More turns make the spring softer, so the spring constant becomes smaller. If you cut a spring into two halves of equal length, each half has twice the spring constant. The **wire diameter** has a very strong effect: if you double it, the spring constant becomes 16 times greater. This is because it appears in the formula to the fourth power.

If you hang a weight on a spring and give it a push, you get a **spring pendulum**. Its period is calculated with T = 2π · √(m/D). A pendulum with 0.5 kg and 50 N/m needs about 0.63 seconds for one oscillation. If a pendulum with 1 kg is to take exactly 1 second, the spring constant must be about 39.5 N/m. If you quadruple the spring constant, the **period** is halved.

Springs are found in mattresses, trampolines, clothes pegs and bike forks. In physics lessons, a **spring balance** is used to measure forces, because the extension corresponds to the force. In mechanical Swiss watches, the **balance wheel** swings back and forth with a hair-thin spiral spring and sets the beat. Its spring constant must be very precise so that the watch keeps the right time. Shock absorbers on cars and bikes also work with springs.

begriffe.erklaerung: A number that shows how stiff a spring is, in newtons per metre.
The rule that the force of a spring grows evenly with its extension.
The unit of force, abbreviated N.
A weight on a spring that oscillates up and down.
An oscillating little wheel with a spiral spring that sets the beat in mechanical watches.

gewusst: Robert Hooke first published his spring law as a letter puzzle so that nobody could steal his idea.
The balance wheel of a mechanical wristwatch often swings back and forth several times a second, day and night.
A rubber band also behaves roughly like a spring when stretched a little.

teile.einleitung: A spring rider is a piece of playground equipment on which children sit and rock back and forth. It often looks like a horse, a duck, a motorbike or another animal. Under the seat there is a large spring that makes the rocking possible.
wichtigste: Under a spring rider there is a large, coiled spiral spring made of steel.
If you push the spring rider forwards, the spring wants to return to its starting position.
A spring rider can rock in all directions: forwards, backwards and to the side.
With a light child, the same spring rider rocks back and forth faster than with a heavy one.
A heavier child bends the spring more.
After you get off, the spring rider keeps rocking for a moment because the spring is still oscillating.
There are handles to hold on to and often footrests.

abschnitte.text: A **spring rider** is a rocking toy for younger children. The seat is shaped like an animal or vehicle and is usually made of tough, coloured plastic or wood. It sits on a strong steel spring that is firmly anchored in the ground. On the sides there are **handles** for the hands and rests for the feet.

The spring under the spring rider is a **coil spring**, which looks like a winding spiral. If you push the animal to the side, the spring bends. In doing so it stores energy, rather like a drawn bow. When you let go, it gives the energy back and straightens the animal up. Because the spring is round, this works in all directions.

The back and forth of a spring rider is an **oscillation**. The animal swings past the middle and then comes back again. A heavy child bends the spring more and swings more slowly; a light child rocks faster. Through friction in the spring and through the air, the movement slowly loses energy, which is why the rocking soon stops after you get off.

Spring riders are among the safest pieces of playground equipment, because you sit only a little above the ground. Even so, there are rules, for example that the spring is built so that no fingers can get trapped. Around the equipment there is often soft **impact protection** such as sand, wood chips or rubber mats. In Switzerland, European safety standards apply to playground equipment.

Spring riders stand in many playgrounds in Switzerland, at schools, in parks and at restaurants. There are ones for one child and large rockers for several children. Small children practise their **balance** while rocking and train their muscles. At the same time they learn in a playful way how a spring works.

begriffe.erklaerung: A metal component that bends and then returns to its shape.
A regular movement back and forth around a middle position.
Soft ground under playground equipment that cushions falls.
The ability to move or change something.

gewusst: The steel spring of a spring rider is so strong that it can be bent every day for many years.
Spring riders come not only as horses, but also as snails, hens, fire engines or dragons.
An empty spring rider that you push once oscillates faster than one with a child on it.

teile.einleitung: A spark is a small particle of light that flashes up briefly, or a tiny electrical flash. There are glowing sparks, for example from a sparkler, and electric sparks, for example when touching a door handle. Sparks can be useful, for example in an engine, but also dangerous if they start a fire.
wichtigste: On 1 August burning sparklers give off lots of sparks.
An electric spark can be seen in the dark as a bright flash of light.
You often hear a soft crack at the same time.
When the charge between your finger and the door handle balances out, a small spark is produced.
The spark plug in a petrol engine produces sparks.
At a petrol station you must be careful with sparks, because petrol fumes can burn.
With flint and steel you can strike sparks for a fire.

abschnitte.text: Many sparks are tiny glowing particles of metal or wood. In a **sparkler**, like the ones lit in Switzerland on 1 August, fine metal powder burns and gives off shining sparks. When metal is ground, glowing shavings also fly off. In a campfire, sparks from burning wood rise with the hot air.

An electric spark is produced when a high **voltage** breaks through the air. The air is heated so strongly that it glows brightly and crackles. Dry air needs a voltage of about 3000 volts per millimetre of distance for a spark. **Lightning** in a thunderstorm is basically a giant spark.

If you walk across a carpet in rubber soles, your body becomes electrically charged; this is **static electricity**. If you then touch a metal door handle, the charge balances out with a small spark. Many gas cookers light the gas with an electric spark. In a petrol engine the **spark plug** makes a spark many times a second, which ignites the mixture of petrol and air.

Even in the Stone Age people struck sparks by rubbing a flint against a stone containing iron. Later, flint and steel were used, and the sparks lit dry tinder. Modern lighters produce the spark with a friction wheel or a small crystal that produces a voltage under pressure. This **piezo ignition** is also found in many gas barbecues.

Sparks can be dangerous when there are flammable fumes or dust in the air. That is why you should switch off the engine at a petrol station and not light a fire. In 1886 the German physicist Heinrich Hertz was the first to detect electromagnetic waves using sparks. The first radio transmitters worked with sparks; that is where the German word **Funk** for radio comes from, and in German a spark is called a Funke.

begriffe.erklaerung: A glowing particle that flashes up briefly, or a small electrical discharge.
Electrical pressure that drives charges, measured in volts.
Electric charge that builds up, for example through rubbing.
A component in an engine that ignites the fuel with a spark.
Material that catches fire easily, used for making fire.

gewusst: In winter you get a shock from the door handle more often, because the air in heated rooms is dry.
A small spark from the door handle can have several thousand volts, but it is harmless because the current is tiny.
In German, the word Funk for radio and walkie-talkie dates from the time of the first spark transmitters.

teile.einleitung: Felix Bloch was a Swiss physicist from Zurich who received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1952. He studied how electrons move in metals and how atomic nuclei behave in a magnetic field. His work is one of the foundations of magnetic resonance imaging, which doctors use today to look inside the body.
wichtigste: Felix Bloch was born in Zurich in 1905 and also died in Zurich, in 1983.
He studied at ETH Zurich and did his doctorate under Werner Heisenberg in Leipzig.
Bloch's theorem describes the wave function of electrons in a periodic crystal lattice.
The Bloch equations describe how the magnetisation of nuclear spins in a magnetic field changes over time.
Because the Nazis had seized power and because of his Jewish origins, he left Germany in 1933.
In 1952 he received the Nobel Prize in Physics together with Edward Purcell for nuclear magnetic resonance.
He was the first Director-General of the CERN research centre in Geneva.

abschnitte.text: **Felix Bloch** was born in Zurich on 23 October 1905. At first he wanted to become an engineer, but at ETH Zurich he switched to physics. There he attended lectures by famous researchers such as Erwin Schrödinger. Then he went to Leipzig to Werner Heisenberg, one of the founders of quantum mechanics, and wrote his doctoral thesis there in 1928.

In his doctoral thesis Bloch investigated why metals conduct electricity. He showed that electrons in a regular **crystal lattice** spread out like waves that adapt to the pattern of the lattice. This result is now called **Bloch's theorem** and is a foundation of solid-state physics. He also predicted that an electron in an ideal crystal under a constant electric field swings back and forth; these are the so-called Bloch oscillations.

abschnitte.titel: Escape and a new life in the USA
abschnitte.text: When the Nazis came to power in Germany in 1933, Bloch had to leave the country because of his Jewish origins. In 1934 he got a post at **Stanford University** in California. There he researched and taught for most of his life. In 1940, together with Luis Alvarez, he measured the magnetic moment of the neutron precisely.

abschnitte.titel: Nuclear magnetic resonance and the Nobel Prize
abschnitte.text: After the Second World War, Bloch developed a method for measuring the tiny magnetic fields of atomic nuclei: **nuclear magnetic resonance**. At the same time, Edward Purcell at Harvard also succeeded. Both received the Nobel Prize in Physics together for this in 1952. Bloch's equations describe how the magnetisation builds up again after a disturbance, for example with the time constant T1, the longitudinal relaxation time.

Nuclear magnetic resonance gave rise to **magnetic resonance imaging**, MRI for short. With it, hospitals make detailed images of the inside of the body without X-rays. Chemists also use the method to work out the structure of molecules. In quantum physics, a sphere used to show the states of a qubit is named after him: the Bloch sphere.

In 1954 Bloch became the first Director-General of **CERN** near Geneva, the European centre for particle physics. He led it for about a year and then returned to Stanford. In old age he again lived more often in Zurich, where he died in 1983. He is considered one of the most important physicists born in Switzerland.

begriffe.erklaerung: A famous award for outstanding achievements in science, literature and peace.
A property of atomic nuclei that makes them behave like tiny magnets.
A regular arrangement of atoms in a solid substance.
A hospital examination in which a strong magnet creates images of the inside of the body.

gewusst: Felix Bloch originally wanted to become an engineer and only came to physics at ETH.
He was the first head of CERN, which is today one of the largest research centres in the world.
Without his research there would be no MRI scanners, which are found today in almost every larger hospital.

teile.einleitung: A Geiger counter is a measuring device that detects radioactive radiation. For every particle it detects, it makes a short click. In this way the invisible radiation becomes audible.
wichtigste: A Geiger counter detects radioactive radiation.
It is named after the German physicist Hans Geiger.
In 1928 Hans Geiger and Walther Müller developed the Geiger-Müller tube.
Inside the tube there is a gas between two electrodes.
Every particle detected produces an electrical pulse and a click.
The number of pulses per unit of time is called the count rate.
Even without a radiation source the counter clicks now and then, because of natural background radiation.

abschnitte.text: Radioactive substances give off **radiation** that we can neither see, hear nor feel. A Geiger counter makes this radiation noticeable. It detects mainly beta and gamma radiation, and with a thin window alpha radiation too. It counts the particles, but does not say directly which substance they come from.

Inside the **Geiger-Müller tube** there is a gas between two **electrodes**, which have a high voltage across them. If a particle of radiation flies in, it knocks electrons out of the gas atoms. These are strongly accelerated and set off a whole avalanche of further electrons. As a result a current flows briefly, which is counted as a **pulse** and made audible as a click.

At the beginning of the 20th century the German physicist **Hans Geiger** worked in England with the famous researcher Ernest Rutherford. There, in 1908, he built a first counter for alpha particles. Together with his doctoral student **Walther Müller** he developed the Geiger-Müller tube in Kiel in 1928. This device was so simple and reliable that it is still used today.

The number of pulses per second or per minute is called the **count rate**. The stronger the radiation, the faster the clicks. If you move away from a radiation source, the count rate falls markedly. That is why distance is one of the best ways to protect yourself from radiation.

Even without an artificial radiation source, a Geiger counter clicks now and then. It is measuring the natural **background radiation**, which comes from rock, from the ground and from space. In Switzerland the radioactive gas **radon** from the ground contributes most to it. In the Alps and in an aeroplane the radiation from space is stronger than in the lowlands.

begriffe.erklaerung: The property of some atoms of decaying and giving off radiation in the process.
The gas-filled tube in the Geiger counter that detects the radiation.
The number of pulses measured per unit of time.
Natural radiation that is found everywhere in the environment.
A radioactive gas that can get into houses from the ground.

gewusst: A Geiger counter can detect individual particles, so it is incredibly sensitive.
The typical clicking of the Geiger counter is often used in films to signal danger.
Bananas also contain a little natural radioactivity, because a small share of the potassium in them is radioactive.

teile.einleitung: Fritz Zwicky was a Swiss astronomer who did research in the USA at the California Institute of Technology. He is considered one of the first to suspect the existence of mysterious dark matter. He also coined the term supernova together with Walter Baade and predicted neutron stars.
wichtigste: Fritz Zwicky was born in 1898 in Varna in Bulgaria and was a citizen of Mollis in the canton of Glarus.
He studied at ETH Zurich and from 1925 did research at Caltech in California.
In 1933 he concluded from the speeds of the galaxies in the Coma Cluster that there was invisible mass: dark matter.
To do so he used the virial theorem of mechanics.
With a Schmidt telescope on Mount Palomar he searched systematically for supernovae.
With colleagues he compiled a large catalogue of galaxies and galaxy clusters.
The Zwicky Transient Facility at the Palomar Observatory bears his name today.

abschnitte.text: **Fritz Zwicky** was born in 1898 in Varna in Bulgaria, where his father worked as a merchant. As a child he was sent to the family's home town of Glarus and went to school there. He studied physics at **ETH Zurich** and did his doctorate there. In 1925 he went to the California Institute of Technology, Caltech for short, in Pasadena, where he did research until the end of his life. He always kept his Swiss citizenship and died in 1974.

In 1933 Zwicky studied the **Coma Cluster**, a huge group of galaxies. He measured how fast the galaxies in it move and used the **virial theorem** to calculate how much mass is needed for the cluster to hold together. According to this theorem, for a bound system 2·K + U = 0, where K is the kinetic energy and U the potential energy. He found much more mass than the shining stars could explain. He called this invisible mass **dark matter**, a puzzle that still occupies researchers today.

Together with the German astronomer Walter Baade, Zwicky coined the term **supernova** in 1934 for enormous explosions of stars. The two suspected that an extremely dense **neutron star** is formed in the process. This idea was only confirmed decades later by the discovery of pulsars. With a wide-field Schmidt telescope on Mount Palomar, Zwicky searched systematically for supernovae and found more than a hundred of them.

In 1937 Zwicky predicted that galaxies could bend the light of objects lying behind them with their gravity and act like a lens. Such **gravitational lenses** were actually observed from 1979 onwards. If a light source lies exactly behind the lens, an Einstein ring forms. With colleagues at the Palomar Observatory, Zwicky also compiled an extensive catalogue of galaxies and galaxy clusters. Not all his ideas held up, for example the tired light hypothesis of 1929, which is now considered disproved.

During the Second World War Zwicky also worked on the development of jet and **rocket engines**. He also developed a way of thinking, **morphological analysis**, with which you systematically search for all the solutions to a problem. Zwicky was considered brilliant, but also quarrelsome, and he often clashed with colleagues.

Zwicky was buried in Mollis in the canton of Glarus. An asteroid and a crater on the far side of the Moon bear his name. The sky survey project **Zwicky Transient Facility** at the Palomar Observatory has been searching since 2018 for short-lived events in the sky such as supernovae. Today he is considered one of the most important Swiss astronomers.

begriffe.erklaerung: Invisible mass in the universe that can only be detected by its gravity.
An enormous explosion of a star at the end of its life.
The extremely dense remains of an exploded star.
A large group of galaxies held together by gravity.
A large mass that bends light like a lens.

gewusst: Zwicky suspected dark matter as early as 1933, but only decades later did most researchers take the idea seriously.
He discovered more than a hundred supernovae, more than almost anyone else at the time.
Although he spent almost his whole life in California, he remained a Swiss citizen.

teile.einleitung: A gas balloon is an aircraft whose envelope is filled with a gas lighter than air, usually hydrogen or helium. It rises like a cork in water, because the surrounding air pushes it upwards. People have been flying in gas balloons for over 240 years, and Switzerland plays a special part in their history.
wichtigste: Helium is lighter than air and, unlike hydrogen, does not burn.
In 1783 Jacques Charles launched the first balloon filled with hydrogen in Paris.
To rise higher, the crew drops sand as ballast.
To sink, gas is let out through a valve.
As it rises, the envelope expands because air pressure decreases with height.
Near the ground, one cubic metre of helium can carry about 1 kilogram.
Since 1906 there has been the Gordon Bennett Cup, the most famous race for gas balloons.

abschnitte.text: Every body in the air is pushed upwards by it with a **buoyant force**. This is as great as the weight of the air the body displaces; this is Archimedes' principle. Because the gas in the balloon is much lighter than the displaced air, force is left over to carry the envelope, the basket and the people. Near the ground one cubic metre of helium carries about 1 kilogram.

A gas balloon has no engine and cannot steer; it travels with the wind. To rise, the crew throws out **ballast**, usually fine sand from bags. To sink, they let a little gas escape through a **valve** at the top of the envelope. As it rises, the envelope expands because air pressure decreases with height.

**Hydrogen** is the lightest gas and carries the most, but it catches fire easily. **Helium** carries a little less, but it does not burn and is therefore safer. On the other hand, helium is rare and expensive. By the way, gas balloons are not the same as hot-air balloons, which simply use air heated with a burner.

In 1783 the Montgolfier brothers launched the first hot-air balloons in France. In the same year the physicist **Jacques Charles** launched the first balloon filled with hydrogen in Paris, and shortly afterwards he flew in one himself. Since 1906 balloonists have competed in the **Gordon Bennett Cup**: whoever travels furthest in their gas balloon wins. The flights often last several days.

In 1931 the Swiss physicist **Auguste Piccard** became the first person to rise into the stratosphere, over 15 km high, with a gas balloon and a closed capsule. His grandson **Bertrand Piccard** set off in 1999 with the Briton Brian Jones from Château-d'Oex in the canton of Vaud. In the balloon Breitling Orbiter 3 they were the first to fly around the Earth without landing. This balloon was a **Rozière**, which combines gas and hot air.

begriffe.erklaerung: The force with which air or water pushes a body upwards.
Weight, usually sand, that can be thrown out in order to rise.
An opening through which gas can be let out in a controlled way.
A balloon that combines gas and hot air.
The layer of air above a height of about 10 to 15 km.

gewusst: When the first hydrogen balloon landed in 1783, frightened farmers attacked the unknown balloon with pitchforks.
Bertrand Piccard and Brian Jones's flight around the world lasted almost three weeks.
Château-d'Oex holds an international balloon festival every winter.

teile.einleitung: Uniformly accelerated motion is movement in which the speed increases or decreases by the same amount every second. So the acceleration always stays the same. A falling stone or a train pulling away moves roughly like this.
wichtigste: In uniformly accelerated motion the acceleration is constant.
The speed increases by the same amount in equal times.
Starting from rest: speed equals acceleration times time.
The distance from rest is half the acceleration times the time squared.
In a speed-time graph the result is a sloping straight line.
In a distance-time graph, starting from rest, the result is a parabola.
Braking evenly is also uniformly accelerated motion, only with negative acceleration.

abschnitte.text: **Acceleration** shows how quickly the speed changes. It is measured in metres per second squared. An acceleration of 2.5 m/s² means that the speed grows by 2.5 metres per second every second. In **uniformly accelerated motion** this value stays the same the whole time.

If a body starts from rest, the speed is v equals a times t. A car that accelerates for 8 seconds at 2.5 m/s² therefore reaches 20 m/s. For the distance, s equals one half times a times t squared. A body that accelerates for 6 seconds at 3 m/s² covers 54 metres in this way.

If you plot the speed against time, you get a **sloping straight line**. The steeper it is, the greater the acceleration. If you plot the position against time, starting from rest you get a **parabola** that keeps getting steeper. The area under the straight line in the speed-time graph corresponds to the distance covered.

When **braking**, the speed decreases evenly. A car at 108 km/h, that is 30 m/s, braking at 5 m/s² needs 6 seconds to come to a stop. In doing so it covers a **braking distance** of 90 metres. Because the braking distance grows with the square of the speed, it is four times as long at twice the speed.

The most important case of uniformly accelerated motion is **free fall**. Without air resistance every body on Earth falls with about 9.81 m/s². Around 1600 the Italian scientist **Galileo Galilei** used balls on slopes to study how bodies accelerate. He realised that the distance fallen grows with the square of the time.

begriffe.erklaerung: How quickly the speed changes.
With uniform acceleration, the mean of the starting and final speeds.
A falling movement in which only gravity acts.
A curved line that arises, for example, in a distance-time graph.

gewusst: A skateboard that accelerates evenly from 4 m/s to 10 m/s has an average speed of 7 m/s during this phase.
A train that accelerates from 0 to 30 m/s in 60 seconds has an acceleration of only 0.5 m/s², which you hardly notice.
In a vacuum a feather and a hammer fall equally fast, as an astronaut showed on the Moon in 1971.

teile.einleitung: A spring pendulum is a body that hangs on a spring and oscillates up and down. Together with the simple pendulum, it is the most important example of an oscillation in physics. Its principle is found in cars, trampolines and even mechanical Swiss watches.
wichtigste: The period is calculated with T = 2π · √(m/D).
m is the mass of the body and D the spring constant, that is the stiffness of the spring.
If the mass becomes nine times as large, one oscillation takes three times as long.
On the Moon a spring pendulum oscillates exactly as fast as on Earth.
The period does not depend on how far you pull the spring.
If the pendulum hangs vertically, only the rest position shifts.
For an exact result, about a third of the spring's mass must be added to the mass of the pendulum.

abschnitte.text: A spring pendulum consists of a **coil spring** and a body attached to it. If you pull the body down and let go, the spring pulls it back. It shoots past the **rest position**, is slowed down again and turns round. Without friction it would keep oscillating for ever; in reality the oscillation slowly gets smaller.

The further you stretch a spring, the greater its force. The Englishman Robert Hooke described this in the 17th century: F = D · s. The **spring constant** D in newtons per metre says how stiff a spring is. Because the restoring force is exactly proportional to the displacement, a particularly even **harmonic oscillation** results.

T = 2π · √(m/D) applies. A mass of 0.2 kg on a spring with D = 80 N/m oscillates back and forth once in about 0.31 s. A heavy mass oscillates more slowly, a stiff spring faster. If you hang the body on two identical springs in parallel, the spring becomes twice as stiff and the period falls to about 71 per cent.

Unlike the simple pendulum, gravity makes no difference to the period. That is why a spring pendulum oscillates exactly as fast on the Moon as on Earth. The **amplitude** does not change anything either: if you pull it twice as far, the body simply moves faster. A body of 1 kg on a spring with D = 100 N/m reaches a top speed of 1 m/s with an amplitude of 10 cm.

In mechanical wristwatches a small **balance wheel** swings back and forth on a hair-thin spiral spring and sets the beat. This technique has been perfected especially in the Swiss watch industry in the Jura. Cars have springs and shock absorbers that quickly calm the up-and-down movement after a bump. When jumping on a trampoline and in a bungee jump, you also oscillate as if on a spring.

begriffe.erklaerung: A number that shows how stiff a spring is.
The point where the body comes to rest without oscillating.
The greatest displacement from the rest position.
A particularly even oscillation that follows a sine curve.
An oscillating little wheel with a spiral spring that sets the beat of a mechanical watch.

gewusst: The balance wheel of a mechanical wristwatch often swings several times a second, which adds up to hundreds of thousands of oscillations a day.
Astronauts on the space station measure their mass with a kind of spring pendulum, because normal scales do not work in weightlessness.
A spring pendulum in a train moving at a steady speed oscillates exactly as fast as in a room at rest.

teile.einleitung: Bicycle gears let you choose an easy or a hard gear when cycling, depending on the route. In an easy gear you can ride up a hill comfortably; in a hard gear you ride fast on the flat. Behind this is the principle of the gear ratio with toothed wheels.
wichtigste: Gears help you ride more easily or faster.
Going uphill you choose an easy gear.
A hard gear is suitable for riding fast on the flat.
The small toothed wheels on the back wheel are called sprockets.
With derailleur gears the chain is moved from one toothed wheel to another.
With hub gears the gears are hidden in the centre of the back wheel.
A bike with 2 chainrings at the front and 10 sprockets at the back has 20 gears.

abschnitte.text: Our legs work best when they pedal steadily and not too slowly. Uphill you need a lot of force; on the flat, on the other hand, you want to be fast. Gears adjust the ratio between pedalling and the turning of the wheel. This means that in hilly Switzerland you can ride up steep roads without getting off.

At the front by the pedals there are one to three **chainrings**, and at the back on the wheel several **sprockets**. If the chainring has 40 teeth and the sprocket 20, the back wheel turns twice for one turn of the pedals. That is a hard gear: you get far, but you need a lot of force. If you choose a large sprocket at the back, the gear becomes easy: you pedal more often but with less force, rather like the **law of the lever**.

With **derailleur gears**, a part at the back, the rear derailleur, pushes the chain from one sprocket to the next. At the front the front derailleur does this at the chainrings. So that the chain can jump, you have to keep pedalling while changing gear. The number of gears is the number of chainrings times the number of sprockets: 2 times 10 gives 20 gears.

With **hub gears**, the gears lie well protected in the centre of the back wheel, the hub. Inside there are small toothed wheels, called planetary gears. You can even change gear while standing still, for example in front of traffic lights. Hub gears are tough and not very sensitive to dirt, which is why they are often found on town bikes.

On most bikes the **gear lever** sits on the handlebars, as a twist grip or a small lever. Good riders change into an easy gear before a climb. Modern racing bikes often have electronic gears that work at the press of a button. Cars and motorbikes also have gears; there they are called a gearbox.

begriffe.erklaerung: A setting of the gears with a particular gear ratio.
A small toothed wheel on the back wheel.
A large toothed wheel at the front by the pedals.
How often the wheel turns for each turn of the pedals.
The centre part of the wheel, around which it turns.

gewusst: For a long time gears were banned in the Tour de France; riders had to turn the back wheel round to use a different sprocket.
Some hub gears have 14 gears inside a single hub.
Many gears overlap, so a bike with 20 gears has fewer than 20 really different ratios.

teile.einleitung: A Foucault pendulum is a very long pendulum that can be used to show that the Earth turns. The plane in which it swings slowly turns over the hours, although nobody pushes it. The Frenchman Léon Foucault demonstrated this experiment in Paris in 1851.
wichtigste: The Foucault pendulum proves that the Earth turns on its own axis.
The slow turning of the plane of swing is explained by the Coriolis force.
In the northern hemisphere the plane of swing turns clockwise, seen from above.
Exactly at the equator the plane of swing does not turn.
In Zurich the plane of swing needs about 32.5 hours for a full turn.
Foucault's famous pendulum in the Panthéon in Paris hung on a wire about 67 m long.
Modern pendulums in museums are often given electromagnetic pushes to make up for energy losses.

abschnitte.text: A **Foucault pendulum** consists of a heavy ball on a very long wire. The mounting is built so that the pendulum can swing freely in any direction. You set it swinging in one direction and watch it for hours. It then looks as if the direction in which it swings slowly turns.

In fact the pendulum keeps its **plane of swing**, but the floor beneath it turns away with the Earth. Someone standing on the Earth does not notice this and only sees the plane of swing shift. This effect is described with an apparent force, the **Coriolis force**. In the northern hemisphere the plane turns clockwise as seen from above; in the southern hemisphere it turns the other way.

How fast the plane turns depends on the **latitude**. At the poles it turns all the way round in about a day. Exactly at the equator it does not turn at all. In Zurich, at about 47.4 degrees north, one full turn takes about 32.5 hours. You calculate this by dividing the length of a day by the sine of the latitude.

The French physicist **Léon Foucault** first showed his experiment in 1851 in his cellar and then at the Paris Observatory. The demonstration in the **Panthéon** in Paris became famous, where a ball of about 28 kg hung on a wire about 67 m long. Such a long pendulum needs about 16 seconds for one swing there and back. The visitors watched in amazement as the ball gradually drew marks in the sand in a different place.

For a Foucault pendulum you use a long wire and a heavy bob. This means that air resistance and small disturbances make little difference, and the pendulum swings for a long time. Even so, it gradually loses energy through **air friction**. Modern pendulums in museums and universities therefore get a small electromagnetic push with every swing, which makes up for the losses.

Today Foucault pendulums hang in many museums, universities and planetariums all over the world. In Switzerland, too, you can see such pendulums at some universities and museums. Often small pegs stand in a circle around the pendulum, which it knocks over one after another. In this way the **Earth's rotation**, which we otherwise cannot feel, becomes directly visible.

begriffe.erklaerung: A weight on a thread or wire that swings back and forth.
The surface in which the pendulum moves back and forth.
An apparent force that acts on moving bodies on the turning Earth.
The turning of the Earth on its own axis in about a day.

gewusst: At the North Pole the plane of swing of a Foucault pendulum would turn all the way round in about a day.
Foucault's experiment was the first to show the Earth's rotation without looking at the sky.
The pendulum in the Panthéon hung on a wire about as long as a 20-storey building is tall.

teile.einleitung: Colour is what our eyes and our brain make of the light that comes to us from objects. An object has its colour because it reflects some parts of the light and absorbs others. Without light, therefore, there are no colours.
wichtigste: For us to see colours, there must be light.
A banana looks yellow because it mainly reflects yellow light.
White reflects almost all light, black absorbs almost all light.
Leaves are green in summer because chlorophyll reflects green light.
Light-coloured clothes are safer on a bike at night because they reflect more headlight.
Sunlight can destroy dyes over time, which is why curtains fade.
Glow-in-the-dark stars on the bedroom ceiling keep glowing for a while after the light is switched off.

abschnitte.text: White sunlight is really a mixture of many colours. **Isaac Newton** showed this around 1666 when he split light with a glass prism. This produces a colourful band from red through orange, yellow, green and blue to violet, the **spectrum**. You see the same thing in a rainbow, where drops of water split the light. Each colour corresponds to a different **wavelength** of light.

An object usually does not shine itself, but reflects light. A banana looks yellow because it mainly reflects **yellow light** and absorbs the other colours. Leaves are green because **chlorophyll** reflects green light and uses red and blue light for photosynthesis. White reflects almost all light, black absorbs almost all of it. That is why black clothes get warmer in the sun than white ones.

In the retina of our eyes there are visual cells called **cones**. There are three kinds, which react mainly to red, green or blue light. The brain compares their signals and creates all the colours we see from them. At dusk almost only the rods are working, and they cannot tell colours apart. That is why people say that at night all cats are grey.

If you mix coloured **light**, it gets brighter: red, green and blue together make white. This is how the screens of mobile phones and televisions work; it is called **additive colour mixing**. If you mix paints, on the other hand, each colour absorbs part of the light, and the mixture gets darker. Printers use the primary colours cyan, magenta and yellow for this. This is called **subtractive colour mixing**.

Light-coloured clothes are safer on a bike at night because they reflect more headlight. Reflectors and high-visibility vests make this effect even stronger. Colourful curtains at a sunny window fade over time because **sunlight** destroys the dyes. Glow-in-the-dark stars on the bedroom ceiling store light and give it off for a while after the light is switched off. This property is called **phosphorescence**.

begriffe.erklaerung: A coloured band into which white light can be split.
A property of light that decides which colour we see.
Visual cells in the eye with which we recognise colours.
Mixing coloured light, which becomes brighter together.
A substance glowing on after it has been lit up.

gewusst: Bees can see ultraviolet light, which is invisible to humans.
The colour magenta does not appear in the rainbow at all; the brain creates it from red and blue.
An object that looks blue in the shop can look quite different in the yellowish light of a street lamp.

teile.einleitung: A generator is a machine that uses magnetic fields to convert kinetic energy into electric current. Almost all the electricity in the world is produced by generators, from the small bike dynamo to the huge machine in a power station. It works like an electric motor, only the other way round.
wichtigste: A generator uses magnetic fields to convert kinetic energy into electric current.
It is based on electromagnetic induction, which Michael Faraday discovered in 1831.
A generator consists of a turning part, the rotor, and a fixed part, the stator.
It is driven by turbines, engines, wind or muscle power.
Most generators produce alternating current, at 50 hertz in the Swiss grid.
An electric motor and a generator are in principle the same machine.
In 1866 Werner von Siemens discovered the dynamo-electric principle.

abschnitte.text: A **generator** is an electrical machine that converts **mechanical energy** into electrical energy. The word comes from the Latin generare, which means to produce. It needs a drive to turn it, such as a water turbine, a steam turbine, a wind turbine or an engine. Without this drive it supplies no electricity.

Inside, the **rotor**, often an electromagnet, turns within the fixed **stator** with its coils of wire. The turning makes the magnetic field in the coils change constantly. According to the law of **induction**, this produces an electrical voltage. Because the direction of the field keeps reversing, **alternating current** is produced.

In 1831 Michael Faraday built a first simple generator, a copper disc turning between magnetic poles. In 1866 **Werner von Siemens** discovered the dynamo-electric principle, in which the generator supplies its own magnet with electricity. This made powerful generators possible, which were called **dynamos**. From about 1880 the first power stations supplying electricity to towns were built.

In **hydroelectric power stations**, such as those in the Swiss Alps, the water drives a turbine that is connected directly to the generator. In nuclear and coal power stations, **steam turbines** turn the generator. The largest generators produce over 1000 megawatts, enough for hundreds of thousands of households. They turn so that the grid in Europe oscillates at exactly **50 hertz**.

A **bicycle dynamo** is a small generator that supplies electricity for the bike lights. Emergency generators on building sites or in hospitals are driven by diesel engines. Wind-up torches and wind-up radios also have a generator. In electric cars and trains, the motor works as a generator when braking, charging the battery or feeding electricity back into the grid.

An **electric motor** turns electricity into movement; a generator does exactly the opposite. In principle it is the same machine with magnets and coils. **Pumped-storage power stations** make use of this reversibility: when there is surplus electricity, the same machine pumps water uphill, and later, as a generator, it produces electricity again. This is important for storing electricity from sun and wind.

begriffe.erklaerung: The turning part of a generator.
The fixed part of a generator, with the coils.
Producing a voltage through a changing magnetic field.
Current that keeps changing its direction.
A wheel with blades that is turned by water, steam or wind.

gewusst: Almost every light bulb and every mobile phone in the world ultimately gets its electricity from a turning generator.
Solar cells are one of the few ways of producing electricity without any generator at all.
The generators of large power stations must be cooled constantly, some of them even with hydrogen.

teile.einleitung: An electric circuit is a closed path through which current flows from a source to a device and back again. Only when the circuit is closed does a lamp light up or a motor run. Every electrical device, from a torch to a train, works with circuits.
wichtigste: A simple circuit consists of a source, wires, a device and often a switch.
The battery supplies the electrical energy; the lamp is a device that uses it.
If you open the switch, the circuit is broken and the lamp goes out.
The current must be able to flow through both terminals of the source.
Outside the source, the conventional direction of current runs from the positive to the negative terminal.
In a short circuit a very large current flows, and cables can become very hot.
Water conducts electricity, so a hairdryer near the bath is life-threatening.

abschnitte.text: The **source**, for example a battery or socket, supplies the electrical energy. Metal wires, usually made of copper, connect all the parts. The **device**, such as a lamp or a motor, converts the electrical energy into light, heat or movement. With a **switch** you can open and close the circuit.

Current only flows if the path from one terminal of the source through the device to the other terminal is unbroken. If you connect both wires of a lamp only to the positive terminal, it stays dark. If you open the switch, the circuit is broken and the lamp goes out. The **conventional direction of current** points from the positive to the negative terminal outside the source; the electrons actually flow the other way.

In a **series circuit** lamps are connected one after the other, and the current flows through all of them in turn. If one breaks, the whole circuit is broken. In a **parallel circuit** each lamp has its own path to the source. This is how the sockets in a house are connected, so that each appliance works on its own.

Metals such as copper and aluminium are good **conductors**. Salt water conducts electricity much better than pure water, because dissolved particles in it carry charge. Plastic, rubber, glass and dry wood hardly conduct at all; they are called **insulators**. That is why cables are covered in plastic on the outside, so that nobody gets an electric shock and no short circuit occurs.

In Switzerland, sockets supply a voltage of 230 volts, which is dangerous for people. If two wires touch directly, a **short circuit** occurs with a very large current, and the cable can glow and start a fire. A fuse then breaks the circuit. A residual current circuit breaker switches off immediately if current flows through a person. Electrical appliances never belong near water.

begriffe.erklaerung: A part that supplies electrical energy, for example a battery.
An appliance that converts electrical energy into another form of energy.
A direct connection of the terminals without a device, in which a dangerously large current flows.
A substance that hardly conducts electric current at all.

gewusst: The direction of current from plus to minus was decided before electrons were known.
Birds can sit on a high-voltage line because they do not close the circuit to the ground.
Humans themselves are conductors of electricity, because the body contains a lot of salty water.

teile.einleitung: A light bulb, or incandescent lamp, is a lamp that turns electric current into light by making a thin wire glow. For over a hundred years it lit up homes all over the world. Today it has been replaced almost everywhere by more economical LED lamps.
wichtigste: The light bulb turns electric current into light.
Inside, a very thin wire made of tungsten glows.
The filament gets hotter than 2000 degrees.
The glass bulb is airless or filled with a protective gas so that the wire does not burn up.
Only about 5 per cent of the energy becomes light; the rest becomes heat.
Around 1880 Thomas Edison and Joseph Swan made the light bulb suitable for everyday use.
In Switzerland and the EU traditional light bulbs were taken off the market step by step from 2009.

abschnitte.text: The light bulb consists of a **glass bulb**, a threaded base and a fine wire inside. If you screw it into a holder and switch on the current, the wire starts to shine brightly. Because it is often pear-shaped, in German it is called a Glühbirne, a glowing pear. It comes in many shapes, for example as a candle bulb or a small bulb for torches.

The current flows through a very thin, coiled wire, the **filament**. This wire has a high resistance and therefore gets extremely hot, about 2500 degrees Celsius. Every very hot body gives off light, just like glowing iron at a blacksmith's. So that the filament does not melt, it is made of **tungsten**, the metal with the highest melting point of about 3400 degrees.

abschnitte.titel: Why no oxygen may get in
abschnitte.text: In air the hot wire would immediately react with the oxygen and burn through. That is why the glass bulb is either pumped empty of air or filled with a **protective gas** such as argon. Even so, the wire slowly evaporates over time. At some point it becomes so thin in one place that it breaks, and the bulb has blown.

As early as the 19th century many inventors experimented with glowing wires. The Briton Joseph Swan and the American Thomas Alva Edison developed light bulbs with carbon filaments that lasted long enough around 1879 and 1880. Edison also built power stations and cables so that the bulbs got electricity. From about 1910 tungsten filaments won out, which were brighter and lasted longer.

A light bulb is a poor source of light: about 95 per cent of the energy becomes heat. You notice this if you touch a light bulb that is on, which you should not do because of the risk of burns. That is why traditional light bulbs were banned step by step in Switzerland and the EU from 2009. Today **LED** lamps are mostly used, which need about a fifth to a tenth of the electricity for the same brightness.

begriffe.erklaerung: A thin wire in the lamp that gets hot from the current and shines.
A metal that only melts at very high temperatures.
A gas such as argon that does not react with the hot wire.
A light-emitting diode, a modern and economical source of light.

gewusst: In a fire station in Livermore in California, a light bulb has been burning almost without a break since 1901.
The light bulb is so well known that in comics a little bulb is a sign of a good idea.
Special bulbs are still used in ovens today, because they can withstand the great heat.

teile.einleitung: An optical fibre is a wafer-thin thread of very pure glass through which light is guided. Optical fibres transmit data as pulses of light and are therefore the backbone of fast internet. A typical optical fibre for data lines is about as thick as a hair.
wichtigste: An optical fibre carries light over long distances.
It consists of a core and a cladding made of glass.
Total internal reflection keeps the light trapped in the core.
In optical fibres, data are transmitted as pulses of light.
Fibre-optic cables are used today mainly for fast internet.
Electrical appliances hardly disturb the transmission, because light is not affected by electromagnetic interference.
In 2009 Charles Kao received the Nobel Prize in Physics for his work on guiding light in optical fibres.

abschnitte.titel: How an optical fibre is built
abschnitte.text: An optical fibre consists of two main layers: the **core** in the middle and the **cladding** around it. Both are made of very pure quartz glass, but the core bends light slightly more strongly. On the outside a layer of plastic protects the delicate fibre. A fibre for data lines, including the cladding, is about a tenth of a millimetre thick, roughly as thick as a hair.

When light hits the boundary between core and cladding at a very shallow angle, it is reflected back completely. This effect is called **total internal reflection**. In this way the light is trapped in the core and travels through the fibre in a zigzag or straight line, even round gentle bends. In a similar way, light stays trapped in a jet of water, which you can see in illuminated fountains.

Data are transmitted as **pulses of light**: light on and off stands for ones and zeros. A laser can send many billions of such pulses per second. All the continents are connected to each other by **undersea cables** made of optical fibres. In Switzerland, too, more and more houses are being connected directly to the **fibre-optic network**.

Bundles of many optical fibres can also carry images. In an **endoscope** they bring light into the body and the image back to the camera. In this way doctors can look into the stomach or joints without cutting the body wide open. Optical fibres are also used in lamps, sensors and measuring devices.

It was already known in the 19th century that light can be guided in glass or water. But early glass swallowed up too much light for long distances. In 1966 the physicist **Charles Kao** showed that very pure glass could carry light over long distances. For this he received the **Nobel Prize** in Physics in 2009, and from the 1970s such fibres were actually produced.

begriffe.erklaerung: The complete reflection of light at the boundary between two substances.
The inner part of the optical fibre, in which the light travels.
A thin device with which you can look inside the body.
A cable on the sea floor that connects continents.

gewusst: In an optical fibre light is about a third slower than in empty space, but it still travels at about 200,000 kilometres per second.
The glass for data lines is so clear that you could still see through a window of it a kilometre thick.
Optical fibres are drawn from a thick glass rod, which is heated and then pulled out into a thin thread kilometres long.

teile.einleitung: A thunderstorm is a weather event with lightning and thunder, often accompanied by heavy rain, hail and gusts of wind. It forms in huge, towering clouds. In Switzerland thunderstorms happen mainly on hot summer days.
wichtigste: Thunderstorms form in tall storm clouds, the cumulonimbus clouds.
Lightning is a giant electrical discharge between a cloud and the ground or within the clouds.
Thunder is produced because the air in the lightning channel suddenly becomes very hot and expands.
You see the lightning first and hear the thunder later, because light is much faster than sound.
From the time between lightning and thunder you can estimate how far away the storm is.
During a thunderstorm, open areas, mountain tops, water and single trees are dangerous.
In a car or a building you are well protected from lightning.

abschnitte.text: Thunderstorms need warm, moist air that rises quickly. As the air rises, it cools, the water vapour forms clouds and a mighty **cumulonimbus** cloud is created. It can grow more than ten kilometres high and often looks like an anvil at the top. Inside the cloud, water droplets, ice crystals and soft hail swirl wildly about.

As the ice and water particles collide, parts of the cloud become electrically charged. When the voltage is great enough, it is released in a flash of **lightning**. A lightning flash lasts only fractions of a second, but it is extremely powerful. In the lightning channel the air becomes about 30,000 degrees hot for a moment, hotter than the surface of the Sun.

The suddenly heated air expands explosively. This produces a pressure wave, which we hear as **thunder**. Because light reaches us almost instantly, but sound travels only about 340 metres per second, we hear the thunder later. If you count the seconds between lightning and thunder and divide by three, you get roughly the distance in kilometres.

Thunderstorms often bring heavy rain, which can make streams swell in a short time. In the strong updraughts, ice grains can be carried upwards again and again and grow into **hail**. Hailstones can become as large as table tennis balls or even larger and damage cars, roofs and fields. On top of that come strong gusts of wind that break off branches.

In Switzerland there are thunderstorms mainly from May to September, often in the afternoon or evening after a hot day. Lightning is especially frequent in Ticino and along the northern edge of the Alps. MeteoSwiss issues severe weather warnings that you can see in its app. For hikes in the mountains it is important to read the weather forecast and to set off early in the day.

In a thunderstorm it is best to go into a building or a car, because their outer shell leads the current around the outside. Outdoors you should avoid summits, ridges, open fields, water and single tall trees. If there is no shelter you can reach, crouch down in a hollow with your feet together. Houses are protected by a **lightning conductor**, which leads the current safely into the ground.

begriffe.erklaerung: A very tall, dark storm cloud, often with a flat anvil at the top.
A large electrical discharge in the air.
The bang and rumble produced by the hot, expanding air of a lightning flash.
A metal rod with a wire that leads the lightning current safely into the earth.

gewusst: Across the whole Earth there are about 40 to 50 lightning flashes every second.
The saying “Lightning never strikes twice in the same place” is not true: tall towers are even struck often.
Thunder can usually only be heard up to about 20 kilometres away, but at night you can see lightning much further.

teile.einleitung: Frost means that the temperature falls below 0 °C and water freezes into ice. In Switzerland there is frost mainly in winter, but in the mountains also in summer. Frost creates ice flowers and hoar frost, but it can also damage plants, roads and pipes.
wichtigste: There is frost when the air temperature drops below 0 °C.
Frost is most likely on clear nights without clouds.
Ice flowers form on cold window panes.
Ice needs more space than water, which is why a full glass bottle can burst in the frost.
Salt or grit is spread on icy pavements, and roads on bridges often become slippery first.
After the Ice Saints in mid-May, little frost is expected.
Ground in the Alps that stays frozen all year round is called permafrost.

abschnitte.text: We speak of **frost** when the temperature falls below the freezing point of 0 °C. A distinction is made between air frost, measured at a height of about 2 m, and **ground frost** directly on the ground. Ground frost often occurs even when the air above is still a little warmer. In Switzerland there are many days of frost each year on the Central Plateau, and considerably more in the Alps.

Frost forms especially on **clear nights**. Without clouds the ground gives off its heat as radiation into space and cools down a lot. Clouds, on the other hand, act like a blanket and hold the heat in. Cold air is heavier than warm air and collects in hollows and valleys, which is why it is often coldest there. On **bridges** the road becomes slippery first, because they also cool from below.

When water vapour from the air turns directly into ice, fine ice crystals form. On grass and car roofs this is called **frost**, and on branches in fog and cold the jagged **hoar frost** forms. On cold window panes **ice flowers** grow with branching patterns. Today they are seen less often, because modern windows insulate well.

Water expands by about a tenth when it freezes, because ice needs more space than water. That is why a full glass bottle can burst in the frost. If water gets into cracks in rock and freezes, it can break the rock apart; this is called **frost weathering**. Outdoor water pipes must also be emptied or protected in winter, otherwise they can burst.

Many plants cannot stand frost, especially young blossoms in spring. That is why gardeners often wait until after the **Ice Saints** in mid-May before putting sensitive plants such as tomatoes outdoors. When there is a risk of frost, plants are covered with fleece. Fruit growers sometimes even spray their trees with water, because heat is released when it freezes and the layer of ice protects the blossoms.

High up in the Alps there is ground that stays frozen all year round: **permafrost**. In Switzerland it is usually found above about 2500 m and covers about 5 per cent of the country's area. Permafrost holds rocks and debris together like putty. Because of global warming it is thawing in some places, which can make rockfalls and debris flows more likely.

begriffe.erklaerung: The temperature of 0 °C at which water turns into ice.
Jagged ice crystals on branches and grass in fog and cold.
Ground that stays permanently frozen.
Rock is broken apart because freezing water expands.

gewusst: When it freezes, water gives off heat, which is why fruit growers protect blossoms with a layer of ice.
Because ice is lighter than water, lakes freeze from the top and fish can survive underneath.
The village of La Brévine in the Neuchâtel Jura is known for its especially cold frosty nights.

teile.einleitung: In uniform motion a body always moves at the same speed. If it is also in a straight line, the direction does not change either. It is the simplest of all movements and the starting point of the whole of mechanics.
wichtigste: Uniform motion in a straight line has a steady speed in the same direction.
For the distance, the formula s = v · t applies.
If you double the time, the distance also doubles.
In a speed-time graph it is a horizontal line.
According to Newton's first law, the forces on such a body cancel each other out.
A moving escalator comes very close to uniform motion.

abschnitte.text: Uniform means that a body always covers distances of the same length in equal periods of time. So its **speed** stays constant. If it moves along a straight line, it is called **uniform motion in a straight line**. Movement in a circle at a steady speed is called uniform circular motion, but in that case the direction keeps changing.

For the distance, s = v · t applies, that is distance equals speed times time. A toy car at 3 m/s gets 21 metres in 7 seconds. A passenger boat on Lake Zurich at 24 km/h travels 18 kilometres in 45 minutes. A snail at 1.5 mm/s needs exactly 60 seconds for 9 centimetres.

In a **distance-time graph**, uniform motion is a sloping straight line. The steeper it is, the faster the body is. In a speed-time graph it is a horizontal line, because the speed does not change. Distance and time are **proportional**: twice the time means twice the distance.

In 1687 Isaac Newton described in his first law of motion, the **law of inertia**, that a body without a force acting on it stays in uniform motion. Galileo Galilei had already studied this idea with balls on slopes. On Earth, however, friction and air resistance slow down almost every movement. A car only travels at a steady speed when the engine exactly balances these braking forces and all the forces cancel each other out.

An **escalator** or a conveyor belt in operation moves almost uniformly. A train on a straight stretch at a set speed, or a ski lift, also comes close. An aeroplane at cruising altitude flies straight ahead at almost the same speed for a long time. In reality, though, there are always small fluctuations, which is why uniform motion is an ideal case.

begriffe.erklaerung: Distance divided by time, for example in metres per second or kilometres per hour.
Two quantities grow in the same ratio: twice as much of one gives twice as much of the other.
The property of a body of keeping its state of motion.
A graph that shows how far a body has moved at each moment.

gewusst: In empty space a space probe without a drive keeps flying almost perfectly uniformly.
Inside a train moving at a steady speed, you cannot tell that you are moving without looking outside.
The space probe Voyager 1 has been moving further away from the Sun without a drive for decades.

teile.einleitung: An energy flow diagram uses arrows to show where the energy in a device or process comes from and where it goes. The wider an arrow is, the more energy flows there. This lets you see at a glance how much energy is used and how much flows away as loss.
wichtigste: An energy flow diagram with arrows of different widths is called a Sankey diagram.
The width of an arrow shows the amount of energy.
Together, the outgoing arrows are always as wide as the incoming arrow.
The energy that serves the desired task is called useful energy.
The Sankey diagram is named after an Irish engineer.
For a light bulb, the arrow for heat is the widest.

abschnitte.text: An **energy flow diagram** shows how energy flows through a device or a system. On the left a wide arrow usually comes in with the energy supplied. Then it splits into several arrows, for example for light, movement, heat or sound. The **width** of each arrow corresponds to the amount of energy. This shows you immediately where most of the energy goes.

In an energy flow diagram the **law of conservation of energy** must always apply. Together, the outgoing arrows are exactly as wide as the incoming arrow. If a device receives 500 J and gives out 350 J as useful energy, the loss arrow shows 150 J. If an electric motor receives 2000 J and gives out 200 J as heat and 100 J as sound, 1700 J of **useful energy** remain. With this rule you can easily calculate missing values.

In an old **light bulb**, electrical energy flows in. Only a small part, about five per cent, becomes visible light. The rest becomes heat, which is why the heat arrow is the widest. In an LED lamp the light arrow is much wider and the heat arrow narrower. The diagram therefore shows very clearly why LED lamps save electricity.

Diagrams with arrows of different widths are called **Sankey diagrams**. They are named after the Irish engineer **Matthew Henry Phineas Riall Sankey**. In 1898 he drew such a diagram to show the energy flows of a steam engine. He wanted to show how much of the fuel's energy is actually converted into work. Since then this kind of diagram has been used in engineering, economics and schools.

abschnitte.titel: The energy flow of a country
abschnitte.text: Sankey diagrams show not only individual devices but also whole countries. Every year the Swiss Federal Office of Energy publishes **energy statistics** for Switzerland. They show how much oil, gas, hydroelectric power and other energy sources flow into the country. You can also see how much of it is used in transport, households and industry. Similar diagrams show flows of money, materials or water.

begriffe.erklaerung: A diagram with arrows whose width shows the amount.
Energy that is used for the desired task.
Energy that does not help with the task, usually heat.
A unit of energy, abbreviated J.
Energy is never lost; it only changes its form.

gewusst: One of the most famous flow diagrams shows Napoleon's Russian campaign, where the width of the line represents the number of soldiers.
In a petrol car, often less than a third of the fuel's energy becomes movement.
The human body can also be drawn as an energy flow diagram, with food as the input and a lot of heat as the output.

teile.einleitung: Empa is a Swiss research institute for materials science and technology. It tests how strong, safe and environmentally friendly materials are, and develops new materials for the future. It was founded in 1880 and today belongs to the ETH Domain.
wichtigste: Empa was founded in 1880.
Its first director was Ludwig von Tetmajer.
Empa has three sites: Dübendorf, St Gallen and Thun.
It belongs to the ETH Domain, together with ETH Zurich, EPFL and other research institutes.
In 1891 Tetmajer investigated the collapse of the railway bridge at Münchenstein.
In 1937 a testing institute for textiles in St Gallen became part of Empa.
In the NEST research building in Dübendorf, Empa and Eawag test new building technologies in everyday use.

abschnitte.text: The name Empa originally stood for **Swiss Federal Laboratories for Materials Testing and Research**. It does research on materials such as metals, concrete, wood, plastics and textiles. It also tests products on behalf of companies and authorities. Empa belongs to the **ETH Domain**, which also includes ETH Zurich, EPFL in Lausanne, the Paul Scherrer Institute, WSL and Eawag.

Empa began in 1880 as a testing institute for building materials at the Polytechnic, today's ETH Zurich. Its first director was **Ludwig von Tetmajer**. At that time many railway bridges were being built in Switzerland, and people needed to know how much load steel, iron and cement could bear. Tetmajer developed standard testing methods so that materials would be tested in the same way everywhere.

In 1891 a railway bridge at **Münchenstein** in the canton of Basel-Landschaft collapsed under a fully occupied train. It was one of the worst railway accidents in Switzerland, with many deaths. Tetmajer investigated the accident and showed that slender compression struts of the bridge had buckled. His experiments led to a correction of **Euler's buckling formula**, which describes when a rod under pressure gives way sideways.

Empa's headquarters is in **Dübendorf** near Zurich. In **St Gallen**, a testing institute specialising in textiles became part of Empa in 1937, fitting the tradition of St Gallen embroidery. Today research there includes high-tech fibres and materials for medicine. In **Thun**, Empa works among other things on surfaces and new manufacturing methods.

In the **NEST** building in Dübendorf, Empa and Eawag test new building and energy technologies directly in everyday use. People live and work there while individual living units are exchanged and tried out. Empa also does research on hydrogen as a fuel, on batteries, on recycling and on better air quality. In this way it helps to make buildings, vehicles and products safer and more environmentally friendly.

begriffe.erklaerung: A substance from which things are made, for example steel, concrete or wood.
Tests in which you measure how strong or durable a material is.
The group made up of the two federal institutes of technology and several federal research institutes.
When a long, thin rod gives way sideways under pressure.

gewusst: Empa also tests everyday products such as bike helmets, climbing ropes and sportswear for safety.
At NEST they try out how houses of the future could be built while people live in them quite normally.
The Münchenstein accident led to bridges in Switzerland being tested much more strictly afterwards.

teile.einleitung: Escape velocity is the minimum speed a body must have to free itself from the pull of a body in space without any further drive. On Earth this is about 11.2 kilometres per second. It explains why the Moon has hardly any air and why not even light can escape from a black hole.
wichtigste: Escape velocity is the minimum speed needed to escape from a body in space without a drive.
At the Earth's surface it is about 11.2 km/s.
On the Moon it is only about 2.4 km/s.
It depends only on the mass and radius of the body in space, not on the mass of the flying object.
It is greater by a factor of the square root of 2 than the circular orbital speed at the same place.
At the Schwarzschild radius of a black hole it equals the speed of light.
Because of its low escape velocity, the Moon has practically no atmosphere.

abschnitte.text: If you throw a ball upwards, it falls back down because of **gravity**. The faster you throw it, the higher it flies. Above a certain speed it would never come back; that is the **escape velocity**. This assumes that no air slows it down and no engine keeps pushing it.

At the Earth's surface the escape velocity is about 11.2 km/s, which is about 40,000 km/h. On the Moon about 2.4 km/s is enough, on Mars about 5 km/s. Giant Jupiter demands almost 60 km/s, and at the surface of the Sun it is over 600 km/s. Rockets do not have to be this fast straight away, because their engines keep pushing for a long time, but the number shows how much energy a journey into space needs.

Escape velocity depends only on the **mass** and radius of the body in space. Whether a grain of sand or a heavy space probe is flying makes no difference. The formula is v = square root of 2GM/r, where G is the gravitational constant. If a planet has four times the Earth's mass but the same radius, its escape velocity is twice as great. It is also greater by a factor of the square root of 2 than the **circular orbital speed** that a satellite needs for an orbit at the same place.

abschnitte.titel: Why the Moon has no air
abschnitte.text: Gas particles are constantly whizzing about in all directions, and in the heat of the Sun they become fast. On the Moon many of them easily reach the low escape velocity and disappear into space. That is why the Moon has practically no **atmosphere**. The Earth, on the other hand, is heavy enough to hold on to its blanket of air; only the very light hydrogen gas slowly escapes.

In a **black hole** the mass is squeezed into a tiny space. At the Schwarzschild radius the escape velocity is as great as the speed of light, about 300,000 km/s. That is why not even light can escape from inside. If you wanted to turn the Earth into a black hole, you would have to squeeze it to a radius of about 9 mm, roughly the size of a marble.

begriffe.erklaerung: The force of attraction with which masses pull on each other.
The speed a satellite needs to stay in a circular orbit around a body in space.
The size below which a body becomes a black hole.
The blanket of air around a body in space.

gewusst: At the Earth's escape velocity you would get from Zurich to Milan in less than a minute.
The space probes Voyager 1 and 2 are so fast that they are even leaving the solar system.
The whole Earth as a black hole would be smaller than a marble.

teile.einleitung: Sliding friction is the braking force that acts when a body slides over a surface. It occurs when a sledge races over the snow or a crate is pushed across the floor. How strong it is depends on the two materials and on how firmly the body presses on the surface underneath.
wichtigste: When a body slides over a surface, sliding friction acts.
The force of sliding friction is calculated as the coefficient of sliding friction times the normal force.
If you double the normal force, the force of sliding friction also doubles.
