Friction is caused mainly by tiny bumps that catch on each other.
Steel on ice has a particularly small coefficient of sliding friction.
If you pull a body at a steady speed, the pulling force is as great as the force of sliding friction.
Sliding friction is usually smaller than static friction.

abschnitte.text: Friction is a force that slows down movement between two surfaces. A distinction is made between **static friction**, which holds a body at rest in place, **sliding friction** when sliding, and rolling friction when rolling. Sliding friction always acts against the direction of movement. When a sledge slides down the slope, it keeps slowing it down a little.

Even a surface that seems smooth is full of hills and valleys under the microscope. When two surfaces lie on top of each other, these tiny **bumps** catch on each other. In addition, the particles at the points of contact attract each other slightly. When sliding, these connections have to be broken all the time, and this produces heat.

The force of sliding friction is F = μ · F_N. Here μ is the **coefficient of sliding friction** and F_N the **normal force** with which the body presses on the surface. If a wooden crate presses on the floor with 400 N and μ = 0.3, the force of sliding friction is 120 N. If you need 50 N to pull a crate with a normal force of 250 N steadily, the coefficient of sliding friction is 0.2.

The coefficient of sliding friction depends on the materials that rub against each other. At about 0.015, steel on ice has a particularly small value, which is why skates and curling stones glide so well. Wood on wood or rubber on tarmac have much larger values. An ice hockey puck therefore glides much further on ice than on a road.

Friction is sometimes unwanted, for example in engines, where it wastes energy and wears parts out. There, **lubricants** such as oil help. When braking, on the other hand, sliding friction is useful, because brake pads press on brake discs and turn kinetic energy into heat. If a car's wheels lock, it slides with sliding friction, which brakes less strongly than the static friction of rolling tyres; that is why there is ABS.

Around 1500 Leonardo da Vinci was already studying friction with blocks on slopes. Around 1700 the Frenchman **Guillaume Amontons** described that friction depends on the normal force but hardly on the size of the contact area. Charles-Augustin de Coulomb later extended these laws. That is why today people often speak of Coulomb's law of friction.

begriffe.erklaerung: The force with which a body presses at right angles on the surface beneath it.
A number without a unit that shows how strongly two materials rub against each other when sliding.
The friction that stops a body at rest from sliding away.
A substance such as oil or grease that reduces friction between parts.

gewusst: Whether a crate lies on its wide side or its narrow side makes almost no difference to the sliding friction.
If you rub your hands together quickly, they get warm through friction.
A match catches fire because friction on the striking surface produces enough heat.

teile.einleitung: A drop tower is a tall tower in which objects are dropped in order to carry out experiments in weightlessness. The best-known research drop tower in Europe stands in Bremen and is about 146 metres tall. When the capsule and its contents fall together, the things inside float for a few seconds.
wichtigste: The well-known drop tower for weightlessness experiments in Bremen is about 146 m tall.
A research drop tower is used mainly for experiments in weightlessness.
Objects float in a freely falling capsule because the capsule and its contents fall equally fast.
The air is pumped out of the drop tube so that no air resistance slows things down.
A simple drop in Bremen gives about 4.7 seconds of weightlessness.
If the capsule is first catapulted upwards, the time roughly doubles.
At the end the capsule is slowed down in a container of polystyrene beads.

abschnitte.text: A **drop tower** is a tower or shaft in which test capsules are allowed to fall freely. During the fall, there is **weightlessness** in the capsule for a short time. This lets researchers test how flames, liquids or materials behave without noticeable gravity. This is much cheaper than an experiment in space. Such facilities exist, for example, in Germany, the USA, Japan and China.

In free fall, the capsule and everything in it fall at exactly the same speed. So nothing presses against the floor of the capsule, and everything seems to float. Exactly the same happens to astronauts on the space station, who are constantly falling around the Earth. So that the capsule is not slowed down by the air, the air is pumped out of the **drop tube**. Without **air resistance** the capsule really does fall freely.

The **Bremen drop tower** belongs to the University of Bremen and was opened in 1990. It is about 146 m tall; the actual drop distance in the airless tube is about 110 m. In a simple drop, weightlessness lasts about 4.7 seconds. With a **catapult** at the bottom, the capsule can first be shot upwards; then it rises and falls, and the time roughly doubles to over 9 seconds. At the end the capsule lands in a container full of **polystyrene beads**, which slows it down gently.

In drop towers researchers study, for example, how flames burn without gravity. On Earth hot gases rise, but in weightlessness a candle flame forms a round ball. The behaviour of liquids, dust and crystals is also studied. In addition, devices are tested before they fly into space in satellites. Even experiments on the **theory of relativity** have been carried out in a drop tower.

There are also towers for falling in amusement parks. In a **drop tower ride**, a gondola with people in it is pulled up and then falls straight down. For a moment the passengers feel almost weightless, with butterflies in their stomachs. At the end strong magnets or brakes slow the gondola down safely. Because there is air, the fall there is not completely free.

begriffe.erklaerung: A state in which you feel no weight, for example in free fall.
An airtight tube in the drop tower through which the capsule falls.
A space from which the air has been almost completely removed.
A device that hurls something upwards or forwards with great force.

gewusst: Before the capsule in Bremen may be dropped, the air has to be pumped out of the tube, which takes quite a long time each time.
After the fall, the capsule enters the braking container at almost 170 km/h.
Parabolic flights in aeroplanes give longer weightlessness of about 20 seconds per manoeuvre.

teile.einleitung: A rectifier is an electronic circuit that converts alternating current into direct current. This is necessary because alternating current comes out of the socket, but mobile phones, computers and many other devices need direct current. That is why there is a rectifier in almost every power supply.
wichtigste: A rectifier converts alternating current into direct current.
The most important component of a rectifier is the diode.
A half-wave rectifier with only one diode lets through only every second half-wave.
A bridge rectifier needs 4 diodes and uses both half-waves.
The bridge circuit is also called the Graetz circuit, after the physicist Leo Graetz.
A capacitor after the rectifier smooths the pulsing voltage.
On the 50-hertz grid, the voltage after a bridge rectifier pulses at 100 hertz.

abschnitte.text: In Switzerland **alternating current** at 230 volts and 50 hertz comes out of the socket. The direction of the current changes back and forth 50 times a second. But electronic devices such as mobile phones, laptops or televisions need **direct current**, which always flows in the same direction. That is why a rectifier in the charger or power supply takes care of the conversion.

The heart of a rectifier is the **diode**. It lets current through in only one direction, like a valve that lets water flow in only one direction. Today diodes are mostly made of **silicon**. About 0.7 volts are lost at each silicon diode.

A **half-wave rectifier** has only one diode and lets through only every second half-wave; the others are lost. A **bridge rectifier** has 4 diodes connected so that both half-waves are redirected in the same direction. The current always flows through two diodes, so about 1.4 volts are lost. The bridge circuit is also called the Graetz circuit, after the German physicist **Leo Graetz**.

After the rectifier the current flows in only one direction, but it still pulses. On the 50-hertz grid the voltage after a bridge rectifier pulses at 100 hertz, because both half-waves are used. A **capacitor** stores some charge with each pulse and releases it again in the gaps. This makes the voltage much more even; it is said to be **smoothed**.

The 230 volts of the Swiss mains voltage are an average, the **RMS value**. For a moment the voltage reaches a top value, the **peak value**, of about 325 volts. A capacitor after the rectifier charges up to roughly this value. In the past, instead of semiconductor diodes, vacuum tubes or even mercury vapour rectifiers were used, which were large and hot.

begriffe.erklaerung: An electronic component that lets current through in only one direction.
Half of an alternating current cycle, during which the current flows in one direction.
A component that can store electric charge for a short time.
The value of an alternating voltage that has the same effect as a direct voltage of the same size.
The highest value that an alternating voltage reaches.

gewusst: A bridge rectifier is often available as a small black component with four legs, containing all four diodes.
Electric locomotives and charging stations for electric cars also contain large rectifiers.
The faint hum of some old appliances often comes from the 100-hertz ripple after the rectifier.

teile.einleitung: An electron microscope is a microscope that works with a beam of electrons instead of light. With it you can see things that are much smaller than with any light microscope, such as viruses or even individual rows of atoms. It is one of the most important tools of modern biology, medicine and materials research.
wichtigste: In 1931 Ernst Ruska and Max Knoll built the first electron microscope.
Electrons have a much shorter wavelength than light, so they show finer details.
The electron beams are focused with magnetic lenses.
There must be a high vacuum inside, otherwise air molecules would scatter the electrons.
In a transmission electron microscope, electrons pass through an extremely thin sample.
The scanning electron microscope creates images of surfaces using secondary electrons.
In 2017 the Swiss scientist Jacques Dubochet received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry for cryo-electron microscopy.

abschnitte.text: A **light microscope** can only show things separately down to about half the wavelength of light, that is about 200 nanometres. But electrons also behave like waves, and their **wavelength** is much shorter. An electron accelerated with 100 V has a wavelength of only about 0.12 nm. The higher the accelerating voltage, the shorter the wavelength and the finer the details.

An electron source sends out electrons, which are accelerated with a high voltage. Instead of glass lenses, **magnetic lenses** made of coils focus the beam. There is a **high vacuum** throughout the device, because air molecules would deflect the electrons. The image does not form in the eye, but on a fluorescent screen or a camera sensor.

In the **transmission electron microscope** (TEM) the electrons pass through the sample. That is why the sample must be extremely thin, often less than a ten-thousandth of a millimetre. The **scanning electron microscope** (SEM), on the other hand, scans the surface point by point. It mainly records secondary electrons from the sample and so produces three-dimensional-looking images of insect eyes, pollen or fractures in metal.

The German electrical engineer **Ernst Ruska** and his teacher Max Knoll built the first electron microscope in Berlin in 1931. A few years later it already beat the resolution of the best light microscopes. Ruska received the Nobel Prize in Physics for it in 1986. He shared it with Gerd Binnig and Heinrich Rohrer, who had invented the scanning tunnelling microscope at the IBM research laboratory in Rüschlikon near Zurich.

Biological samples contain water, which would evaporate in a vacuum. The biophysicist **Jacques Dubochet** from the canton of Vaud developed a method of freezing samples in a flash into glass-like ice. With this **cryo-electron microscopy** you can image proteins and viruses in their natural form. Dubochet, a professor at the University of Lausanne, received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry for this in 2017, together with Joachim Frank and Richard Henderson.

begriffe.erklaerung: A tiny, negatively charged particle in the shell of atoms.
How close two points may be to each other so that you can still see them separately.
A space from which almost all the air has been removed.
A coil whose magnetic field focuses electron beams as a glass lens focuses light.
A millionth of a millimetre.

gewusst: Images from an electron microscope are actually black and white; the bright colours are often added afterwards.
Modern transmission electron microscopes can resolve distances of less than a tenth of a nanometre and so show individual rows of atoms.
With cryo-electron microscopy, the structure of the coronavirus was made visible shortly after its discovery.

teile.einleitung: Frequency shows how often something vibrates or repeats itself per second. It is measured in hertz, Hz for short, named after the German physicist Heinrich Hertz. Frequencies decide how high a note sounds and play an important part in electricity, radio and mobile phones.
wichtigste: Frequency is the number of vibrations per second.
The unit is the hertz; one hertz means one vibration per second.
The higher the frequency, the higher a note sounds.
Concert A has 440 Hz, and many orchestras tune to it.
An octave higher means double the frequency: 300 Hz becomes 600 Hz.
The current from a Swiss socket changes direction at 50 Hz.
If you tighten a guitar string, its frequency rises and the note gets higher.

abschnitte.text: **Frequency** describes how often a process repeats itself in one second. If a string vibrates 1000 times in 4 seconds, it has a frequency of 250 Hz. The time for a single vibration is called the **period**. Frequency and period are closely linked: if one vibration takes 0.002 seconds, 500 vibrations fit into a second, that is 500 Hz.

Sound consists of vibrations of the air. The faster the air vibrates, the higher we hear the note. People hear notes roughly between 20 Hz and 20,000 Hz; with age the upper limit gets lower. **Concert A** at 440 Hz is used by musicians for tuning. If you double the frequency, the note sounds exactly one **octave** higher.

A guitar string vibrates faster if you tighten it more or make it shorter. That is why you press the strings onto the frets when playing. Bats and dolphins use **ultrasound** with frequencies far above 20,000 Hz, which we cannot hear. Elephants, on the other hand, also communicate with very low infrasound below 20 Hz.

The current from a socket is **alternating current**; it keeps changing direction. In Switzerland and throughout Europe this happens at 50 Hz, in the USA at 60 Hz. The railways in Switzerland, such as the SBB, have their own power network at 16.7 Hz. The power stations must keep the frequency very precise, otherwise there can be disturbances in the grid.

Radio waves also have frequencies, only much higher ones. FM radio stations broadcast at about 100 million hertz, that is 100 **megahertz**. Mobile phones and wifi work with several billion hertz, that is gigahertz. Even light is a vibration whose frequency decides its colour; red light has a lower frequency than blue.

The unit is named after the German physicist **Heinrich Hertz**. Between 1886 and 1888 he was the first to detect electromagnetic waves in the laboratory. In this way he confirmed James Clerk Maxwell's theory. His discovery was the basis for radio, television and mobile communications.

begriffe.erklaerung: The unit of frequency; one hertz is one vibration per second.
The time that a single vibration takes.
Current that keeps changing direction.
Sound with such a high frequency that people cannot hear it.

gewusst: Swiss trains run on electricity at 16.7 Hz, not on the 50 Hz from the socket.
A mosquito beats its wings so fast that an audible humming sound is produced.
A processor in a computer works at a clock rate of several billion hertz.

teile.einleitung: Static electricity builds up when two substances rub against each other and electric charges move from one to the other. Then your hair stands on end, socks stick together or there is a crackle when you take off a jumper. Sometimes you even feel a small shock at the door handle.
wichtigste: When two substances are rubbed together, electrons move from one substance to the other.
You become charged especially easily in dry air in winter.
You become charged when walking on a carpet or sliding down a plastic slide.
Strongly charged hair stands on end because like charges repel each other.
Socks from the tumble dryer stick together because they are electrically charged.
The crackling when you take off a jumper comes from tiny sparks discharging.
To avoid shocks at the door handle, it helps to touch it first with a key.

abschnitte.titel: How does the charge build up?
abschnitte.text: All substances are made of atoms with positively charged nuclei and negatively charged **electrons**. Normally there are equal numbers of positive and negative charges, and the substance is neutral. When two different substances rub against each other, electrons move from one to the other. Afterwards one substance is negatively charged and the other positively charged; this is called **triboelectricity**, or electricity from friction.

Like charges **repel each other**, unlike charges attract. If all your hairs have the same charge, they push each other away and stand out in all directions. A rubbed balloon, on the other hand, can stick to the wall or attract small scraps of paper. Socks from the tumble dryer stick together because they have different charges.

In dry air you become charged especially easily. In winter the air in heated rooms is often very dry. Humid air, on the other hand, slowly carries the charges away before they can build up. Plastics such as plastic slides, carpets made of synthetic fibres or fleece jumpers also encourage charging.

abschnitte.titel: The shock at the door handle
abschnitte.text: Anyone who walks across a carpet collects charges on their body; the voltage can reach several thousand volts. If you then touch a metal door handle, a small **spark** jumps across and you feel a shock. Because only very little charge flows, this is harmless, but unpleasant. One trick helps: first touch the door handle with a **key**, and then the spark jumps from the key and not from your fingertip.

Even in ancient Greece people noticed that rubbed **amber** attracts feathers and straw. The Greek word for amber, elektron, gave electricity its name. Today static electricity is used, for example, in laser printers and photocopiers to put the toner powder onto the paper. In electronics workshops and at petrol stations, on the other hand, you have to be careful, because sparks can destroy sensitive components or ignite fumes.

begriffe.erklaerung: A tiny, negatively charged particle in every atom.
The property of particles of being positively or negatively electric.
When collected charges suddenly flow away, often with a spark.
Electric charge that builds up when two substances are rubbed together.

gewusst: Lightning is basically a giant electrostatic discharge between a cloud and the ground.
If you take off a fleece jumper in the dark, you can sometimes even see the tiny sparks.
A rubbed balloon can bend a thin stream of water from the tap.

teile.einleitung: Electrostatics deals with electric charges at rest and the forces between them. You know it when your hair stands on end after taking off a jumper or a balloon sticks to the wall. The small shock from a door handle also has to do with electrostatics.
wichtigste: Electrostatics studies electric charges at rest.
Rubbing transfers electrons from one substance to another.
Like charges repel each other, unlike charges attract.
A balloon rubbed on a jumper sticks to the wall.
The force between charges is described by Coulomb's law.
Lightning is the discharge of huge electrostatic charges.
Photocopiers and laser printers use electrostatics.

abschnitte.text: If you rub a **balloon** on a woollen jumper or on your hair, electrons move onto the balloon. This makes it **negatively charged**. If you hold it against the wall, the charges in the wall shift a little and the balloon is attracted. That is why it sticks to the wall, and hair stands up towards it.

Every atom has positively charged protons and negatively charged electrons. Normally they balance each other out and the body is **neutral**. If a body has too many electrons, it is negatively charged; if it has too few, it is positively charged. **Like** charges repel each other, **unlike** charges attract.

Around 1785 the Frenchman Charles-Augustin de **Coulomb** measured the force between charges with a delicate torsion balance. He found that the force decreases sharply with distance: at twice the distance it is only a quarter as large. The unit of charge, the **coulomb**, is named after him. With an **electroscope** you can test whether a body is charged.

When you walk on a carpet and then touch a door handle, a small **spark** sometimes jumps across. The charges balance out suddenly; this is called a **discharge**. Such sparks can have several thousand volts, but they are harmless because the charge is tiny. **Lightning** is the same thing on a huge scale.

Laser printers and photocopiers use electrostatically charged drums to which the toner powder sticks. In electrostatic filters in chimneys, dust particles are charged and so removed from the waste air. When cars are painted, electrostatics ensures an even layer of paint. It is dangerous when refuelling or in mills, where sparks can cause **explosions**, and for sensitive computer chips.

begriffe.erklaerung: A property of particles such as electrons and protons that causes forces.
A device that shows whether a body is electrically charged.
The rapid balancing out of charges, often visible as a spark.
A body is neutral if it has as many positive as negative charges.

gewusst: In dry winter air you get small electric shocks much more often than in summer.
A small spark at a door handle can have a voltage of several thousand volts.
Even the ancient Greeks observed that rubbed amber attracts feathers.

teile.einleitung: The bicycle chain, usually called a velo chain in Switzerland, transfers the force from the pedals to the back wheel. It consists of many small metal links that run over toothed wheels. Without a chain you would have to drive the wheel directly, as on the first balance bikes and penny-farthings.
wichtigste: The chain carries the force from the pedals to the back wheel.
A bike chain consists of many metal links.
At the front, by the pedals, the chain runs over the chainring.
The teeth of the toothed wheels fit into the gaps in the chain.
A chain needs oil to run well.
If a chain often gets wet and is never looked after, it rusts.
If the chain is loose, it can come off.

abschnitte.text: When you push the pedals, you turn the **chainring** at the front, a large toothed wheel. From there the chain runs to a smaller toothed wheel on the back wheel, the **sprocket**. In this way it carries the force of your legs to the back wheel, which then turns. Because the back toothed wheel is smaller, the wheel turns faster than the pedals. Such a connection is called a **chain drive**.

A bike chain consists of many small **metal links** made of steel. Each link has two plates, pins and small rollers. The teeth of the toothed wheels fit exactly into the gaps between the rollers. That is why this design is also called a **roller chain**. On bikes the distance from pin to pin is half an inch, about 12.7 millimetres.

Many bikes have several toothed wheels at the back and sometimes at the front too. With **derailleur gears**, a mechanism pushes the chain onto a different toothed wheel. A large sprocket at the back makes pedalling uphill easier; a small one makes you fast on the flat. The ratio of the teeth at the front and back is called the **gear ratio**. With hub gears, on the other hand, the gears are hidden inside the hub of the back wheel.

A chain needs **oil** so that the links slide easily and it runs quietly. If it often gets wet and is never looked after, it starts to **rust**. That is why you should clean it regularly with a cloth and then oil it lightly. A chain stretches a little over time and has to be replaced after a few thousand kilometres. If it is too loose, it can come off.

A **chain guard** made of metal or plastic covers the chain so that your trousers stay clean and do not get caught. The first bikes had no chain yet; on the penny-farthing the pedals were fixed directly to the huge front wheel. Only in the 1880s did the **safety bicycle** appear, with a chain drive to the back wheel. It was safer and became the model for almost all bikes today. Motorbikes still often use chains today too.

begriffe.erklaerung: The large toothed wheel at the front by the pedals.
A small toothed wheel on the back wheel.
The ratio of the teeth at the front and back; it decides how easily or fast you ride.
Gears in which the chain jumps onto other toothed wheels.
A chain with small rollers between the links.

gewusst: A well-oiled bike chain transfers almost all the force; only a few per cent are lost through friction.
A normal bike chain has more than a hundred links.
Some bikes have a toothed belt made of plastic instead of a chain, which needs no oil.

teile.einleitung: Fever is a raised body temperature with which the body defends itself against germs. People speak of fever from about 38 degrees Celsius. Fever is not itself an illness, but a sign that the immune system is working.
wichtigste: People speak of fever from about 38 °C.
The body raises its temperature in order to fight germs.
Fever is not an illness, but a sign.
When the fever rises, there is sometimes strong shivering, the chills.
When the fever falls, you often sweat because the body is giving off heat.
Body temperature is measured with a clinical thermometer.
With a fever, drinking a lot and resting are especially important.

abschnitte.text: The normal body temperature of a person is about 36.5 to 37.5 °C. From about 38 °C it is called **fever**, and above 39 °C high fever. The forehead then often feels hot, you are tired and not very hungry. Fever is not an illness of its own, but a **symptom**, that is a sign, for example of flu.

In the brain there is an area, the **hypothalamus**, which works like the thermostat of a heating system. Normally it keeps the temperature at about 37 °C. When viruses or bacteria get into the body, defence cells release messenger substances that turn the set point higher. Many germs multiply less well at a higher temperature, and the immune system works faster.

When the set point is raised, the body suddenly feels too cold. It produces heat through rapid trembling of the muscles, the **chills**, and you feel cold even though your skin is warm. When the fever falls again, the body is too warm and gives off heat. Then you sweat a lot, because sweat cools the skin as it evaporates; this is **evaporative cooling**.

With a **clinical thermometer** you measure body temperature, for example under the tongue, in the ear or under the armpit. In the past thermometers contained poisonous mercury; today they are mostly digital. In the 19th century the German doctor Carl Reinhold August Wunderlich examined thousands of patients and set the limits for normal temperature and fever. Depending on where you measure, the values differ a little.

With a fever the body needs a lot of fluid, because it loses water through sweating. Rest and sleep help the immune system with its work. Light clothing and a duvet that is not too thick stop too much heat from building up. With very high fever or fever that lasts a long time, especially in small children, a **doctor** should look at the child.

begriffe.erklaerung: A body temperature of about 38 °C or more.
A sign that points to an illness.
A part of the brain that, among other things, controls body temperature.
Strong shivering with which the body produces heat.
Cooling that happens when water evaporates on the skin.

gewusst: Many animals also get fever, and lizards even deliberately lie down in warmer places when they have an infection.
Calf compresses with lukewarm water are an old home remedy that cools through evaporation.
In the evening body temperature is usually a little higher than early in the morning.

teile.einleitung: Hearing protection protects your ears from noise that is too loud. It comes as small earplugs or as ear defenders, which look like large headphones. This is important, because destroyed hearing cells never grow back.
wichtigste: Hearing protection dampens sound before it reaches the inner ear.
Earplugs are put directly into the ears.
Ear defenders look like large headphones.
On building sites, in factories and at shooting ranges, hearing protection is part of the equipment.
For children hearing protection makes sense, for example during loud fireworks.
Damaged hearing cells in the ear do not grow back.
A ringing in the ear is a warning sign that it was too loud.

abschnitte.text: Sound consists of vibrations of the air that reach the ear. The eardrum and the tiny bones of the ear pass them on to the **cochlea** in the inner ear. There sit fine **hair cells**, which turn the vibrations into nerve signals. Very loud noises can permanently damage these delicate cells.

Loudness is measured in **decibels**. A conversation has about 60 decibels; a pneumatic drill or loud music at a concert over 100 decibels. From about 85 decibels, longer exposure to noise can harm your hearing. The louder it is, the shorter the time you may stay there without protection.

**Earplugs** made of foam or silicone are put into the ear canal. **Ear defenders** enclose the whole ears like large headphones and are well suited to children. There are also custom-made earplugs that are produced to the exact shape of your own ear. Musicians use special plugs that make all notes quieter evenly.

In Switzerland Suva, the accident insurance fund, makes sure that workers are protected from noise. On **building sites**, in workshops and when shooting, hearing protection is compulsory. At carnival with Guggenmusik bands, at concerts and on 1 August with fireworks, you should also think of your ears. It is best to keep your distance from loudspeakers and loud instruments.

A **ringing** or rushing in the ear after a loud event shows that your hearing was overloaded. It often goes away after a while, but sometimes it stays for ever. A permanent sound in the ear is called **tinnitus**. Anyone who is often in loud noise without protection can become hard of hearing, and this cannot be reversed.

begriffe.erklaerung: The unit of measurement used to give loudness.
A snail-shaped part of the inner ear in which the hearing cells sit.
A ringing or rushing in the ear that does not come from outside.
Hearing protection that sits over the ears like large headphones.

gewusst: A person is born with only about 15,000 hair cells per ear, and no new ones are ever added.
Headphones can also harm your hearing if you listen to very loud music for a long time.
An increase of 10 decibels makes a noise seem about twice as loud to us.

teile.einleitung: The guitar is a string instrument with a neck and usually six strings, which you pluck with your fingers or a plectrum. It is one of the most popular instruments in the world and is heard in folk music, classical music, pop and rock. The guitar is a good example for showing how notes are made.
wichtigste: A guitar usually has six strings.
It is played with the fingers or with a small plate, the plectrum.
The hollow wooden body amplifies the sound and makes it louder.
The round hole in the body is called the sound hole.
The metal strips across the neck are called frets.
The strings are tuned with the pegs at the top of the neck.
A shorter, tighter or thinner string sounds higher.

abschnitte.text: A guitar consists of the **body**, the neck and the head. The body of an acoustic guitar is a hollow wooden box with a round **sound hole**. On the neck lies the fingerboard with the **frets**, which are metal strips across the neck. On the head sit the pegs, with which the strings are tightened. At the bottom of the body the strings are attached to the bridge.

If you pluck a string, it starts to **vibrate** quickly back and forth. But a string on its own is quiet, because it moves only a little air. The vibration is passed through the bridge to the thin wooden top, which then vibrates along with it. The hollow body acts as a **sound box** and makes the note much louder. The sound gets out through the sound hole.

How high a note sounds depends on how often the string vibrates per second, that is on the **frequency**. Thin strings sound higher than thick ones. If you turn a peg and tighten the string more, its note gets higher. If you press the string onto a fret, the vibrating part becomes shorter and the note rises. At the twelfth fret the string is exactly halved, and then the note sounds an **octave** higher.

The **classical guitar** has nylon strings and sounds soft; it is often used in guitar lessons. The steel-string acoustic guitar has steel strings and sounds brighter and louder. The **electric guitar** usually has a solid body and needs an amplifier. In it, **pickups** turn the vibration of the strings into electrical signals. There is also the bass guitar, usually with four low strings.

Today's guitar developed mainly in Spain. In the 19th century the Spanish guitar maker Antonio de Torres gave it the shape that classical guitars still have today. In the 20th century the electric guitar became the most important instrument of rock music. In Switzerland many children learn the guitar at a music school. You can accompany songs by playing **chords**, that is several notes at the same time.

begriffe.erklaerung: A small plastic plate with which you strike the strings.
A metal strip across the guitar neck that divides up the notes.
A hollow body that vibrates along and amplifies the sound.
Several notes that sound at the same time.
How often something vibrates back and forth per second.

gewusst: The six strings of a guitar are normally tuned to the notes E, A, D, G, B and E.
Between two neighbouring frets there is always exactly one semitone.
The frets are not equally far apart; they get closer and closer together towards the body.

teile.einleitung: The Fosbury flop is the technique with which almost all high jumpers today go over the bar. You cross the bar backwards and head first. The technique is named after the American Dick Fosbury, who won the Olympic title with it in 1968.
wichtigste: The Fosbury flop is a technique in the high jump.
It is named after the American Dick Fosbury.
Fosbury won gold with it at the 1968 Olympic Games in Mexico City.
In the flop you cross the bar backwards and head first.
Before that most jumpers used the straddle.
Only soft foam mats made landing on your back safe.
According to the rules you must take off from one foot.
Javier Sotomayor has held the men's world record since 1993.

abschnitte.text: The **Fosbury flop** is a jumping technique in the **high jump**. The jumper runs up in a curve, takes off from one foot and turns so as to fly with their back to the bar. First the head and shoulders go over the bar, then the body is arched into a bridge. Finally you pull your legs after you and land on your back on the mat.

The American **Dick Fosbury** tried out his unusual technique while still at school, because he did not get on well with the old techniques. At first many coaches laughed at him. At the 1968 Olympic Games in **Mexico City** he won the gold medal with 2.24 m. After that more and more athletes adopted his style, and within a few years it was the most important technique in the world.

Before the flop, most jumpers used the **straddle**. In it you roll over the bar face down. Even earlier there was the scissors jump, in which you swing your legs over the bar one after the other. The flop is easier to learn than the straddle, because the fast, curved run-up brings a lot of momentum into the height.

The secret of the flop lies in the **centre of gravity**. Because the body is strongly arched over the bar, the centre of gravity is at times even below the bar, while the head, back and legs slide over it one after the other. In this way you can get over a higher bar with the same jumping power. The curved run-up also helps, because the jumper leans into the curve and straightens up at take-off.

Before there were thick **foam mats**, people landed in sand or sawdust. Landing on your back or neck there would have been dangerous. Only the soft mats made the flop possible. According to the rules you must take off from one foot, and you have three attempts at each height. Anyone who knocks the bar off has a failed attempt.

Since 1993 the men's high jump world record has been held by the Cuban **Javier Sotomayor** with 2.45 m, jumped with the flop, of course. That is higher than a normal ceiling in many flats. All women today also jump with this technique. In Switzerland children often learn the flop in PE lessons or at an athletics club.

begriffe.erklaerung: An athletics event in which you jump over a bar without any aids.
The point at which you can imagine the whole weight of a body to be concentrated.
An older high jump technique in which you roll over the bar face down.
The pole that has to be jumped over in the high jump.

gewusst: In the Fosbury flop the centre of gravity can pass under the bar while the body flies over it.
Dick Fosbury was only 21 years old when he won the Olympic title.
For more than 30 years nobody has beaten Javier Sotomayor's world record.

teile.einleitung: A generator is a machine that makes electric current from movement. In it, magnets and coils of wire turn relative to each other, and this produces a voltage. Almost all the electricity from our sockets is produced by generators in power stations.
wichtigste: A generator converts kinetic energy into electrical energy.
A generator contains magnets and coils of wire.
The current is produced by electromagnetic induction, which Michael Faraday discovered in 1831.
The faster a generator turns, the greater the voltage.
An electric motor does the opposite: it turns electricity into movement.
In hydroelectric power stations, turbines drive the generators.
Photovoltaic systems produce electricity without any turning generator.

abschnitte.text: A **generator** converts kinetic energy into electrical energy. The word comes from the Latin “generare”, meaning “to produce”. Inside, magnets turn in coils of wire, or coils of wire turn between magnets. You find small generators on bikes; large ones stand in power stations and are as big as a house. The **electric motor** works exactly the other way round: it turns electricity into movement.

If a magnet moves near a coil of wire, the magnetic field in the coil changes. This produces an electrical voltage in the wire; this is called **electromagnetic induction**. It was discovered by the Englishman **Michael Faraday** in 1831. The faster you turn, the greater the voltage becomes. If many appliances are connected, the generator becomes harder to turn, because more energy is being taken out.

On a bike a **dynamo** produces electricity for the lights, and the faster you ride, the brighter they get. A wind-up torch shines when you turn its crank. Hospitals have **emergency generators** that supply electricity at once during a power cut. These generators are usually driven by a diesel engine, just like the ones on building sites. Electric cars also use their motor as a generator when braking and so recharge the battery.

In a **hydroelectric power station**, water flows through a **turbine** and makes it turn, and the turbine drives the generator. In nuclear power stations and many other power stations, steam is produced that drives turbines. In a **wind turbine** the wind turns the rotor blades, which are connected to a generator. A **photovoltaic system**, on the other hand, produces electricity directly from sunlight without any turning generator. In Switzerland more than half of the electricity has come from hydropower for many years.

After Faraday's discovery, inventors built the first simple generators. In 1866 the German engineer **Werner von Siemens** presented a dynamo that worked without permanent magnets and could produce a lot of electricity. This was the start of the age of electricity, with trams, electric light and factories. At the end of the 19th century the first large power stations with alternating current generators were built. In Switzerland, too, hydroelectric power stations were built on many rivers at that time.

begriffe.erklaerung: The creation of an electrical voltage when a magnetic field in a coil changes.
A wire that is wound up many times.
A wheel with blades that is turned by water, steam or wind.
A small generator, for example on a bike.
Current that keeps changing its direction back and forth, 50 times a second in Europe.

gewusst: The generators in Europe's power stations all turn in step, so that the alternating current changes direction 50 times a second.
A large power station generator can supply as much electricity as hundreds of thousands of households need at the same time.
You can use a small electric motor as a generator if you turn its shaft by hand.

teile.einleitung: Black ice is a thin, smooth layer of ice on roads, paths and objects. It forms mainly when rain falls on frozen ground and freezes there immediately. Because you often can hardly see it, black ice is especially dangerous for pedestrians and drivers.
wichtigste: Black ice forms when rain falls on frozen ground and freezes.
You often can hardly see black ice, which is why it is so treacherous.
Wet ice is especially slippery, because a thin film of water lies on it.
Black ice often forms first on bridges.
Drivers should drive more slowly and keep a greater distance when there is black ice.
Salt is often spread on roads so that the ice melts.
Shoes with spikes and walking like a penguin help when walking on black ice.

abschnitte.text: After a cold night the ground can still be frozen, even if the air above is already a little warmer. If rain now falls on it, it freezes immediately into a smooth layer. Sometimes the rain itself is even below zero degrees and freezes on impact; this is called **freezing rain**. Freezing fog or dew can also form slippery patches, which are called **hoar frost glaze**.

There is almost always a wafer-thin **film of water** on ice. It acts like a lubricant, so that shoes and tyres can hardly get a grip. When ice is wet, for example at temperatures around zero degrees, it is therefore especially slippery. The **friction** between shoe and ground becomes very small.

Black ice is usually transparent, and the road underneath just looks wet. When it forms very suddenly, it is called **flash ice** in German. On **bridges** ice often forms first, because they are cooled by cold air from above and below. Shady stretches of woodland and hollows are also especially at risk.

The **winter road services** spread salt on roads, because salt water only freezes at lower temperatures than pure water. So the ice melts, as long as it is not too cold. On pavements grit or sand is often spread too, which gives shoes more grip. In Switzerland MeteoSwiss warns of icy conditions so that everyone can prepare for them.

Anyone walking on black ice should take small steps and keep their weight over their feet, like a **penguin**. Shoes with a good tread or with **spikes** help a lot. Drivers should drive more slowly, brake gently and keep much more distance. In Switzerland good winter tyres are very important for cars in winter.

begriffe.erklaerung: Rain that freezes into ice immediately on impact.
Black ice that forms very suddenly and unexpectedly.
The force that stops things from sliding over each other.
The people and vehicles that clear and grit roads in winter.

gewusst: Penguins walk with short steps and lean slightly forwards, and that is exactly how you are least likely to slip on ice.
Road salt hardly works any more in very severe cold, because salt water also freezes at some point.
Black ice can become so heavy that branches break off and power lines snap.

teile.einleitung: Ferromagnetism is the property of certain substances of being strongly attracted by magnets and being able to become magnets themselves. At room temperature these include mainly the metals iron, nickel and cobalt. Without ferromagnetism there would be no fridge magnets, no compass needles and no electric motors.
wichtigste: At room temperature iron, nickel and cobalt are ferromagnetic.
Inside there are small regions, the Weiss domains, that act like tiny magnets.
When magnetised, the Weiss domains line up in a common direction.
Above the Curie temperature a ferromagnet loses its magnetic properties.
The Curie temperature is named after the physicist Pierre Curie.
The strongest permanent magnets are made of neodymium, iron and boron.
The magnetisation that remains after a field is switched off is called remanence.

abschnitte.text: Most substances hardly react to magnets: wood, glass or aluminium, for example. **Ferromagnetic** substances, on the other hand, are strongly attracted. The name comes from the Latin word ferrum for iron. At room temperature iron, nickel and cobalt are ferromagnetic, as are many of their alloys and the mineral magnetite.

Inside a ferromagnet there are tiny regions in which all the atomic magnets point in the same direction. They are called **Weiss domains**, after the French physicist Pierre-Ernest Weiss, who did research at ETH Zurich for a long time. In an unmagnetised iron nail the domains point every which way, and their effects cancel each other out. If you stroke it with a magnet, they line up in a common direction, and the nail becomes a magnet itself.

If you heat a ferromagnet, the atoms jiggle more and more strongly. Above the **Curie temperature** the order is lost completely, and the substance is no longer ferromagnetic. For iron this limit is about 768 °C. It is named after the French physicist **Pierre Curie**, who studied this at the end of the 19th century.

Substances that quickly lose their magnetisation again after the field is switched off are called **magnetically soft**, for example soft iron in transformers. Magnetically hard substances keep a lot of magnetisation; this **remanence** makes them permanent magnets. Today the strongest permanent magnets are made of neodymium, iron and boron. They are found in headphones, electric motors and wind turbines.

Many stainless steel sinks are hardly attracted by a magnet. This is because many stainless steels have a crystal structure that is not ferromagnetic. A **compass needle** is a small permanent magnet that lines itself up with the Earth's magnetic field. Hard disks, bank cards with magnetic strips and loudspeakers also use ferromagnetic substances.

begriffe.erklaerung: Strongly magnetisable, like iron, nickel and cobalt.
Small regions in which all the atomic magnets point the same way.
The temperature above which a substance is no longer ferromagnetic.
Magnetisation that remains after the external field is switched off.
A magnet that keeps its effect for a long time.

gewusst: If you often drop a permanent magnet or heat it strongly, it can become weaker.
Even in ancient Greece people knew stones of magnetite that attract iron.
A neodymium magnet no bigger than a sugar cube can hold several kilograms.

teile.einleitung: Energy occurs in different forms, which are called forms of energy. A rolling ball has kinetic energy, a reservoir in the mountains has potential energy and an apple has chemical energy. All forms of energy are measured in the same unit, the joule.
wichtigste: Energy is measured in the unit joule.
A rolling ball has kinetic energy.
The water of a high reservoir has potential energy.
Chemical energy is stored in food.
Sunlight carries radiant energy to the Earth.
Other forms are electrical energy, heat and nuclear energy.
Forms of energy can be converted into one another.

abschnitte.text: Everything that moves has **kinetic energy**, also called energy of movement. A rolling ball, a moving car or a flying bird have it. It grows with mass and especially strongly with speed: at twice the speed it is four times as large. That is why an accident at high speed is so much more dangerous.

A body that lies high up has **potential energy**, also called energy of position. The water in a high **reservoir** in the Alps stores a great deal of it. If it is allowed to flow down into the valley, it can drive turbines and produce electricity. A stretched spring or a drawn bow also stores energy; this is called elastic energy.

**Food**, wood, petrol and batteries contain **chemical energy**. It is stored in the bonds between atoms and is released in chemical reactions, for example when burning or during digestion. On food packaging the energy content is given in kilojoules. A litre of petrol contains about 32 million joules.

The Sun sends **radiant energy** to the Earth in the form of light and heat radiation. Plants use it in photosynthesis, and solar cells turn it into electricity. **Thermal energy** is the energy of the disordered movement of the smallest particles. The hotter an object is, the faster its particles jiggle.

**Electrical energy** is especially practical, because it can be carried a long way through cables and easily converted into other forms. **Nuclear energy** is contained in atomic nuclei and is released in nuclear power stations or in the Sun. In Switzerland, for example, there are the nuclear power stations of Gösgen and Leibstadt. For electricity the unit kilowatt-hour is often used, which is 3.6 million joules.

All forms of energy are measured in **joules** (J), named after the English physicist James Prescott Joule. One joule is roughly the energy you need to lift a 100-gram bar of chocolate one metre. Because that is very little, kilojoules (1000 J) or megajoules (a million J) are often used. In the past the calorie was also common; it equals about 4.2 joules.

begriffe.erklaerung: The unit in which all forms of energy are measured.
Another word for energy of movement.
Another word for energy of position.
Energy carried by light and other radiation.
Energy stored in substances and released in reactions.

gewusst: In theory, the chemical energy in an apple would be enough to lift it more than a hundred kilometres high.
Without the radiant energy of the Sun there would be neither wind nor rain on Earth.
One kilowatt-hour equals exactly 3.6 million joules.

teile.einleitung: Tides are the regular rise and fall of the sea level, that is ebb and flood. They are caused mainly by the pull of the Moon and to a lesser extent of the Sun. On some coasts the difference between high and low water is more than ten metres.
wichtigste: Tides are caused by the pull of the Moon and the Sun on the Earth.
The tidal effect of the Sun is about half as great as that of the Moon.
There are two tidal bulges, one on the side of the Earth facing the Moon and one on the side facing away.
Most coasts have high tide about twice a day and low tide twice.
At full moon and new moon especially strong spring tides occur, at half moon weak neap tides.
The largest tidal ranges in the world are measured in the Bay of Fundy in Canada.
The Moon always shows us the same side because tidal forces have tied its rotation to its orbit.

abschnitte.text: When the water rises, it is called the **flood tide**; when it falls, the **ebb tide**. The highest water level is called high water, the lowest low water. The difference in height between them is called the **tidal range**. Between two high waters about 12 hours and 25 minutes pass, which is why the times shift a little every day.

The Moon pulls on the Earth, but not equally strongly everywhere. On the side facing it, the pull is stronger than at the centre of the Earth, and on the side facing away it is weaker. As a result, two **tidal bulges** form on opposite sides of the Earth. The **tidal force** decreases with the cube of the distance, which is why the nearby Moon has a stronger effect than the much heavier but far more distant Sun.

At new moon and full moon, the Sun, Moon and Earth are roughly in a line. Then their forces add together, and there are especially high **spring tides**. At half moon the Sun and Moon are at right angles to the Earth, and their effects partly cancel each other out. This gives the weak **neap tides**.

How strong the tides are depends very much on the shape of the coast. In the **Bay of Fundy** on the east coast of Canada, the tidal range can be over 15 metres. In the Wadden Sea on the North Sea, a wide stretch of sea floor dries out at low tide. In the Mediterranean, on the other hand, the tides are only weak in most places, and on Lake Geneva there are practically no visible tides, because the lake is too small.

Tidal forces act everywhere in space. They have slowed the Moon's rotation so much that it always shows us the same side; this is called **tidal locking**. A moon that came too close to a planet would be torn apart by tidal forces. This minimum distance is called the **Roche limit**, and the rings of Saturn lie inside this limit.

begriffe.erklaerung: The difference in height between high water and low water.
An especially strong tide at full moon and new moon.
An especially weak tide at half moon.
The distance below which a moon would be torn apart by tidal forces.
A body in space turns so that it always shows the same side to its partner.

gewusst: The solid ground also rises and falls with the tides, in Central Europe by a few dozen centimetres, without us noticing.
In France the tidal power station on the Rance has been producing electricity from ebb and flood since 1966.
Tidal friction very slowly brakes the Earth's rotation, so over millions of years the days become longer.

teile.einleitung: A gas thermometer measures temperature with the help of a gas. It makes use of the fact that the pressure or volume of a gas changes very evenly with temperature. Gas thermometers are among the most accurate thermometers and helped to establish the kelvin scale.
wichtigste: A gas thermometer finds the temperature from the pressure or volume of a gas.
Helium and hydrogen are especially suitable.
If you heat a gas in a closed container, its pressure rises.
At double the absolute temperature, for example 600 K instead of 300 K, the pressure doubles, for example from 1 bar to 2 bar.
An ideal gas expands by about 1/273 of its volume at 0 °C for every degree of warming.
Almost all gases behave the same way here, which is why the gas thermometer is very accurate.
The kelvin scale can be determined especially directly with the gas thermometer.

abschnitte.text: A **gas thermometer** consists of a container with a gas, connected to a pressure gauge or a movable piston. When the gas gets warmer, either its **pressure** or its **volume** rises. From this change the temperature is calculated. Such devices are found mainly in research laboratories and measurement institutes, not in the living room.

In a constant-volume thermometer the gas is enclosed in a rigid container. If you heat it, the gas particles move faster and hit the walls harder, so the pressure rises. The pressure is proportional to the **absolute temperature** in kelvin. If the gas has a pressure of 1 bar at 300 K, then at 600 K it is exactly 2 bar.

**Helium** and hydrogen are best suited, because they behave almost like an ideal gas. An **ideal gas** is a simplified model in which the particles do not affect each other. Because different gases behave almost the same at low pressure, it hardly matters which one you use. This makes the gas thermometer so accurate and independent of the material.

At the beginning of the 19th century the French scientist **Joseph Louis Gay-Lussac** studied how gases behave when heated. He found that the volume of a gas at constant pressure grows with temperature. For every degree it expands by about 1/273 of its volume at 0 °C. From this came the idea that there must be a lowest possible temperature at about -273 °C.

The lowest possible temperature is called **absolute zero** and lies at -273.15 °C. The British physicist William Thomson, later Lord Kelvin, proposed a scale that starts at zero there. This **kelvin scale** is today the base unit of temperature in physics. It can be measured especially directly with the gas thermometer, because pressure and kelvin temperature grow in the same proportion.

begriffe.erklaerung: The force with which a gas presses on a surface.
A unit of temperature that starts at zero at absolute zero.
The lowest possible temperature, -273.15 °C.
A simplified model of a gas with which physicists can calculate easily.

gewusst: 0 °C equals 273.15 kelvin, and water boils at about 373 kelvin.
At absolute zero an ideal gas would have no pressure at all.
A gas thermometer with helium still works at temperatures at which almost all other substances have long since become solid.

teile.einleitung: A parachute is a large piece of fabric that opens in the air and strongly slows down a falling person or object. This makes it possible to land slowly and safely from a great height. Parachutes are used in sport, for rescue, in space travel and even on racing cars.
wichtigste: A parachute makes sure that you land slowly and safely.
It brakes through air resistance, and for that it needs a large surface.
Today a parachute is usually made of light, strong synthetic fabric such as nylon.
Leonardo da Vinci drew a parachute more than 500 years ago.
You open the parachute by pulling a handle.
Shortly after it opens, the jumper is slowed down sharply.
Dandelion seeds also fly through the air on little parachutes.

abschnitte.text: When something falls through the air, it keeps bumping into countless particles of air. This force is called **air resistance**. The larger the surface, the more air has to be pushed aside and the stronger the braking effect. An open parachute has many square metres of surface and therefore brakes so strongly that you sink only about as fast as if you jumped off a wall.

A parachute consists of the **canopy**, that is the fabric roof, many suspension lines and a harness that the person wears. The fabric is light, tear-resistant and lets almost no air through; in the past it was made of silk, today it is usually nylon. Before the jump the parachute is carefully packed into a backpack. When you pull the handle, a small pilot chute shoots out and pulls the large parachute out of its pack.

The classic **round canopy** looks like a giant mushroom cap and sinks almost straight down. Modern sport parachutes are rectangular **ram-air parachutes**, which work like a wing. With them you can steer and land almost exactly on target. A close relative is the **paraglider**, with which people glide down into the valley from many mountains in Switzerland.

Around 1485 Leonardo da Vinci drew a parachute in the shape of a pyramid made of fabric and wood. In 1797 the Frenchman André-Jacques Garnerin jumped from a balloon over Paris with a parachute. In the 20th century parachutes became important for rescuing aeroplane pilots. Since 1919 there have been parachutes that you release yourself during the fall.

Space capsules returning to Earth often land on several large parachutes. Mars probes also use parachutes to slow down in the thin Martian atmosphere. Very fast **dragster** racing cars open a braking parachute at the end of the track. Aid organisations also use parachutes to drop food and supplies into areas that are hard to reach.

begriffe.erklaerung: A braking force that arises when something moves through air.
The large fabric roof of the parachute.
The many cords between the canopy and the harness.
A second parachute for emergencies.
A steerable wing with which people glide through the air from mountains.

gewusst: In 2000 a Briton tested a replica of Leonardo's parachute, and it really worked.
Dandelion seeds have little parachutes that can carry them many kilometres.
Without a parachute a falling person reaches about 200 km/h; with an open parachute only about 20 km/h.

teile.einleitung: A spring is a technical component that changes shape under a force and then springs back into its original shape. In doing so it stores energy and releases it again. Springs are found in ballpoint pens, mattresses, cars, trampolines and every mechanical watch.
wichtigste: After being squeezed or stretched, a spring springs back into its original shape.
When it is tensioned it stores energy, called elastic energy.
According to Hooke's law, the deformation is proportional to the force.
How stiff a spring is, is given by the spring constant.
Springs are usually made of especially elastic spring steel.
Important designs are the coil spring, the leaf spring, the spiral spring and the disc spring.
If a spring is loaded too heavily, it stays permanently bent.

abschnitte.text: A **spring** is a component that changes shape under a force and returns to its old shape when let go. This property is called **elasticity**. If you squeeze a metal spring and let it go, it springs back. The work put in when tensioning it is stored as **elastic energy** and is released again when it relaxes.

In the 17th century the English natural scientist **Robert Hooke** found out that a spring stretches twice as far when the force is doubled. This **Hooke's law** is written F = D · s, where s is the extension. The **spring constant** D says how stiff the spring is; it is measured in newtons per metre. The **spring balance**, used in physics lessons to measure forces, is based on this law.

The best-known form is the **coil spring**, a wire wound in a helix, for example in a ballpoint pen. **Leaf springs** are curved steel strips found on lorries and railway wagons. **Spiral springs** are rolled up flat and drive clocks and toys. Disc springs, torsion springs in clothes pegs and gas springs on office chairs are further examples.

In cars and bikes, springs provide the **suspension**, which absorbs the jolts from bumps. In mattresses and sofas they make lying down soft. A trampoline is fixed to its frame all the way round with many springs. Door handles, staplers, mousetraps and locks also only work with springs.

A mechanical watch is driven by a wound-up **mainspring**. The tiny **balance spring** makes the balance wheel swing back and forth evenly and so sets the beat of the watch. It is often thinner than a hair. The Swiss watch industry in the Jura and in Geneva is known worldwide for such precision parts.

A spring only works within its **elastic limit**. If you pull it too far apart, it stays permanently bent and no longer returns fully. That is why springs are usually made of special **spring steel**, which is especially elastic. Frequently repeated loading can also tire a spring out and make it break.

begriffe.erklaerung: The ability of a body to return to its shape after being deformed.
A value that shows how stiff a spring is.
The deformation of a spring is proportional to the force.
Energy stored in a tensioned spring.
A measuring device that measures forces with a spring.

gewusst: Hooke first published his law as a coded letter puzzle.
A bow and a jump on a trampoline also use elastic energy, as with a spring.
The balance spring of a wristwatch swings back and forth many millions of times a year.

teile.einleitung: The Energy Strategy 2050 is Switzerland's plan for how it wants to transform its energy supply. Switzerland wants to use energy more economically, produce more renewable energy and gradually phase out nuclear energy. The trigger was the reactor accident at Fukushima in Japan in 2011.
wichtigste: The two main directions are: using energy more efficiently and expanding renewable energy.
New nuclear power stations may no longer be approved in Switzerland.
The trigger was the Fukushima reactor disaster in 2011.
The voters accepted the new Energy Act on 21 May 2017.
At the end of 2019 Mühleberg became the first nuclear power station in Switzerland to be shut down for good.
On 9 June 2024 the voters accepted the Electricity Act with about 69 per cent voting yes.
With the Climate and Innovation Act of 2023, Switzerland aims for net zero by 2050.

abschnitte.text: The **Energy Strategy 2050** is a long-term plan of the Federal Council and Parliament. It is meant to make Switzerland's energy supply secure, affordable and environmentally friendly. To do this it relies on two main directions: **energy efficiency**, that is less energy for the same result, and the expansion of **renewable energy**. It is being put into practice in several packages and laws.

In March 2011, after an earthquake and a tsunami, a severe reactor disaster occurred at the Japanese nuclear power station of **Fukushima**. After that the Federal Council decided to phase out nuclear energy gradually. Parliament drew up a new Energy Act. On 21 May 2017 the voters accepted this law in a popular vote, and it came into force in 2018.

According to the Energy Strategy, new nuclear power stations may no longer be approved. The existing plants may keep running, however, as long as they are safe. At the end of 2019 the **Mühleberg** nuclear power station in the canton of Bern became the first in Switzerland to be shut down for good. Other nuclear power stations are at Beznau, Gösgen and Leibstadt.

Switzerland's most important source of electricity has long been **hydropower**, with its reservoirs and river power stations. In addition, solar panels on roofs and façades above all, but also wind, biomass and geothermal energy, are to be expanded. On 9 June 2024 the voters accepted the **Electricity Act** with about 69 per cent voting yes; it is meant to speed up the expansion. With the Climate and Innovation Act of 2023, Switzerland has also set itself the goal of reaching **net zero** greenhouse gas emissions by 2050.

Municipalities and families also contribute to the Energy Strategy. Municipalities with an exemplary energy policy can receive the **Energy City** label. At home it helps to switch off lights and appliances, buy economical appliances and air rooms properly. Anyone who uses a bike, bus or train instead of a car also saves a lot of energy.

begriffe.erklaerung: Energy from sources that do not run out, such as sun, water and wind.
Achieving the same with less energy, for example with an LED lamp.
No more greenhouse gas is given off than is removed from the air again.
A vote in which those entitled to vote decide on a law themselves.

gewusst: Mühleberg was in operation for about 47 years before it was shut down in 2019.
Swiss voters have voted on the Energy Strategy themselves several times, because referendums were called against the laws.
For decades hydropower has supplied the largest part of Switzerland's electricity.

teile.einleitung: A colour wheel shows colours arranged in a circle so that related colours lie next to each other. Colours opposite each other are called complementary colours and form a strong contrast. Well-known colour wheels come from Isaac Newton, Johann Wolfgang von Goethe and the Swiss artist Johannes Itten.
wichtigste: A colour wheel arranges colours in a circle.
Colours opposite each other are called complementary colours.
Red lies opposite green, blue opposite orange.
Red, orange and yellow are considered warm colours.
Blue, green and violet are considered cool colours.
The Swiss Johannes Itten drew a well-known colour wheel with twelve colours.
The poet Goethe also studied a colour wheel intensively.

abschnitte.text: A **colour wheel** is a diagram in which colours are arranged in a circle like slices of a cake. Neighbouring colours blend gently into each other, such as yellow, orange and red. This shows at a glance how colours are related to each other. Painters, designers and photographers use it to find colours that go together.

Colours that lie exactly opposite each other on the wheel are called **complementary colours**. Examples are red and green, blue and orange, and yellow and violet. Side by side they shine especially strongly, because they form a great contrast. That is why red tomatoes look so bright among green leaves.

Red, orange and yellow are called **warm colours** because they remind us of fire and sun. Blue, green and violet are considered cool colours; they remind us of water, ice and shade. In pictures, warm colours seem to come closer, while cool colours seem to move back. Interior designers use this effect deliberately so that rooms feel cosy or calm.

The English physicist **Isaac Newton** split sunlight into the colours of the rainbow with a prism and arranged them in a circle in 1704 in his book on optics. In 1810 the German poet Johann Wolfgang von Goethe published his “Theory of Colours” with a colour wheel in six parts. Goethe was especially interested in how colours affect people and feelings. He did not agree with Newton's explanation, but in physics Newton's view won out.

**Johannes Itten** was born in 1888 in the canton of Bern and was a painter and art teacher. He taught at the famous Bauhaus in Germany and later in Zurich. His colour wheel has twelve colours: in the centre are the primary colours yellow, red and blue, and on the outside come the mixed colours. This colour wheel is still used in art lessons in many schools today.

begriffe.erklaerung: A colour that lies exactly opposite on the colour wheel.
A strong difference that makes things stand out clearly.
A glass body that splits white light into the colours of the rainbow.
A famous German school of art and design, founded in 1919.

gewusst: If you look at a red dot for a long time and then at a white wall, you briefly see a green spot, the complementary colour.
The colour purple does not appear in the rainbow, but on the colour wheel it closes the circle between red and violet.
Many sports teams choose complementary colours for their kits so that they stand out.

teile.einleitung: Binoculars are an optical device with which you can see faraway things enlarged using both eyes. In Switzerland they are usually called a Feldstecher. They actually consist of two small telescopes joined side by side.
wichtigste: In the marking “8 x 42”, the 8 means eight times magnification.
The 42 gives the diameter of the objective lenses in millimetres.
If you divide the objective diameter by the magnification, you get the exit pupil; for 8 x 42 this is 5.25 mm.
Binoculars with large objective lenses such as 8 x 56 are especially good for dusk.
The great advantage over a one-eyed telescope is comfortable viewing with both eyes.
Binoculars usually contain Porro prisms or roof prisms.
You can bend the binoculars in the middle to adjust them to the distance between your eyes.

abschnitte.text: **Binoculars** consist of two telescopes, one for each eye. At the front are the large lenses, the **objective lenses**, and at the back the small lenses you look through, the **eyepieces**. Because you look with both eyes, you see in three dimensions and get less tired than with a one-eyed telescope. Binoculars are used when hiking, bird-watching, hunting, at sea and in the army.

Every pair of binoculars has two numbers on it, for example “8 x 42”. The first number is the **magnification**: an ibex 800 m away looks as if it were only 100 m away. The second number is the diameter of the objective lenses in millimetres. Larger objective lenses collect more light, but also make the binoculars heavier. Binoculars that magnify more than about 10 times can hardly be held steady by hand.

If you divide the objective diameter by the magnification, you get the **exit pupil**, the bright spot of light behind the eyepiece. For 8 x 42 it is 5.25 mm, for 8 x 56 as much as 7 mm. At dusk the pupil of the eye opens wide, so you then need a large exit pupil. That is why hunters and nature watchers often take binoculars with 56 mm objective lenses in the evening.

A simple telescope made of two converging lenses shows the image upside down. That is why binoculars contain glass **prisms**, which turn the image the right way up and fold the path of the light. With **Porro prisms**, named after the Italian Ignazio Porro, the objective lenses are further apart than the eyepieces, giving the binoculars a zigzag shape. With roof prisms the tubes are straight, so the binoculars are slimmer and lighter.

First you bend the binoculars in the middle until the two images merge into one round image. With the central focusing wheel you make the image sharp. Many people see slightly differently with their left and right eyes; you compensate for this with the **dioptre adjustment** on one eyepiece. People who wear glasses can fold down the eyecups so that they see the whole image.

The first telescopes were built in the Netherlands around 1608. Soon people tried to join two telescopes together, but only prisms made handy binoculars possible. Towards the end of the 19th century the firm Carl Zeiss in Jena began building prism binoculars in large numbers. Small opera glasses for the theatre, on the other hand, work without prisms and magnify only a little.

begriffe.erklaerung: The large front lens that collects the light.
The small lens through which you look into the device.
A cut glass body that redirects light.
The bright circle of light behind the eyepiece, which shows how much light reaches the eye.

gewusst: Binoculars that magnify 10 times also magnify the shaking of your hands tenfold, which is why there are models with built-in image stabilisation.
Many binoculars are filled with nitrogen so that they do not mist up inside in the cold.
The word Feldstecher is used mainly in Switzerland and southern Germany.

teile.einleitung: Free fall is a movement in which a body falls downwards only under the influence of gravity. Without air resistance all objects fall equally fast, a feather just like a hammer. In doing so they get faster by about 9.81 metres per second every second.
wichtigste: In free fall only gravity acts on the body.
Without air resistance all objects fall equally fast.
On Earth the acceleration due to gravity is about 9.81 m/s².
After one second of falling, a body is moving at about 35 km/h and has covered just under 5 metres.
Galileo Galilei studied falling with experiments around 1600.
In everyday life the air slows down light and broad things more strongly.
On the Moon in 1971 an astronaut dropped a hammer and a feather at the same time.

abschnitte.text: If you let go of an object, the Earth's **gravity** pulls it downwards. If no other force acts, it is called **free fall**. The body keeps getting faster; it is **accelerated**. In everyday life, however, the air almost always slows it down a little too.

For a long time people believed that heavy things fall faster than light ones; Aristotle taught this. Around 1600 **Galileo Galilei** showed with balls on slopes that this is not true. Without **air resistance** all objects fall equally fast, no matter how heavy they are. In an airless tube a feather and a coin therefore fall exactly equally fast.

On Earth the speed increases by about 9.81 metres per second every second; this is the **acceleration due to gravity** g. After one second a falling stone is therefore moving at about 35 km/h, after two seconds at about 70 km/h. The distance fallen grows with the square of the time: after 1 second about 5 metres, after 2 seconds about 20 metres. On the Moon the acceleration due to gravity is only about a sixth as large.

In real life the air slows down falling bodies, and the faster they fall, the more strongly it does so. At some point gravity and **air resistance** are equal, and the body carries on falling at a constant speed. A skydiver without an open parachute reaches about 200 km/h in this way. With an open **parachute** they sink at only about 20 km/h.

In 1971, during the **Apollo 15** mission, the astronaut David Scott dropped a hammer and a falcon feather at the same time on the Moon. Because there is no air there, both reached the ground at the same time. In the Bremen **drop tower**, weightlessness is studied by letting capsules fall freely over about 110 metres. In 2012 Felix Baumgartner jumped from a height of about 39 kilometres and was faster than sound during the fall.

On a **drop tower** ride at an amusement park you feel almost weightless for a short time. Astronauts in the ISS space station also float because they are constantly falling around the Earth together with the station. When you jump off the diving tower at the swimming pool, you also experience a short free fall. From a height of 10 metres it lasts only about 1.4 seconds.

begriffe.erklaerung: The force with which the Earth pulls all bodies.
How quickly a falling body gets faster; on Earth about 9.81 m/s².
The slowing force of the air on moving bodies.
A state in which you feel no weight, for example in free fall.

gewusst: Astronauts in the ISS do not float because there is no gravity there, but because they are constantly in free fall.
The story that Galileo dropped balls from the Leaning Tower of Pisa is probably only a legend.
Thanks to air resistance, a raindrop falls at only about 20 to 30 km/h.

teile.einleitung: An electrical conductor is a substance through which electric current can flow easily. Metals such as copper or aluminium are the best-known conductors. Their opposites are insulators such as plastic, glass or porcelain, which hardly let current through.
wichtigste: An electrical conductor lets current flow through it easily.
Copper is one of the best and most widely used conductors.
Plastic, glass and porcelain are good insulators.
Graphite is a non-metal that still conducts electricity.
Tap water conducts electricity, so you must never touch appliances with wet hands.
Substances such as silicon that lie between conductors and insulators are called semiconductors.
In metals, freely moving electrons carry the current.

abschnitte.text: An **electrical conductor** is a material with many freely moving charge carriers. In metals these are **free electrons**, which can move between the atoms like a gas. If a voltage is applied, they travel through the material and a current flows. How well a substance conducts is given by its electrical conductivity.

The best metallic conductor is **silver**, followed closely by **copper**. Because copper is much cheaper, the inside of almost all cables is made of it.
