For high-voltage power lines aluminium is often used because it is light. **Graphite**, a form of carbon, also conducts electricity even though it is not a metal; you find it in pencil leads, for example.

An **insulator** has almost no free charge carriers and therefore hardly lets any current through. Good insulators are plastic, rubber, glass, porcelain and dry wood. That is why cables are covered in plastic. On high-voltage pylons the lines hang from **insulators**, which are traditionally often made of porcelain or glass.

Completely pure water conducts electricity only very poorly. Tap water, however, contains dissolved salts, that is **ions**, and therefore conducts electricity. The human body is also a conductor because it contains a lot of salty fluid. That is why you must never touch electrical appliances with wet hands and never use a hairdryer in the bath.

Between conductors and insulators lie the **semiconductors**; the most important example is **silicon**. Their conductivity can be changed on purpose, for example by heat, light or by adding foreign atoms. Semiconductors are used to build computer chips, light-emitting diodes and solar cells. Without them there would be no mobile phones and no computers.

Metals conduct less well when they get warm, because the atoms vibrate more strongly and slow the electrons down. Some substances lose their resistance completely at very low temperatures; they become **superconductors**. Superconducting magnets are used, for example, in the LHC particle accelerator at CERN near Geneva. There they are cooled to about minus 271 degrees Celsius.

begriffe.erklaerung: Shows how well a substance conducts electric current.
A substance that conducts current hardly or not at all.
A substance such as silicon that conducts current moderately, depending on conditions.
Electrons in metals that are not firmly bound to one atom.
An electrically charged atom or molecule.

gewusst: Silver conducts electricity slightly better than copper, but it is far too expensive for cables.
With a thickly drawn pencil line you can close a small electric circuit.
Even air becomes a conductor when the voltage is very high; that is how lightning happens.

teile.einleitung: A spring combination is formed when you use two or more springs together. You can arrange them side by side, that is in parallel, or one after the other, that is in series. Depending on the arrangement, the whole system becomes stiffer or softer than a single spring.
wichtigste: The spring constant says how stiff a spring is and is given in newtons per metre (N/m).
In a parallel arrangement you add up the spring constants; for example, 200 N/m plus 300 N/m gives 500 N/m.
In a series arrangement the system becomes softer: 200 N/m and 300 N/m become only 120 N/m.
Two identical springs in series together have only half the spring constant of a single spring.
In a series arrangement each spring carries the full force; in a parallel arrangement the springs share the force.
If you hang a second identical spring in parallel, a mass oscillates faster; the period becomes about 0.71 times as long.

abschnitte.text: A single spring stretches by a certain distance when you pull on it. This is described by **Hooke's law**: force equals spring constant times extension, in short F = D · s. It is named after the English researcher Robert Hooke, who lived in the 17th century. If you connect several springs, the whole **spring combination** behaves like a single new spring with its own total spring constant.

In a **parallel arrangement** the springs hang side by side and carry the load together. Each spring stretches by the same amount, but each carries only part of the force. Two identical springs therefore each carry half the load. The total spring constant is the sum of the individual values, so the system becomes stiffer. In this way 200 N/m and 300 N/m become 500 N/m.

In a **series arrangement** one spring hangs below the other. Each spring must carry the full force, and their extensions add up. That is why the system becomes softer. You calculate with the reciprocals: 1 divided by D total equals 1 divided by D1 plus 1 divided by D2. If springs with 100 N/m and 400 N/m hang in series and carry 8 N, the first stretches by 8 cm and the second by 2 cm, together by 10 cm.

You can also combine both kinds. Two parallel springs of 100 N/m each act together like one spring of 200 N/m. If you then hang another spring of 200 N/m in series below them, the result is a **total spring constant** of 100 N/m. In this way you calculate step by step, much as with resistors in a circuit, only with the rules swapped round.

Spring combinations are found wherever something needs cushioning. A **mattress** contains many springs side by side that carry the weight together. A trampoline also has many parallel springs all the way round. In cars and bikes, springs work together in the suspension so that the ride stays comfortable on bumpy roads. Engineers calculate such combinations so that vehicles are neither too stiff nor too soft.

A mass on a spring oscillates up and down; it is a **spring pendulum**. The stiffer the spring combination, the faster the mass oscillates. If you double the spring constant with a second parallel spring, the period becomes about 0.71 times as long, because it depends on the square root of the spring constant. If you connect the springs in series, on the other hand, the mass oscillates more slowly.

begriffe.erklaerung: A number that shows how stiff a spring is, measured in newtons per metre.
Springs hang side by side and share the load.
Springs hang one after the other, and each carries the whole load.
The rule that the extension of a spring grows evenly with the force.

gewusst: For springs, exactly the opposite rules of calculation apply as for electrical resistors.
You can also think of a long rubber band as many small springs in series, which is why a long band is softer than a short one.
If you cut a spring in half, each half becomes twice as stiff as the whole spring.

teile.einleitung: A block and tackle is a simple machine made of pulleys and a rope with which you can lift heavy loads with little force. The more sections of rope carry the load, the less force you need. But in return you have to pull correspondingly more rope.
wichtigste: A block and tackle consists of fixed and movable pulleys and a rope.
The load is shared among several supporting sections of rope.
With 4 supporting sections of rope, without friction you need only a quarter of the force.
In return you have to pull four times as much rope as the load rises.
The work stays the same: you save force, but not work.
In German the block and tackle gets its name from the pulley housings, which are called “bottles”.
Blocks and tackles are found on cranes, on sailing ships and in garages.

abschnitte.text: A **block and tackle** consists of several pulleys and a rope. The **fixed pulleys** are attached at the top, for example to a beam, and do not move. The **movable pulleys** hang at the bottom on the load and move up with it. Several pulleys often sit together in a housing called a **block**. In German this housing is called a bottle, which gives the device its German name.

The rope runs back and forth several times between the upper and lower pulleys. As a result, the load hangs on several **supporting sections of rope**, which share the weight. If a crate of 90 kilograms hangs on 3 sections of rope, you need roughly as much force as for 30 kilograms. With 3 movable pulleys in the lower block there are 6 supporting sections. A load of 1200 newtons then needs a pulling force of only 200 newtons without friction.

What you save in force, you have to make up in distance. With 4 supporting sections of rope you pull 4 metres of rope, and the load rises only 1 metre. If a load on 5 sections of rope is to rise 2 metres, you have to pull 10 metres of rope. This is called the **golden rule of mechanics**: force times distance stays the same. So you save force, but not work.

In reality you need a little more force than calculated. The **friction** in the pulleys and the weight of the lower pulleys are added. In a **compound pulley system**, the movable pulleys hang one above the other, and each halves the force once more. With 3 movable pulleys you need only an eighth of the load there. With the gravitational field strength g = 10 N/kg, you pull about 200 newtons for a crate of 80 kilograms on 4 sections of rope.

abschnitte.titel: Blocks and tackles in everyday life
abschnitte.text: Large **cranes** on building sites and in ports work with blocks and tackles. On a **sailing ship** they are used to haul up the heavy sails and tighten the lines. In the garage you can easily pull a bike up to the ceiling with a small block and tackle. Mountain rescuers, climbers and fire brigades also use systems made of ropes and karabiners. In workshops they are used to lift heavy engines and machine parts.

The ancient Greeks and Romans already knew pulleys and blocks and tackles. The Greek scholar **Archimedes** is said to have moved a loaded ship on his own with a block and tackle. The Romans built treadwheel cranes, in which workers walked inside a large wheel and lifted heavy stones through blocks and tackles. Without such lifting machines many temples, castles and cathedrals would not have been possible. In the Middle Ages, too, they were used to build large churches and castles.

begriffe.erklaerung: A pulley that is attached in one place and changes the direction of pull.
A pulley that moves with the load and saves force.
What you save in force, you must cover extra in distance.
The unit of force, named after Isaac Newton.
A force that slows down movements when things rub against each other.

gewusst: A single fixed pulley saves no force; it only changes the direction in which you have to pull.
The pulley, together with the lever, the inclined plane, the wedge and the screw, is one of the simple machines.
On old sailing ships there were hundreds of pulleys in the rigging.

teile.einleitung: Renewable energy comes from sources that keep renewing themselves or are practically inexhaustible. These include solar energy, hydropower, wind energy, biomass and geothermal energy. They are important for slowing down climate change, because they give off hardly any carbon dioxide.
wichtigste: Renewable energy renews itself again and again or is practically inexhaustible.
Solar energy is a renewable source of energy.
Renewable energy also includes water, wind, biomass and geothermal heat.
Oil, natural gas and coal, on the other hand, are not renewable.
In Switzerland hydropower is the most important renewable source of electricity.
Sun and wind do not always supply the same amount of energy, so storage is needed.
Renewable energy helps to reduce emissions of carbon dioxide.

abschnitte.text: The Sun supplies huge amounts of energy, and it will shine for billions of years yet. **Photovoltaic** systems turn sunlight directly into electricity. **Solar collectors** on roofs heat water for showers and heating. In recent years a great many solar panels have been built in Switzerland, including on dams and noise barriers.

**Hydropower** is the most important source of electricity in Switzerland; it supplies about sixty per cent of the electricity produced in the country. There are run-of-river power stations on rivers such as the Rhine and storage power stations with reservoirs in the Alps. **Pumped-storage power stations** such as Nant de Drance in Valais pump water uphill when there is too much electricity. When needed, they let it flow down again and produce electricity.

**Wind turbines** use the wind; so far there are rather few in Switzerland, for example on Mont Crosin in the Bernese Jura. **Biomass** is energy from wood, plant remains, slurry or green waste, from which heat or biogas is obtained. **Geothermal energy** uses heat from inside the Earth, for example with ground probes for heat pumps. The waste heat from waste incineration plants is also often used for district heating.

**Fossil fuels** such as oil, natural gas and coal formed from plants and animals that lived millions of years ago. They do not renew themselves within human timescales and will be used up at some point. When burned, they release **carbon dioxide**, which warms the Earth. Uranium for nuclear power stations is not renewable either.

Renewable energy causes hardly any greenhouse gases while running and makes a country less dependent on imports. However, the Sun does not shine at night and the wind does not always blow. That is why **storage** such as batteries and pumped-storage plants is needed, as well as well-developed power grids. The impact on the landscape, for example from reservoirs or wind turbines, is also often debated.

With the **Energy Strategy 2050**, Switzerland wants to reduce energy consumption and use more renewable energy. In 2017 the voters decided that no new nuclear power stations may be built. By 2050 Switzerland is to give off no more greenhouse gases on balance. Everyone can help, for example by saving energy or cycling.

begriffe.erklaerung: Technology that uses solar cells to turn sunlight directly into electricity.
Plant and animal material from which energy is obtained.
A power station that pumps water uphill in order to store energy.
Coal, oil and natural gas from living things of prehistoric times.
A gas such as carbon dioxide that holds heat in the atmosphere.

gewusst: Hydropower and wind power actually come from the Sun too, because it drives the water cycle and the winds.
The Nant de Drance pumped-storage power station lies in a huge cavern deep in the rock.
Centuries ago people were already using renewable energy with watermills and windmills.

teile.einleitung: Speed shows how fast something moves, that is what distance it covers in a certain time. In everyday life it is usually measured in kilometres per hour, in physics in metres per second. The cheetah is the fastest land animal, and nothing is faster than light.
wichtigste: Speed tells you what distance something covers in a certain time.
Average speed is calculated as distance divided by time.
The speedometer in a car shows the speed in kilometres per hour.
10 m/s is 36 km/h; you multiply by 3.6.
In Switzerland the limit in built-up areas is usually 50 km/h, and on motorways at most 120 km/h.
The cheetah is the fastest animal on land.
Light travels through a vacuum at about 300,000 km/s.
In uniform motion the speed always stays the same.

abschnitte.text: **Speed** v shows how much distance is covered in a certain time. You calculate the **average speed** with the formula v = s / t, that is distance divided by time. If a train travels 240 km in 2 hours, its average speed is 120 km/h. If Lea runs 100 metres in 20 seconds and Tim in 25 seconds, Lea is faster, because she needs less time for the same distance.

In everyday life speed is measured in **kilometres per hour** (km/h), which is also what the **speedometer** in a car shows. In physics **metres per second** (m/s) are used. To convert from m/s to km/h, you multiply by 3.6, so 10 m/s is exactly 36 km/h. Ships and aeroplanes often measure their speed in knots.

If the speed always stays the same, it is called **uniform motion**. Then the distance grows evenly with time. A bike that travels 15 km in one hour gets 30 km in 2 hours. A cyclist at 18 km/h covers 6 km in 20 minutes, that is a third of an hour.

The **cheetah** is the fastest land animal and can reach about 100 km/h for a short time. The peregrine falcon even gets faster than 300 km/h in a dive. The fastest man, Usain Bolt, ran the 100 metres in 9.58 seconds in 2009, which is almost 38 km/h on average. A snail, on the other hand, manages only a few metres per hour.

In Switzerland there are fixed **speed limits**: usually 50 km/h in built-up areas, 80 km/h outside them, 100 km/h on expressways and 120 km/h on motorways. In many residential areas there are **30 km/h zones** and shared zones with 20 km/h. Speed limits protect lives, because at higher speeds the braking distance becomes much longer. Anyone who drives too fast gets a fine or even loses their driving licence.

Sound travels through the air at about 340 m/s, which is about 1200 km/h. **Light** is much faster still: in a vacuum it covers about 300,000 kilometres per second. In one second it could travel more than seven times around the Earth. According to Albert Einstein's **theory of relativity**, nothing can be faster than light.

begriffe.erklaerung: The total distance divided by the total time.
A device in a vehicle that shows the speed.
Movement at a speed that always stays the same.
The highest speed there is, about 300,000 km/s.
A unit of speed in shipping and aviation.

gewusst: Light from the Sun takes about 8 minutes to reach the Earth.
Even when you sit still, you are racing around the Sun with the Earth at about 30 km per second.
Passenger trains travel through the Gotthard Base Tunnel at up to 200 km/h.

teile.einleitung: A bell is a sounding body, usually made of metal, that produces a loud, long-ringing note when struck. Bells ring in church towers, hang round the necks of cows and ring at the front door. In Switzerland they are part of many customs and of everyday life on the Alpine pastures.
wichtigste: Bells are usually made of metal, large church bells of bronze.
Inside, the clapper strikes the wall of the bell.
The largest bell sounds the lowest.
If you hold a bell with your hand, its sound quickly gets quieter.
Cows on the Alpine pastures wear bells so that they can be heard and found.
In Switzerland a large cowbell made of forged sheet metal is called a Treichel.
In the Chalandamarz custom in the Engadine, children go through the village with bells to drive away the winter.

abschnitte.text: A bell has the shape of an upside-down cup. Inside hangs the **clapper**, a heavy beater that strikes the wall of the bell when it swings. At the top the bell is hung by its **crown**, and at the bottom the rim is thickest. Where the clapper strikes, the rim is called the sound bow.

When struck, the whole metal starts to **vibrate**, and this vibration makes the air ring. A bell rings on for a long time because it is only very weakly damped. If you hold it with your hand, the sound quickly gets quieter. The larger and heavier a bell is, the lower its note.

Large church bells are cast from **bell bronze**, a mixture of about four parts copper and one part tin. To do this, the bell founder builds a mould out of clay and pours the liquid metal into it. After cooling, the bell is dug out, cleaned and tested. In Aarau, the Rüetschi bell foundry is a very old bell foundry in Switzerland.

On the **Alpine pastures** cows wear bells so that they can be heard and found in fog or in the forest. A **Treichel** is a large cowbell made of forged and bent sheet metal, whereas a cast bell is often called a **Schelle**. The cattle wear splendid Treicheln with decorated leather straps when they are driven up to the summer pastures. Treichler groups also parade through the villages with large Treicheln at festivals.

On 1 March children in the Engadine and other parts of the Grisons celebrate **Chalandamarz**. They go through the village with cowbells and Treicheln, sing and so symbolically drive away the winter. Church bells ring for services, weddings, on holidays and to tell the hour. On the evening of 1 August, bells ring in many Swiss municipalities for the national holiday.

begriffe.erklaerung: The beater inside the bell that strikes the wall.
A large cowbell made of forged sheet metal.
A mixture of copper and tin from which church bells are cast.
A spring custom in the Engadine on 1 March.

gewusst: The Tsar Bell in Moscow is the largest bell in the world, but it has never rung, because a piece broke off it.
A bell does not sound with just one note, but with many partial tones at the same time.
The doorbell at the front door is also a bell, even though today it usually rings electrically.

teile.einleitung: The cheetah is a slender big cat from Africa and Asia and the fastest land animal in the world. For a short sprint it reaches over 90 kilometres per hour. Its body is built like a racing car: light, narrow and designed entirely for speed.
wichtigste: The cheetah is the fastest land animal on Earth.
Its body is slender, with long legs and a long tail.
Unlike a house cat, it cannot fully pull in its claws.
It eats meat and hunts mainly smaller antelopes such as gazelles.
Before it starts running, it creeps as close as possible to its prey.
Most wild cheetahs today live in Africa south of the Sahara.
In Asia there are only a few wild cheetahs left, in Iran.
The cheetah is considered threatened because its habitat keeps getting smaller.

abschnitte.text: The cheetah has yellowish fur with many small, round, black **spots**. Typical are two black stripes that run like tear tracks from the eyes to the mouth. An adult weighs about 30 to 70 kilograms, much less than a leopard or a lion. The head is small, the chest deep and the back very flexible.

When sprinting, the cheetah stretches and bends its **spine** like a spring, which makes its strides especially long. Its half-extended **claws** grip the ground like the spikes of a running shoe. The long tail acts as a rudder when it changes direction quickly and helps it keep its balance. Large nostrils and powerful lungs supply plenty of oxygen. Because the sprint costs an enormous amount of energy, it can only keep up the speed for a few hundred metres.

Cheetahs live in open **savannahs**, grassland and semi-deserts, where they can see far and run freely. Most of them today live in countries such as Namibia, Botswana, Kenya and Tanzania. In the past cheetahs were also found in large parts of Asia as far as India. Today only very few survive in Asia, in **Iran**. In India, cheetahs from Africa have been reintroduced in a national park since 2022.

The cheetah eats only meat; it is a **carnivore**. It prefers to hunt during the day, usually in the morning or late afternoon. First it creeps up crouching, then it starts a short, lightning-fast sprint. It brings its prey down with a swipe of its paw. After the hunt it is so exhausted that it often has to catch its breath for a while before it can eat.

Females usually live alone and raise their young without help. Young cheetahs have a long, pale mane on their backs that camouflages them well in tall grass. Males, often brothers, sometimes live together in small groups. Cheetahs cannot roar like a lion; they purr and make chirping sounds. Lions and hyenas often steal their prey, because the cheetah is too lightly built for a fight.

The cheetah is classed as **vulnerable** by the World Conservation Union, IUCN. Its habitat is being cut up by fields, roads and settlements. Some farmers kill cheetahs because they fear for their goats and sheep. Conservation projects, for example, use guard dogs so that farmers and cheetahs can live side by side better. In Switzerland you can only see cheetahs in zoos.

begriffe.erklaerung: A cat that hunts other animals, for example the lion, tiger or cheetah.
A wide grassland with only a few trees, mainly in Africa.
A very short, very fast run with full power.
The term for an animal species that could die out in the future if it is not protected.

gewusst: A cheetah accelerates almost as fast as a sports car in a few seconds.
With their pale back mane, young cheetahs look like a small, fierce honey badger, which is meant to scare off enemies.
Cheetahs purr like house cats, but they cannot roar.

teile.einleitung: Electromagnetic waves are waves of electric and magnetic fields that travel at the speed of light. Light, radio waves, mobile phone signals, X-rays and microwaves all belong to them. They need no medium and even travel through empty space.
wichtigste: Electromagnetic waves travel through a vacuum at about 300,000 km/s.
The electric and magnetic fields are at right angles to each other and to the direction of travel.
Unlike sound, they need no medium and can also pass through a vacuum.
James Clerk Maxwell predicted their existence with his equations.
Heinrich Hertz proved them by experiment at the end of the 1880s.
Gamma radiation has the highest frequency, radio waves the lowest.
The Poynting vector gives the direction and strength of the flow of energy.

abschnitte.text: An **electromagnetic wave** consists of an electric field and a magnetic field that create each other. When one field changes, the other is created, and so the wave travels on. Both fields vibrate at right angles to each other and to the direction of travel; this is called a **transverse wave**. In a vacuum it always has the same speed, about 300,000 km per second.

Electromagnetic waves differ in their **wavelength** and frequency. Arranged by increasing frequency, they form the **electromagnetic spectrum**: radio waves, microwaves, infrared, visible light, ultraviolet, X-rays and gamma radiation. Visible light is only a tiny part of it. The higher the frequency, the more energy the radiation carries.

In the 1860s the Scottish physicist **James Clerk Maxwell** brought electricity and magnetism together in his famous equations. From them it followed that there must be waves that move at the speed of light, and that light itself is such a wave. From 1886 the German physicist **Heinrich Hertz** was the first to produce and receive such waves in the laboratory, in Karlsruhe. The unit of frequency, the hertz, is named after him.

Radio waves are sent and received by **aerials**. A simple dipole aerial is about half as long as the wavelength it is tuned to. Wavelength is calculated as the speed of light divided by frequency. A mobile phone signal at 900 MHz thus has a wavelength of about 33 cm. Radio, television, wifi, GPS and mobile phones all work with electromagnetic waves.

Electromagnetic waves carry energy; that is how sunlight warms us across 150 million kilometres. The **Poynting vector** describes in which direction and how strongly this energy flows. Ultraviolet radiation can cause sunburn, and X-rays pass through the body and make bones visible. Microwaves heat food by setting water molecules in motion.

begriffe.erklaerung: The distance between two crests of a wave.
The number of vibrations per second, measured in hertz.
A space that contains almost no particles, like outer space.
A wave that vibrates across the direction of travel.
The ordered range of all wavelengths from radio waves to gamma radiation.

gewusst: Light from the Sun takes about eight minutes to reach the Earth.
With radio telescopes, researchers receive electromagnetic waves from galaxies that are billions of light years away.
The heat you feel in front of a fire is also electromagnetic radiation, namely infrared.

teile.einleitung: An emission spectrum is the colourful pattern of light that a glowing substance gives off when you split its light into the individual colours. Every chemical element has its very own lines, like a fingerprint. This lets you find out what a star is made of without ever travelling there.
wichtigste: An emission spectrum shows which wavelengths a glowing substance gives off.
Glowing gases of low density give off a line spectrum.
An emission line forms when an electron moves to a lower energy level and gives off a photon.
Every element has its own typical pattern of lines.
Strontium colours fireworks bright red, sodium glows yellow.
In 1860 Bunsen and Kirchhoff discovered the element caesium using spectral analysis.
Helium was first discovered in 1868 in the spectrum of the Sun.

abschnitte.text: A **spectrum** forms when you split light into its colours with a prism or a grating. Glowing solid bodies such as the filament of a light bulb give off a **continuous spectrum**, that is all colours without gaps. Glowing gases of low density, on the other hand, give off only individual colours. You then see bright lines on a dark background, a **line spectrum**.

The electrons in an atom can only occupy certain **energy levels**. When an atom is excited by heat or electric current, an electron jumps to a higher level. When it falls back, it gives off the difference in energy as a **photon**, that is a particle of light. Because the energy levels are different for each element, very particular colours are produced.

Hydrogen is the simplest atom and has a particularly clear spectrum. The lines in the visible range belong to the **Balmer series**, in which the electron falls back to the second level. The transition from n = 4 to n = 2 produces blue-green light with a wavelength of about 486 nm. If the electron falls all the way to the lowest level, the Lyman series is produced in the **ultraviolet**, which we cannot see.

In 1859 and 1860 Robert Bunsen and Gustav Kirchhoff developed **spectral analysis** in Heidelberg. With it, in 1860, they discovered the element **caesium** from new blue lines; its name comes from the Latin word for sky blue. In 1868 an unknown yellow line was found in the light of the Sun and recognised as a new element. It was named **helium** after the Greek word for sun and was only found on Earth years later.

The colours of **fireworks** come from emission spectra: strontium glows red, sodium yellow, barium green and copper blue-green. A tube filled with neon glows red-orange, because neon's strongest lines lie in the red range. Yellow street lamps with sodium vapour glow in almost only one colour. At school you can use the flame test to identify salts in a gas flame.

begriffe.erklaerung: Splitting light into its individual colours or wavelengths.
A spectrum made of individual bright lines instead of an unbroken band of colour.
A tiny particle or packet of light.
A particular energy step on which an electron in an atom can be found.
A method of finding out what a substance is made of from its spectrum.

gewusst: The yellow light of sodium is so typical that even a crumb of table salt turns a gas flame yellow.
From shifted spectral lines, astronomers can tell whether a galaxy is moving away from us or towards us.
The northern lights glow green and red because oxygen atoms high in the atmosphere give off particular lines.

teile.einleitung: An energy carrier is a substance or medium in which energy is stored that we can use. These include wood, oil, natural gas, coal, uranium and hydrogen, but also electric current. Without energy carriers there would be no warm flats, no moving trains and no glowing screens.
wichtigste: An energy carrier is a substance or medium that stores energy.
Oil, natural gas and coal are fossil energy carriers.
Oil and natural gas formed mainly from dead marine plankton.
Electric current is a secondary energy carrier, because it is obtained from other energy carriers.
Biogas consists mainly of methane.
When hydrogen is burned, water is produced.
In 2017 Swiss voters accepted the new Energy Act for the Energy Strategy 2050.

abschnitte.text: An **energy carrier** stores energy that can be released when needed. Wood or petrol contains chemical energy, which is released as heat when burned. The water of a reservoir contains potential energy, uranium contains nuclear energy. Energy carriers can be stored, transported and then converted into heat, movement or electricity. You cannot see the energy itself; you only see the substance that carries it.

Experts distinguish between **primary energy carriers** and **secondary energy carriers**. Primary energy carriers occur in nature, for example coal, crude oil, natural gas, wood, wind or sunlight. Secondary energy carriers are made from them, such as petrol from crude oil or **electricity** from hydropower. Pellets and hydrogen are also secondary energy carriers. With every conversion, part of the energy is lost as heat.

Oil, natural gas and coal are called **fossil energy carriers** because they formed from the remains of living things. Oil and natural gas formed mainly from dead **marine plankton**, which sank to the sea floor millions of years ago. Coal formed from huge swamp forests. When burned, they release carbon dioxide, which makes climate change worse. In addition, their reserves are limited and do not grow back within human timescales.

**Renewable** energy carriers grow back or are available again and again. They include hydropower, sun, wind, geothermal heat and **biomass** such as wood. In a pellet heating system, pressed wood shavings are burned. Biogas is produced when bacteria break down slurry or green waste, and it consists mainly of methane. Hydrogen is particularly clean, because burning it produces only water.

Switzerland has hardly any fossil energy carriers of its own and imports oil and natural gas. For years most electricity has come from **hydropower**, at about 60 per cent, and from nuclear power, at about a third. In 2017 the voters accepted the new Energy Act for the **Energy Strategy 2050**. It provides for no new nuclear power stations to be built and for renewable energy to be promoted. The Mühleberg nuclear power station in the canton of Bern was shut down in 2019.

begriffe.erklaerung: A substance or medium in which usable energy is stored.
Formed from the remains of living things that lived millions of years ago.
An energy carrier made from another one, for example electricity.
Plant or animal material that serves as a source of energy.
A flammable gas, the main component of natural gas and biogas.

gewusst: The energy in coal, oil and wood originally comes from the Sun, which made plants and plankton grow.
In Switzerland there are farms that produce biogas from slurry and then electricity and heat from it.
Hydrogen is the most common element in the universe, but on Earth it occurs almost only in compounds such as water.

teile.einleitung: A residual current circuit breaker is a small device in the fuse box that protects people from dangerous electric shocks. In Switzerland it is usually called an FI switch for short. It switches off the electricity in a flash as soon as current takes a wrong path anywhere.
wichtigste: An RCD constantly compares the current flowing out with the current flowing back.
A fault current is current that flows to earth along a wrong path, for example through a person.
To protect people, an RCD typically trips at 30 milliamperes, which is 0.03 amperes.
It switches off in a fraction of a second.
It is especially important in the bathroom and outdoors, where water increases the danger.
You should use the test button regularly to check that it still works.

abschnitte.text: The **residual current circuit breaker**, or RCD, sits in the distribution board of a house, often next to the normal fuses. It monitors one or more circuits, for example all the sockets in a room. Unlike a fuse, it does not protect the wires from overload, but protects people directly. That is why it is sometimes also called a personal protection switch.

Normally current flows to the appliance through one wire and back through another with exactly the same strength. The RCD measures both currents with a **summation current transformer**, a ring with a coil. If both currents are equal, nothing happens. If something is missing on the way back, a **fault current** has arisen somewhere. Then the switch trips and cuts off the circuit.

Even small currents through the body can be dangerous, especially for the heart. From about 50 milliamperes, ventricular fibrillation can occur, which is life-threatening. That is why an RCD for personal protection trips at just 30 **milliamperes**, which is 0.03 amperes. It reacts in a fraction of a second, much faster than the heart can be harmed.

In the **bathroom**, in the kitchen and outdoors, the danger of an electric shock is higher. Wet skin conducts electricity better, and you often stand on damp ground. If, for example, a hairdryer falls into the water or a cable is damaged while mowing the lawn, the RCD switches off. In Switzerland the installation regulations now require RCDs in many circuits, especially for sockets.

Every RCD has a **test button**, usually marked T. When you press it, a small fault current is created artificially, and the switch must trip immediately. Experts recommend pressing the button regularly, about twice a year. Afterwards you push the lever back up, and the electricity is back.

If the RCD keeps tripping, an appliance is usually faulty or has become damp. You then unplug everything and switch the appliances back on one after the other to find the fault. A broken appliance should no longer be used. Work on the electrical installation may only be carried out by experts.

begriffe.erklaerung: Current that flows to earth along a wrong path instead of back through the cable.
A thousandth of an ampere, a very small current.
A protective device that protects wires from too great a current.
Connecting electrical parts to the earth so that fault currents can flow away safely.

gewusst: An RCD can detect a difference of just a few thousandths of an ampere between the outward and return paths.
An RCD alone does not protect against short circuits; for that you also need the normal fuse.
There are also plug-in RCDs, which you put between the socket and the cable for garden tools.

teile.einleitung: A spring balance is a device with which you can measure forces. It contains a coil spring that stretches more the greater the force. You read the force directly in newtons on a scale.
wichtigste: A spring balance measures forces with the help of a spring.
It is based on Hooke's law.
In the elastic range, twice the force causes twice the extension.
The spring constant shows how stiff a spring is.
For large forces a stiff spring with a large spring constant is used.
If you stretch a spring too far, it stays permanently deformed.
When a body hangs on it at rest, the spring force and the weight are equal.

abschnitte.text: A **spring balance**, also called a dynamometer or newton meter, usually consists of a transparent tube with a coil spring inside. At the top it has a ring to hold it, at the bottom a hook. When you pull on the hook, the spring stretches and a pointer moves along a scale. The force is shown in the unit **newton**, abbreviated N.

The spring balance is based on **Hooke's law**, named after the English researcher Robert Hooke from the 17th century. It says that the extension of a spring is proportional to the force. If the force is doubled, the extension is also doubled. As a formula it is written F = D · s, where F is the force, D the spring constant and s the extension.

The **spring constant** D says how much force you need for a certain distance. If a force of 10 N stretches a spring by 5 cm, the spring constant is 2 N/cm. If a spring has a spring constant of 50 N/m, 10 N stretches it by 0.2 m, that is 20 cm. For large forces you use a stiff spring with a large spring constant, for small forces a soft one.

A spring is **elastic**, which means it returns to its old shape after being let go. But this only applies up to the elastic limit. If you pull harder, the spring is overstretched and stays permanently deformed. Then the spring balance measures incorrectly, which is why you should never load it beyond its measuring range.

When a body hangs on the spring balance at rest, the spring force and the **weight** are equal. On Earth one kilogram has a weight of about 9.81 N, roughly 10 N. On the Moon the same body would show only about a sixth as much force. A beam balance, on the other hand, compares masses and shows the same on the Moon as on Earth.

Luggage scales, with which you weigh your bags before a flight, work on the same principle. Anglers also use small spring scales to weigh their catch. In the past many kitchen scales and bathroom scales had a spring inside. Today electronic scales mostly measure with sensors that detect tiny deformations.

begriffe.erklaerung: The unit of force, named after Isaac Newton.
A number that shows how stiff or soft a spring is.
A body is elastic if it returns to its shape after being deformed.
The force with which the Earth pulls on a body.

gewusst: Robert Hooke first published his law as a coded letter puzzle so that nobody could steal the idea.
A 100-gram bar of chocolate pulls on a spring balance with about 1 newton.
There are spring balances for tiny forces of fractions of a newton up to large forces of many thousands of newtons.

teile.einleitung: Freezing is the name for the change of a substance from the liquid to the solid state, for example when water turns into ice. At normal air pressure, pure water freezes at 0 °C. We come across freezing everywhere: in the freezer compartment, with ice lollies, on frozen lakes and on the washing line in winter.
wichtigste: When water turns into ice, this is called freezing.
At normal air pressure pure water freezes at 0 °C.
The same amount of water freezes faster in a shallow dish than in a tall cup.
When fruit freezes, ice crystals damage its cells, which is why strawberries go mushy after thawing.
A fast-flowing stream rarely freezes over completely, because the water is constantly moving.
The stars on a freezer compartment show how cold it gets inside.
Frost is a thin, white coating of ice that forms on cold nights.

abschnitte.text: In liquid water the **molecules** move about freely. As it cools, they slow down, and at 0 °C they arrange themselves into a fixed **crystal lattice**. In the process the water gives off heat, which is why the temperature stays the same during freezing until everything is solid. The reverse change, from solid to liquid, is called melting.

Water has a special property: when it freezes, it expands by about a tenth. That is why ice floats on water and lakes freeze from the top down. This is why fish can survive the winter under the ice. But the expansion can also burst water pipes, glass bottles and garden hoses and split rocks in the mountains; this is called **frost weathering**.

A small puddle freezes over faster on a cold night than a deep pond, because less water has to cool down. In the same way, water freezes faster in a shallow dish, because it has a larger surface through which heat escapes. A fast-flowing stream rarely freezes over completely, because the moving water keeps mixing. Salt lowers the **freezing point**, which is why salt is spread on the roads in winter.

In the freezer compartment food is preserved, because bacteria hardly grow in the cold. The stars show the temperature: one star means about minus 6 °C, three stars minus 18 °C. When food freezes slowly, large **ice crystals** form that pierce the cells of fruit such as strawberries, which is why they are soft after thawing. With frozen squash in small moulds with sticks, you can make your own ice lollies.

If you hang wet washing outside in a hard frost, it freezes as stiff as a board. Amazingly, it still dries slowly, because the ice can turn directly into water vapour. On clear, cold nights **frost** forms on meadows and car roofs, a thin white coating of ice from water vapour in the air. If rain freezes when it hits the cold ground, dangerous black ice forms.

begriffe.erklaerung: The temperature at which a liquid becomes solid; for water 0 °C.
A regular arrangement of the particles in a solid substance.
Rock is split by water freezing in cracks.
A thin white coating of ice from water vapour on cold surfaces.
Water that has been cooled below 0 °C but is still liquid.

gewusst: Very pure water can stay liquid well below 0 °C and then freezes in a flash at a small jolt.
Because ice is lighter than water, icebergs float, and only about a tenth sticks out of the sea.
Every snowflake is a frozen ice crystal with six arms.

teile.einleitung: An electric car does not run on petrol or diesel, but on an electric motor and electricity from a large battery. It is quiet, has no exhaust pipe and can recover energy when braking. In Switzerland you see more and more electric cars on the roads.
wichtigste: An electric car is driven by an electric motor that draws electricity from a battery.
The distance it can travel on a full battery charge is called its range.
When braking it feeds energy back into the battery through regenerative braking.
Rapid charging stations charge the battery directly with direct current.
A fully electric car has no exhaust pipe and gives off no exhaust gases while driving.
It is most climate-friendly when it runs on electricity from renewable sources.
As early as 1899 the electric car “La Jamais Contente” was the first car to go faster than 100 km/h.

abschnitte.text: In an electric car an **electric motor** drives the wheels. The energy for it comes from a large **battery**, usually a lithium-ion battery in the floor of the car. An electric motor converts most of the energy into movement, whereas a petrol engine turns a large part into waste heat. A gearbox with many gears, a fuel tank and an exhaust pipe are not needed.

When braking, the electric motor works as a **generator** and turns kinetic energy back into electricity. This flows back into the battery, which is called **regenerative braking**. It is especially worthwhile in the mountains: on a long descent from an Alpine pass the battery can be charged up a little again. The normal brakes also wear out less as a result.

The **range** of modern electric cars is usually a few hundred kilometres. At home you charge with alternating current at a wallbox, which takes a few hours. At rapid charging stations **direct current** flows straight into the battery, so a charge often takes less than an hour. If a car uses 18 kWh per 100 km, it needs 45 kWh for 250 km. At 30 centimes per kWh, a charge of 20 kWh costs 6 francs.

Electric cars are older than many people think. Around 1900 many electric vehicles drove through cities such as Paris and New York. In 1899 the Belgian Camille Jenatzy was the first to break the 100 km/h mark, with the electric car **“La Jamais Contente”**. After that, petrol cars won out because they could travel further and petrol was cheap. Only with better batteries did the electric car return from about 2010.

An electric car gives off no exhaust gases while driving and is quieter than a petrol car. How climate-friendly it is overall depends strongly on the **electricity mix**. In Switzerland a lot of electricity comes from hydropower and other sources with little CO₂, which is good for electric cars. Making the battery, however, takes a lot of energy and raw materials such as lithium. That is why research is being done on long-lasting batteries and on recycling.

begriffe.erklaerung: A rechargeable energy store that stores electricity chemically.
The distance an electric car can travel on a full battery charge.
Recovering energy when braking, which flows back into the battery.
A charging station that you mount on the wall at home.
The make-up of electricity from different types of power station.

gewusst: Because electric cars are so quiet, new models have to make an artificial sound when driving slowly so that pedestrians can hear them.
An electric motor has its full power as soon as it starts, which is why many electric cars accelerate very quickly.
Normal cars are banned in Zermatt; small electric vehicles have been driving through the village there for decades.

teile.einleitung: The energy label is a coloured label on appliances such as fridges, washing machines or televisions. It shows at a glance how much energy an appliance uses. This lets you choose economical appliances when shopping and save money and electricity.
wichtigste: The new energy label uses the letters A to G.
The most economical class, A, is dark green; the worst class, G, is red.
The label on a fridge also shows the annual consumption in kWh.
Differences in consumption can have a big effect on the electricity bill over the years.
In Switzerland there is also an energy label for cars.
In Switzerland the Swiss Federal Office of Energy is responsible for the energy label.

abschnitte.text: The **energy label** is a sign with coloured bars that is stuck on many electrical appliances. Each level has a letter, the **efficiency class**. The dark green bar A stands for very economical appliances, the red bar G for appliances with high consumption. In between, the colours go from light green through yellow and orange to red.

In the past there were classes such as A+, A++ and A+++, because appliances kept becoming more economical. That was confusing, because almost all appliances were some kind of A. That is why a new scale from **A to G** was introduced in Switzerland and the EU in 2021. Many appliances that used to have A+++ are now only in class C or D, and class A is reserved for even more economical appliances.

Next to the class, the label shows the **annual consumption** in kilowatt-hours. Depending on the appliance there is further information; for a fridge, for example, the volume of the fridge and freezer compartments and the noise level. For a washing machine you can see the water consumption and the length of the programme. A **QR code** lets you call up more information from a database.

If fridge X needs 150 kWh a year and fridge Y 250 kWh, X uses 100 kWh less. If a kilowatt-hour costs 30 centimes, you save 30 francs a year with X. A fridge often runs for 10 to 15 years, so several hundred francs quickly add up. That is why it is worth looking not only at the purchase price, but also at the **running costs**.

In Switzerland the **Swiss Federal Office of Energy** (SFOE) is responsible for the energy label. It exists not only for household appliances and lamps, but also for **cars**. The car label shows, among other things, a car's energy consumption and CO2 emissions. The rules in Switzerland are largely aligned with those of the European Union, so that appliances can be compared across Europe.

begriffe.erklaerung: A letter from A to G that shows how economical an appliance is.
A measure of electrical energy, abbreviated kWh.
Costs that arise when using an appliance, for example for electricity.
The federal office that deals with energy matters in Switzerland.

gewusst: An appliance in class C on the new scale can be more economical than one that used to be advertised as A+++.
Televisions, lamps and dishwashers also carry an energy label.
A fridge runs day and night, which is why it is one of the appliances where being economical is especially worthwhile.

teile.einleitung: A simple pendulum is a weight that hangs on a thread and swings back and forth. It is one of the simplest and most important experiments in physics. Because it swings so regularly, it was used to build clocks for centuries.
wichtigste: For small swings the period is T = 2π · √(l/g).
The period depends only on the length of the thread and the acceleration due to gravity, not on the mass.
A pendulum 2.5 m long needs about 3.2 seconds for one full swing.
On the Moon a pendulum swings about 2.5 times more slowly than on Earth.
For large swings such as 60°, the period is somewhat longer than the formula says.
A pendulum can be used to measure the acceleration due to gravity g.
Christiaan Huygens built the first pendulum clock in 1656.

abschnitte.text: A simple pendulum consists of a **bob** on a thread that is fixed at the top. If you pull it to one side, gravity pulls it back; it swings through the lowest point and up again on the other side. Physicists often calculate with the **ideal pendulum**: a point mass on a thread that has no mass and cannot stretch. Real pendulums come quite close to this ideal.

The **period** T is the time for one full swing there and back. For small swings T = 2π · √(l/g), where l is the length of the thread and g is the acceleration due to gravity. On Earth g is about 9.81 m/s², so a pendulum 2.5 m long needs about 3.2 seconds. Amazingly, a heavy bob and a light bob swing equally fast.

The formula only applies to small angles, because there you may treat sin φ as roughly equal to φ. At a swing of 60°, one oscillation already takes somewhat longer. The Dutchman **Christiaan Huygens** found out that a pendulum moving along a **cycloid**, a special curve, takes exactly the same time for every amplitude. In practice, pendulum clocks are therefore only allowed to swing a little.

Because T depends on g, a pendulum can be used to measure gravity. A pendulum 0.80 m long with a period of 1.80 s gives, for example, a g of about 9.75 m/s². On the Moon g is only 1.62 m/s², so the pendulum swings about 2.5 times more slowly there. In a lift accelerating upwards, gravity seems stronger and the period becomes shorter.

According to legend, **Galileo Galilei** watched a swinging chandelier in Pisa Cathedral and noticed that each swing took the same time. In 1656 Huygens built the first pendulum clock, which kept much better time than earlier clocks. A pendulum just under one metre long takes exactly one second for one swing. In 1851 Léon Foucault showed in Paris with a huge pendulum that the Earth turns.

begriffe.erklaerung: The time for one full oscillation there and back.
The greatest displacement from the rest position.
How strongly gravity accelerates a body; on Earth about 9.81 m/s².
An imaginary perfect pendulum with a point mass and a thread without mass.
The curve traced by a point on a rolling wheel.

gewusst: A swing in the playground is also a pendulum, and the child's mass hardly changes its period.
A Foucault pendulum slowly changes the direction of its swing during the day, because the Earth turns beneath it.
In the past, pendulum clocks had to be readjusted when they were taken to a place with slightly different gravity.

teile.einleitung: The electromagnetic spectrum includes all kinds of electromagnetic waves, from long radio waves to tiny gamma rays. Visible light is only a small part of it. All these waves travel at the same speed, but differ in wavelength, frequency and energy.
wichtigste: The spectrum includes radio waves, microwaves, infrared, visible light, ultraviolet, X-rays and gamma radiation.
All electromagnetic waves travel through a vacuum at the speed of light.
Wavelength times frequency gives the speed of light, about 300,000 kilometres per second.
The shorter the wavelength, the more energy a photon has.
In the 1880s Heinrich Hertz was the first to prove electromagnetic waves by experiment.
A thermal imaging camera makes infrared radiation visible.
From short-wave ultraviolet upwards, radiation can ionise atoms.

abschnitte.text: Electromagnetic waves consist of electric and magnetic fields that vibrate together. They need no material and can cross even empty space. If you arrange them by their **wavelength**, you get the **electromagnetic spectrum**. Our eyes see only the range from about 380 to 780 nanometres, from violet to red.

**Radio waves** are very long; an FM transmitter at 100 MHz has a wavelength of 3 metres. Microwaves range from about 300 MHz to 300 GHz; a microwave oven works at 2.45 GHz with a wavelength of about 12 cm. Then come infrared, visible light and ultraviolet. At the short-wave end lie **X-rays** and gamma rays.

For all waves: the speed of light equals wavelength times **frequency**. Green light at 500 nm therefore has a frequency of 6 times 10 to the power of 14 hertz. The energy of a particle of light, a **photon**, rises with frequency. A photon at 500 nm has about 2.5 eV, whereas an X-ray photon at 0.1 nm has about 12 keV, almost 5000 times more.

Around 1800 the astronomer William Herschel discovered infrared radiation, and soon afterwards Johann Wilhelm Ritter found ultraviolet. In the 1860s James Clerk Maxwell predicted that light is an electromagnetic wave. In the 1880s **Heinrich Hertz** was the first to produce and receive such waves in the laboratory. In 1895 Wilhelm Conrad Röntgen discovered the rays named after him in German, which we call X-rays.

Mobile phones, wifi and radio transmit with radio waves and microwaves. A **thermal imaging camera** shows the infrared radiation of warm bodies, even in the dark. UV radiation from the Sun causes sunburn, which is why you need sun cream. From short-wave ultraviolet upwards, radiation is **ionising**: it can knock electrons out of atoms and damage cells, which is why X-rays are used sparingly.

begriffe.erklaerung: The distance between two wave crests.
The number of vibrations per second, measured in hertz.
The smallest packet of energy of electromagnetic radiation.
Radiation with so much energy that it can knock electrons out of atoms.

gewusst: The unit of frequency, the hertz, is named after Heinrich Hertz.
Bees can see ultraviolet light, which is invisible to us.
Radio telescopes receive radio waves from space that have been travelling for many billions of years.

teile.einleitung: Galileo Galilei was an Italian scientist, mathematician and astronomer who lived from 1564 to 1642. He was one of the first to point a telescope at the sky, and in doing so he discovered moons of Jupiter and craters on the Moon. Because he taught that the Earth moves around the Sun, he got into a famous dispute with the Church.
wichtigste: Galileo Galilei was born in Pisa in 1564 and died near Florence in 1642.
In 1609 he improved the telescope and pointed it at the sky.
In 1610 he discovered the four large moons of Jupiter.
On the Earth's Moon he saw mountains and craters.
He defended the view of the world with the Sun at the centre.
In 1633 he was condemned by the Roman Inquisition.
He realised that without air resistance all bodies fall equally fast.

abschnitte.text: Galileo Galilei was born on 15 February 1564 in **Pisa**, the city with the famous leaning tower. He first studied medicine, but soon became more interested in mathematics. From 1592 to 1610 he taught mathematics at the University of **Padua**. After that he worked in Florence for the powerful Medici family. He died on 8 January 1642 in Arcetri near Florence.

In 1609 Galileo heard of a new device from the Netherlands with which you could see faraway things more closely. He built a better **telescope** himself and was one of the first to point it at the sky. On the Moon he discovered **mountains and craters**, so it was not a smooth sphere. He saw that the Milky Way consists of countless stars. He also observed the phases of Venus and dark spots on the Sun.

In January 1610 Galileo discovered four points of light circling Jupiter. These four large moons are now called Io, Europa, Ganymede and Callisto; they are known as the **Galilean moons**. The discovery was important because it showed that not everything circles the Earth. Galileo published his observations in 1610 in a small book entitled “Sidereus Nuncius”, which means Starry Messenger.

abschnitte.titel: The dispute about the view of the world
abschnitte.text: At that time most people believed that the Earth stood still at the centre of the world. Galileo, on the other hand, supported the **heliocentric view of the world** of Nicolaus Copernicus, according to which the Earth moves around the Sun. The Catholic Church rejected this teaching at the time. In 1632 Galileo published a book in which he compared the two views of the world. In 1633 the Roman **Inquisition** condemned him, and he had to take back his teaching and spend the rest of his life under house arrest.

abschnitte.titel: Laws of falling and the pendulum
abschnitte.text: Galileo studied how bodies fall, letting balls roll down slopes to do so. He realised that without **air resistance** all bodies fall equally fast, no matter how heavy they are. He also studied the **pendulum** and found that one swing always takes about the same time. This discovery later helped in building accurate pendulum clocks. Galileo is considered one of the founders of modern science because he tested ideas with experiments and measurements.

In 1992 Pope John Paul II officially declared that Galileo's condemnation had been a mistake. A NASA space probe that explored Jupiter bears his name. The European satellite navigation system **Galileo** is also named after him. In Florence you can marvel at his telescopes in the Museo Galileo. His way of understanding nature through observation and experiment still shapes science today.

begriffe.erklaerung: A device with lenses that makes faraway things appear closer.
The idea that the Sun is at the centre and the Earth circles around it.
A church court that in the past took action against differing teachings.
A weight on a string or rod that swings back and forth.
The slowing force of the air on a moving body.

gewusst: In 1971 an astronaut dropped a hammer and a feather on the Moon, and both reached the ground at the same time, just as Galileo had predicted.
Galileo is said to have timed the swinging of a chandelier in Pisa Cathedral with his own pulse.
One of Galileo's middle fingers is shown today as an exhibit in the Museo Galileo in Florence.

teile.einleitung: The Basel geothermal project, also called Deep Heat Mining, aimed to obtain electricity and heat from hot rock deep beneath the city. In December 2006, however, it triggered noticeable earthquakes. After that the project was abandoned, and today it is seen as an important lesson for geothermal energy in Switzerland.
wichtigste: The Basel project was called Deep Heat Mining.
A hole was drilled about 5000 metres deep into the rock.
Water was forced into the ground under high pressure to make the rock permeable.
In December 2006 this caused an earthquake with a magnitude of about 3.4.
Basel lies in the Upper Rhine Graben, an earthquake-prone zone.
The project was abandoned after the earthquakes.
In 2013 St Gallen also experienced an earthquake linked to a geothermal project.

abschnitte.text: The deeper you drill into the Earth, the warmer it gets, on average by about 3 °C per 100 metres. At a depth of 4000 metres it is therefore about 130 °C if it is 10 °C at the surface. This heat from the Earth is called **geothermal energy**. In Basel, the **Deep Heat Mining** project aimed to get this heat out of the hard granite rock and turn it into electricity and district heating.

abschnitte.titel: How it was meant to work
abschnitte.text: From 2006 a hole about 5000 metres deep was drilled in the Kleinhüningen district. The rock there is about 200 °C hot, but very dense. So water was forced into the borehole at high pressure to open up fine cracks. This method is called **hydraulic stimulation**. Later, cold water was supposed to flow through the cracks, heat up and come back up through a second borehole.

As the water was forced in, the ground began to shake. On 8 December 2006 there was a quake with a **magnitude** of about 3.4, and many people in Basel felt the jolt and heard a bang. Nobody was injured, but many homeowners reported small cracks in their buildings. There were also aftershocks in the following weeks and months.

Basel lies in the **Upper Rhine Graben**, a large rift in the Earth's crust between the Black Forest and the Vosges. There the layers of rock are under stress, and earthquakes are more frequent than elsewhere in Switzerland. In 1356 a severe earthquake destroyed large parts of the city of Basel. The water forced in released the existing stress in the rock earlier than it would otherwise have been.

After the quakes, the pumping of water was stopped at once. A risk study showed that continuing could lead to further damaging quakes. In 2009 the project was finally abandoned. In **St Gallen**, too, a geothermal project caused a noticeable earthquake in 2013, and that project was also later given up.

The events in Basel were studied closely by experts all over the world. Today it is better understood how to increase the pressure carefully and how to monitor the ground with many measuring devices. Geothermal energy is still considered an important renewable energy for the future. Smaller **ground probes** for single-family houses are very common in Switzerland and are harmless.

begriffe.erklaerung: Heat from inside the Earth that can be used for heating or for electricity.
A number that shows how strong an earthquake is.
Water is forced into the rock at high pressure so that cracks form.
A long rift in the Earth's crust from Basel to Frankfurt.
A pipe in a borehole with which a house gets heat from the ground.

gewusst: A quake of magnitude 3.4 is rather weak, but because it was directly beneath a city, a great many people felt it.
The borehole in Basel was more than ten times as deep as the Prime Tower in Zurich is tall.
The Basel earthquake of 1356 is considered the strongest known earthquake in Central Europe north of the Alps.

teile.einleitung: In an energy conversion, energy changes from one form into another. A hydroelectric power station turns potential energy into electricity, a solar cell turns light into electricity and an electric motor turns electricity into movement. No energy is ever lost, but unwanted heat is often produced.
wichtigste: Energy can be converted from one form into another.
In a hydroelectric power station, potential energy becomes electrical energy.
In a solar cell, light becomes electrical energy.
An electric motor converts electrical energy into kinetic energy.
When a ball bounces lower and lower, its energy becomes heat and sound.
Efficiency shows what share of the energy is converted usefully.
Every conversion also produces some heat.

abschnitte.text: Energy never disappears; it only changes its form. Such an **energy conversion** happens all around us all the time. When you ride a bike, chemical energy from food becomes kinetic energy. A series of conversions is called an **energy chain**, for example from the Sun through plants and food to your muscles.

In a **hydroelectric power station**, water flows down from a reservoir, and **potential energy** becomes kinetic energy. The water drives a turbine, and a generator turns this into electrical energy. A **solar cell** converts light directly into electrical energy. A plant, on the other hand, stores sunlight as chemical energy during photosynthesis.

An **electric motor** converts electrical energy into kinetic energy, for example in an SBB train or a drill. A petrol engine turns chemical energy into heat and then into movement. A **generator** does the opposite of a motor and turns movement into electricity. A rechargeable battery stores electrical energy as chemical energy and releases it again later.

If you drop a ball, potential energy becomes kinetic energy. On impact it is briefly squashed and bounces back up. But each time it bounces a little less high, because part of the energy becomes **heat** and **sound**. So the energy has not disappeared; it has only passed into a form that we can no longer use.

**Efficiency** shows what share of the energy put in is converted into the desired form. Large electric motors and hydroelectric power stations reach over 90 per cent. A petrol engine in a car uses only about 20 to 35 per cent; the rest becomes waste heat. An old **light bulb** turned only about 5 per cent of the energy into light; an LED is many times better.

begriffe.erklaerung: Several energy conversions one after the other.
The share of energy that is converted usefully, usually given as a percentage.
Heat that is produced unintentionally during a conversion.
A wheel with blades that is turned by water, steam or wind.

gewusst: No device has an efficiency of 100 per cent, because some heat is always produced.
The brakes of modern electric cars and trains can turn kinetic energy back into electricity.
Your body is itself an energy converter: during sport a large part of the food energy becomes heat, which is why you sweat.

teile.einleitung: Colour mixing means making many new colours from a few primary colours. There are two quite different kinds: mixing light and mixing paints. If you know both, you understand why a screen can show all colours from red, green and blue.
wichtigste: Yellow and blue paint make green.
Red and yellow make orange, red and blue make violet.
Red with a lot of white makes pink, black and white make grey.
If you mix a great many paints, you usually get a dark brownish grey.
Red and green light together make yellow.
Red and blue light make magenta, a bright pink.
You cannot mix white from paints.

abschnitte.text: When painting, you mix dyes; this is called **subtractive colour mixing**. Each colour absorbs part of the light and reflects only the rest. If you mix two colours, even more light is absorbed, which is why the mixture gets darker. Yellow and blue make green, red and yellow make orange, red and blue make violet.

With light it is the other way round; this is called **additive colour mixing**. Each lamp adds new light, which is why the mixture gets brighter. Red and green light make yellow, red and blue make magenta, green and blue make cyan. When red, green and blue shine together, white is produced.

Each pixel of a mobile phone or television consists of tiny red, green and blue parts, which is why the system is called **RGB**. Depending on the brightness of the three parts, our eyes see millions of colours. Printers, on the other hand, work with cyan, magenta, yellow and black, abbreviated **CMYK**. Because paper is white, the printer needs no white ink.

In our retina there are three kinds of **cones**, which react especially to red, green or blue light. The brain puts together every colour from the three signals. That is why three primary colours are enough to imitate almost all colours. This three-colour theory goes back to Thomas Young and Hermann von Helmholtz in the 19th century.

abschnitte.titel: Colour theory and the colour wheel
abschnitte.text: The Swiss painter and art teacher **Johannes Itten** from the canton of Bern taught at the famous Bauhaus in Germany. He developed a colour wheel with twelve colours, which is still used in many schools today. In the centre are the primary colours yellow, red and blue, and on the outside the mixed colours. Colours that lie opposite each other on the wheel are called **complementary colours**, for example red and green.

begriffe.erklaerung: Colours from which others are mixed, but which cannot themselves be mixed.
Mixing light; the result becomes brighter.
Mixing dyes; the result becomes darker.
Colours that lie opposite each other on the colour wheel.
Red, green and blue, the light colours of screens.

gewusst: If you go very close to a screen with a magnifying glass, you can sometimes see the individual red, green and blue dots.
Yellow appears on a screen even though no yellow light shines there at all, only red and green together.
Around 1666 Isaac Newton showed with a prism that white light consists of all the colours of the rainbow.

teile.einleitung: Gay-Lussac's law describes how gases expand when heated. At constant pressure, the volume of a gas grows in the same proportion as its absolute temperature in kelvin. It is named after the French scientist Joseph Louis Gay-Lussac.
wichtigste: At constant pressure, the volume of a gas is proportional to its absolute temperature.
Absolute temperature is measured in kelvin; 0 °C is about 273 K.
When a gas warms up, it expands; when it cools down, it contracts.
If you extend the volume-temperature line down to zero volume, you arrive at absolute zero.
Joseph Louis Gay-Lussac came from France.
At constant pressure a gas at 0 °C doubles its volume at about 273 °C.
In English the rule is often called Charles's law, after Jacques Charles.

abschnitte.text: Gay-Lussac's law applies to a fixed amount of gas at constant **pressure**. It says that the volume is proportional to the **absolute temperature**. If the absolute temperature doubles, the volume also doubles. As a formula it is written as V divided by T stays the same, that is V1/T1 = V2/T2.

For the law you have to give the temperature in **kelvin**; to do so you add about 273 to the degrees Celsius. If 3 litres of gas at 27 °C, that is 300 K, are heated to 127 °C, that is 400 K, they grow to 4 litres. From 10 °C to 20 °C the volume increases by only about 3.5 per cent, because 293 K is only a little more than 283 K. A balloon of 2 litres at 20 °C shrinks to about 1.74 litres in a freezer at -18 °C.

If you plot volume and temperature on a graph, you get a straight line. If you extend it down to zero volume, it meets the temperature axis at about -273 °C. This is **absolute zero**, the lowest possible temperature. Real gases, however, become liquid before that, so this is only an imaginary extension.

Joseph Louis Gay-Lussac lived from 1778 to 1850 and was a French chemist and physicist. He published the law in 1802. His fellow countryman Jacques Charles had observed something similar earlier, but had not published it, which is why the rule is called Charles's law in English. In 1804 Gay-Lussac rose in a **balloon** to a height of over 7000 metres to collect samples of air and measure the Earth's magnetic field.

A **hot-air balloon** rises because the heated air expands and is therefore lighter than the cold air outside. An inflated balloon that you put in the fridge goes limp. A football seems softer outside in winter than in a warm room. The expansion of warm gases also helps dough to rise when baking.

begriffe.erklaerung: The space a body or gas takes up, for example in litres.
A unit of temperature that starts at 0 at absolute zero.
The lowest possible temperature, about -273 °C.
Two quantities grow in the same ratio.

gewusst: Gay-Lussac flew higher in his balloon than the highest mountain in Europe rises.
The kelvin temperature scale is named after the British physicist Lord Kelvin.
Car tyres have less pressure in cold winter weather, which is why you should check them in the cold season.

teile.einleitung: Boyle's law, known in German as the Boyle-Mariotte law, describes how the pressure and volume of a gas are connected. If you squeeze a gas to half its volume, its pressure doubles, as long as the temperature stays the same. Anyone who has ever held a bicycle pump closed and pushed the piston in knows this.
wichtigste: For a fixed amount of gas at the same temperature, pressure times volume is constant.
If you halve the volume, the pressure doubles.
The Englishman Robert Boyle described the law in 1662.
The Frenchman Edme Mariotte found it independently a few years later.
In a p-V diagram an isotherm has the shape of a hyperbola.
If you double the pressure, the density of the gas also doubles.
The law applies exactly to ideal gases and quite well to air under normal conditions.

abschnitte.text: For a certain amount of gas at **constant temperature**: pressure times volume always gives the same value. This is written as p times V equals a constant. If the volume gets smaller, the **pressure** rises in the same proportion. If the volume gets larger, the pressure falls.

6 litres of gas at 100 kilopascals are squeezed to 2 litres, that is to a third. The pressure then rises to three times as much, to 300 kilopascals. A 50-litre **gas cylinder** at 200 bar contains so much gas that at 1 bar it would take up 10,000 litres. That is why a great deal of gas can be stored in a small cylinder.

Under water the pressure rises by about 1 bar every 10 metres. A balloon with 3 litres at the surface has a volume of only about 1 litre at a depth of 20 metres, where the pressure is about 300 kilopascals. That is why divers must keep breathing calmly when **surfacing**. The air in their lungs expands again as they rise.

abschnitte.titel: A crisp packet on the Jungfraujoch
abschnitte.text: If you seal a crisp packet in Zurich and take it up to the **Jungfraujoch** at 3454 metres, it puffs up tightly. Up there the outside **air pressure** is much lower than on the Central Plateau. The gas in the packet expands until the pressure inside and outside is almost the same again. The same thing happens to sealed yoghurt pots on an aeroplane.

The Anglo-Irish natural scientist **Robert Boyle** published the law in 1662 after experiments with mercury in a bent glass tube. The Frenchman **Edme Mariotte** discovered it independently in 1676. The law was one of the first mathematical relationships in the physics of gases. Together with other gas laws, it forms the basis of the **ideal gas equation**.

begriffe.erklaerung: The force acting on a certain area, measured for example in pascals or bar.
The space a substance takes up, for example in litres.
A curve in a diagram along which the temperature is the same everywhere.
A simplified model of a gas whose particles do not attract each other.
A curved line produced when the product of two quantities stays the same.

gewusst: A syringe with its opening held closed shows the law very nicely: the further you push, the harder the air pushes back.
In many countries the law is called just Boyle's law, while in France it is often called Mariotte's law.
Because the air on mountain tops is thinner, each breath there contains less oxygen.

teile.einleitung: An endoscope is a device that lets you look inside the body or into narrow cavities without cutting them wide open. The name comes from Greek: “endo” means inside and “skopein” means to look. Doctors, but also mechanics and tradespeople, use endoscopes every day.
wichtigste: An endoscope is used to look inside the body or into cavities.
The Greek prefix “endo” means inside.
In modern video endoscopes a tiny camera sits at the tip of the tube.
The examination of the stomach is called gastroscopy, that of the bowel colonoscopy.
In keyhole surgery, doctors operate through small cuts with an endoscope and fine instruments.
A capsule endoscope is a swallowable camera the size of a tablet.
In engineering, endoscopes are used to check engines or pipes from the inside.

abschnitte.text: An endoscope usually consists of a thin rod or a flexible **tube**, a light source and an optical system or camera. The light illuminates the inside, and the image is transmitted to the outside. There are rigid endoscopes made of metal and flexible endoscopes that can bend round curves. In modern **video endoscopes** the camera sits directly at the tip of the tube, and the image appears on a screen.

In the past, light and images were carried through the tube with lenses or with bundles of fine **optical fibres**. An optical fibre is thinner than a hair and can carry light even round corners. Today a small camera chip usually records the image directly at the tip. Many endoscopes also have fine channels through which air, water or small instruments such as forceps can be pushed. With the little wheel on the handle, the tip can be steered in different directions.

In medicine, an examination with an endoscope is often called an **endoscopy**. In a **gastroscopy** the tube is pushed through the mouth and oesophagus into the stomach. In a bowel examination, in technical language a **colonoscopy**, the large intestine is examined. This makes it possible to detect inflammation, ulcers or growths early, and sometimes small tissue samples can be taken. Patients are often given a sedative and feel little.

With endoscopes you can also operate without opening the abdomen wide. In **keyhole surgery** only a few small cuts of about one centimetre are made. The endoscope goes in through one cut and fine instruments through the others. In this way, for example, an inflamed appendix or the gallbladder can be removed. The wounds are small, heal faster, and patients can go home sooner.

A **capsule endoscope** is a tiny camera the size of a tablet that you simply swallow. On its way through the digestive tract it takes a great many photos and sends them by radio to a device that the person wears on their body.
