This also makes it possible to see parts of the small intestine that are hard to reach with a normal tube. After the examination the capsule leaves the body naturally.

Endoscopes are very useful outside medicine too. Mechanics use them to look into **engines** and aircraft engines without taking them apart. Plumbers check pipes and drains from the inside. On building sites you can look into a wall through a small drill hole. Such technical endoscopes are often called **borescopes**.

begriffe.erklaerung: A device with a light and a camera for looking into the body or into cavities.
The technical word for an examination of the bowel.
A very thin thread of glass that carries light.
An operation through tiny cuts with an endoscope and fine instruments.
A camera the size of a tablet that you swallow.

gewusst: As early as 1806 the doctor Philipp Bozzini built a “light conductor” with which he wanted to look into body openings by candlelight.
During its journey through the body, a capsule endoscope can take tens of thousands of pictures.
Archaeologists sometimes also use endoscopes to look into sealed tombs or cavities.

teile.einleitung: Electromagnetism is the part of physics that shows that electricity and magnetism belong closely together. An electric current creates a magnetic field, and a changing magnetic field creates current. Motors, generators, radio and even light are based on this connection.
wichtigste: Electricity and magnetism are two sides of the same force of nature.
In 1820 Hans Christian Ørsted discovered that a current deflects a compass needle.
In 1831 Michael Faraday discovered electromagnetic induction.
According to Lenz's law, the induced current opposes its cause.
The Lorentz force acts on moving charges in a magnetic field.
In the 1860s James Clerk Maxwell brought everything together in a system of equations.
Light is an electromagnetic wave.

abschnitte.text: In 1820 the Danish physicist **Hans Christian Ørsted** noticed that a wire carrying current deflects a compass needle. This proved that electric current creates a **magnetic field**. The field lines run in circles around the wire. Soon afterwards the Frenchman André-Marie Ampère studied the forces between wires carrying current.

When a charge moves through a magnetic field, it is deflected sideways. This **Lorentz force** is calculated for movement at right angles with F = q · v · B. An electron at 2 · 10^6 m/s in a field of 0.5 tesla thus feels about 1.6 · 10^-13 newtons. The Lorentz force makes **electric motors** turn and steers particles in the accelerator at CERN.

In 1831 **Michael Faraday** found the opposite effect: a changing magnetic field creates a voltage in a wire. This is **electromagnetic induction**, the basis of all generators. In 1834 Heinrich Lenz realised that the induced current always opposes its cause. This **Lenz's law** follows from the conservation of energy.

A **transformer** consists of two coils on a shared iron core. Alternating current in the first coil induces a voltage in the second. The ratio of the voltages equals the ratio of the numbers of turns. With 500 turns on the primary side and 25 on the secondary side, 230 V thus becomes 11.5 V.

In the 1860s the Scottish physicist **James Clerk Maxwell** summed up all the laws of electricity and magnetism in **Maxwell's equations**. From them he predicted that there are **electromagnetic waves** that travel at the speed of light. Heinrich Hertz proved them by experiment in 1886. Today we know that light, radio waves, microwaves and X-rays are all such waves.

Without electromagnetism there would be no electric motors, no power stations and no power grid. Mobile phones, wifi and radio transmit information with electromagnetic waves. The **Earth's magnetic field** also protects us from charged particles from space and creates the northern and southern lights. Electromagnetism is one of the four **fundamental forces** of nature.

begriffe.erklaerung: An area in which magnetic forces act.
The force on a moving charge in a magnetic field.
The unit of magnetic flux density, that is the strength of a magnetic field.
Four equations that describe all electric and magnetic phenomena.
One of the four basic forces of nature, for example gravity.

gewusst: Ørsted is said to have made his discovery during a lecture in front of students.
The unit of frequency, the hertz, is named after Heinrich Hertz.
The northern and southern lights form when charged particles from the Sun are steered towards the poles by the Earth's magnetic field.

teile.einleitung: A freezer compartment is an especially cold compartment in the fridge, or a separate freezer. It is about minus 18 degrees inside, so that food freezes and keeps for many months. There is a lot of physics behind the freezer: heat is pumped from the inside to the outside.
wichtigste: In the freezer compartment it is about minus 18 degrees Celsius.
Food is frozen so that it keeps longer.
In this cold, bacteria and moulds can hardly multiply any more.
Water expands when it freezes, which is why a full glass bottle can burst.
Hot food does not belong in the freezer; you let it cool down first.
Over time ice forms on the walls, which is why the compartment has to be defrosted now and then.
When frozen food becomes soft again, this is called thawing.

abschnitte.text: A normal fridge has about 5 degrees, but a freezer compartment about **minus 18 degrees**. On many appliances **stars** show how cold the compartment gets. Three or four stars mean at least minus 18 degrees. At this temperature many foods stay edible for several months.

A cooling appliance does not produce cold; it carries **heat** from the inside to the outside. To do this a **refrigerant** flows round in a circuit of pipes. Inside, it evaporates and takes in heat; a **compressor** squeezes it, and at the back of the appliance it gives the heat off again. That is why the back of a fridge is often warm.

Water is a special substance: when it turns into ice, it needs about a tenth more space. A full glass bottle has no room for this **expansion** and can therefore shatter. That is why drinks are only put in the freezer briefly and taken out again in good time. Ice cube trays are open at the top so that the ice can expand upwards.

Food should be well wrapped before freezing so that it does not dry out. Dried-out patches are called **freezer burn**. You do not put hot soup in, because it would partly thaw other food and form a lot of ice. The cold does not kill bacteria; it only puts them out of action, which is why thawed food should be eaten quickly and not frozen again.

After taking something out you should close the door quickly so that no warm, damp air gets in. This dampness is what forms the ice on the walls. A thick layer of ice acts like insulation and makes the appliance use more electricity. That is why you should **defrost** the freezer compartment regularly, if it cannot do this by itself.

begriffe.erklaerung: A substance that circulates in the pipes of a cooling appliance and carries heat outside.
A pump that squeezes the gaseous refrigerant.
Dried-out, grey patches on badly wrapped food.
To let the ice in the freezer compartment melt and remove it.

gewusst: In the 1920s the American Clarence Birdseye made quick-freezing of food well known, after seeing how the Inuit let fish freeze in the icy wind.
If you touch an ice-cold ice lolly directly with your tongue, your tongue can stick to it, because your saliva freezes immediately.
A freezer compartment gives off at the back exactly as much heat as it removes inside, plus the energy of the motor.

teile.einleitung: Electrical resistance shows how strongly a component or material hinders the flow of current. The greater the resistance, the less current flows at the same voltage. It is measured in ohms, with the Greek letter Ω as its symbol.
wichtigste: Resistance, measured in ohms, shows how strongly a material hinders current.
Ohm's law says: voltage equals resistance times current, that is U = R · I.
Long, thin wires have a greater resistance than short, thick ones.
In a series circuit the resistances add up.
In a parallel circuit the total resistance is smaller than the smallest single resistance.
When a metal wire is heated, its resistance rises.
In 1911 Heike Kamerlingh Onnes discovered superconductivity, in which resistance disappears completely.

abschnitte.text: When electrons flow through a wire, they keep bumping into the atoms of the material. This slows them down and produces **heat**. This braking effect is called **electrical resistance**, symbol R. Its unit, the **ohm**, is named after the German physicist Georg Simon Ohm, who studied the link between voltage and current around 1826.

**Ohm's law** links voltage, current and resistance: U = R · I. If a resistor has 100 Ω and 10 V is applied, a current of 0.1 A flows. A resistance of 1 Ω lets exactly 1 A through at 1 V. With a **multimeter** you can measure resistance directly.

The resistance of a wire depends on its length, its cross-section and the material. You calculate R = ρ · l / A, where ρ is the **resistivity** of the material. For copper, ρ = 0.0172 Ω·mm²/m, so a wire 100 m long with a cross-section of 1.5 mm² has about 1.15 Ω. That is why thick cables are needed for high currents, so that they do not get too hot.

In a **series circuit** the current flows through all the resistors one after the other, and their values are simply added. In a **parallel circuit** the current splits, and 1/R = 1/R1 + 1/R2 applies. So 6 Ω and 3 Ω in parallel make only 2 Ω together. If you connect 100 Ω in series with a parallel circuit of 60 Ω and 40 Ω, which is 24 Ω, you get 124 Ω in total.

In metals, resistance rises when they get warmer, because the atoms vibrate more strongly. Such components are called **PTC thermistors**. In an **NTC thermistor**, on the other hand, resistance falls when the temperature rises, which is why it is often used as a temperature sensor. In 1911 the Dutchman Heike Kamerlingh Onnes discovered that mercury loses its resistance completely at about minus 269 degrees Celsius; this is called **superconductivity**.

In kettles, toasters and hairdryers, heating wires with high resistance are deliberately made hot. In electronics, small **resistors** are important components that you can recognise by their coloured bands. A rotary knob, a so-called **potentiometer**, is an adjustable resistor, for example in a volume control. In long power lines, on the other hand, you want to keep resistance as small as possible so that little energy is lost.

begriffe.erklaerung: The unit of resistance, symbol Ω.
The rule U = R · I, which links voltage, resistance and current.
A material value that shows how strongly a substance slows down current.
A component whose resistance becomes smaller when it is warm.
A state in which a material has no resistance at all at a very low temperature.

gewusst: The coloured bands on a small resistor reveal, like a code, how many ohms it has.
When hot, the filament of a light bulb has about ten times more resistance than when cold.
Kamerlingh Onnes received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1913 for his research at low temperatures.

teile.einleitung: An electric motor is a machine that converts electrical energy into movement. It is found in trains, electric cars, washing machines, fans and even electric toothbrushes. Its secret is the interplay of electricity and magnets.
wichtigste: An electric motor converts electrical energy into kinetic energy.
A magnetic field exerts a force on a wire carrying current.
In a DC motor, the commutator reverses the current every half turn.
If you reverse the battery, a simple DC motor turns the other way.
More turns in the coil make the electromagnet stronger.
Large electric motors have an efficiency of over 90 per cent.
SBB locomotives are driven by electric motors that get their electricity from the overhead line.

abschnitte.text: When current flows through a wire, a magnetic field forms around the wire. If this wire lies between the poles of a magnet, it is pushed to the side. This force is called the **Lorentz force**. If you wind the wire into a **coil**, the force acts on many pieces of wire at once and becomes much greater. More turns and an iron core strengthen the electromagnet even more.

A motor consists of a fixed part, the **stator**, and a part that turns, the **rotor**. In a simple DC motor the coil sits on the rotor. Its poles are attracted and repelled by the poles of the fixed magnet. So that the rotor does not get stuck after half a turn, the **commutator** reverses the current in the coil each time. In this way the motor keeps turning without a break.

Small motors in toys run on **direct current** from batteries. If you reverse the battery, the direction of rotation changes. Many large motors in factories, pumps and trains work with **alternating current** or three-phase current. These motors often need no commutator, because the magnetic field in the stator itself turns in a circle. Modern electronics can control the speed and force of these motors very precisely.

Switzerland has one of the densest electrified railway networks in the world. **SBB** locomotives and multiple units take electricity from the overhead line through the pantograph and use it to drive their electric motors. When braking, these motors can work as generators and feed electricity back into the grid. Trams, trolleybuses, cable cars and rack railways in the mountains also run on electricity. More and more cars and bikes on Swiss roads have an electric motor too.

In 1821 the English researcher Michael Faraday showed that current and a magnet together can produce continuous rotation. In the following decades inventors such as Moritz Jacobi built the first usable motors. Towards the end of the 19th century, Nikola Tesla among others developed the three-phase motor. Today electric motors are the most common drives of all. They are quiet, give off no exhaust gases where they are used and have a high **efficiency**.

begriffe.erklaerung: A rotating switch that keeps reversing the current in the coil of a DC motor.
A wound-up wire that becomes a magnet when current flows through it.
Shows what share of the energy is really used and how much is lost as heat.
The part of the motor that turns.
The fixed part of the motor.

gewusst: An electric motor can also work the other way round: if you turn it from outside, it produces electricity like a generator.
A modern household often contains dozens of electric motors, for example in the fridge, hairdryer, vacuum cleaner and computer fan.
Large electric motors turn more than nine tenths of the energy into movement; a petrol engine manages much less.

teile.einleitung: A bicycle dynamo is a small generator on a bike that turns the turning of the wheel into electricity for the lights. This makes the front and rear lights shine without any batteries. It works on the principle of electromagnetic induction.
wichtigste: The dynamo on a bike turns the movement of the wheel into electricity for the lights.
It is a small generator and needs no battery.
Inside, a magnet turns close to a coil of wire.
There are sidewall dynamos and hub dynamos.
The faster you ride, the more electricity it supplies.
The kinetic energy comes from the muscle power of the rider.
A classic bike dynamo supplies about 6 volts and 3 watts.

abschnitte.text: A **bicycle dynamo** is a small **generator** fixed to the bike. It converts the kinetic energy of the turning wheel into electrical energy. This powers the headlight at the front and the rear light at the back. So a bike with a dynamo always has lights as long as it is moving.

Inside the dynamo a **permanent magnet** turns close to a **coil** of copper wire. This makes the magnetic field in the coil change constantly. Through the principle of **induction**, an electrical voltage is produced and alternating current flows to the lamp. The faster the magnet turns, the more electricity is produced.

With a **sidewall dynamo**, a small ridged wheel presses against the side of the tyre and is turned along with it. It is flipped against the tyre when needed, but it sometimes slips in the wet. The **hub dynamo** is built into the hub of the front wheel and runs almost silently and reliably. Less common are spoke dynamos, in which small magnets pass by on the spokes.

A typical bike dynamo supplies a voltage of about **6 volts** and a power of about **3 watts**. In the past this was just enough for a weak light bulb. Today the same power lights bright **LED lamps**. Many modern lights have a **standlight**, which keeps shining for a few minutes thanks to a small store of energy when you stop at traffic lights.

The first bike dynamos appeared towards the end of the 19th century; before that there were oil and carbide lamps. For a long time the sidewall dynamo with its typical whirring was part of almost every bike. Today many bikes are lit with rechargeable lamps, while everyday and touring bikes often have a hub dynamo. In Switzerland a bike must have a white light at the front and a red one at the back in the dark.

begriffe.erklaerung: A device that converts kinetic energy into electrical energy.
A dynamo built into the hub of the front wheel.
Producing a voltage through a changing magnetic field.
A light that keeps shining briefly even when you stop.

gewusst: With an old sidewall dynamo, pedalling feels noticeably harder when the light is switched on.
A hub dynamo causes so little resistance that you hardly notice it when riding.
The word dynamo comes from the Greek word dynamis for power.

teile.einleitung: Weight is the force with which a body is pulled downwards by the attraction of a body in space. It is what makes a rucksack sit heavily on your shoulders and a book press down on the table. The exciting thing is that on the Moon you would have the same mass, but a much smaller weight.
wichtigste: Weight is the force with which a body presses vertically on its support or pulls on what it hangs from.
On Earth, weight always points towards the centre of the Earth.
It is measured in newtons, abbreviated N.
On Earth a body with a mass of 1 kg has a weight of about 10 N.
The formula is: weight equals mass times gravitational field strength.
On the Moon the gravitational field strength is only about 1.6 N/kg, which is why you are much lighter there.
Mass stays the same everywhere; only the weight changes depending on the place.

abschnitte.text: Every body is attracted by the Earth. You feel this attraction as **weight**. It is the reason why an apple you let go of falls to the ground and why the scales show something when you stand on them. If a body lies on a support, it presses on it vertically with its weight.

Weight is calculated with the formula F = m · g. Here m is the **mass** in kilograms and g the **gravitational field strength** in newtons per kilogram. On Earth the gravitational field strength is almost exactly 9.81 N/kg; in everyday life people often simply calculate with 10 N/kg. A rucksack with a mass of 5 kg therefore has a weight of about 50 N on Earth.

In everyday life we often say “I weigh 40 kilos”, but what we actually mean is our **mass**. Mass says how much matter there is in a body, and it is the same everywhere in the universe. Weight, on the other hand, depends on how strongly the body in space you are standing on pulls. Bathroom scales actually measure weight and convert it into kilograms.

abschnitte.titel: On the Moon and other planets
abschnitte.text: The Moon has much less mass than the Earth and therefore pulls more weakly. Its gravitational field strength is only about 1.6 N/kg, roughly a sixth of the value on Earth. An astronaut with a mass of 60 kg has a weight of only about 97 N there instead of about 590 N. On Jupiter, on the other hand, she would weigh more than twice as much as on Earth.

On Earth, weight always points towards the **centre of the Earth**. That is why things fall “down” in Switzerland just as they do in Australia, even though down there points in a different direction from our point of view. A plumb line, that is a weight on a string, shows this direction exactly. Bricklayers use it to build walls straight.

Forces are measured with a **force meter**, which contains a spring. The greater the weight, the further the spring is stretched. A spring balance at the market works in the same way. At school small weights are often hung on a force meter to investigate the connection between mass and weight.

begriffe.erklaerung: The unit of force, named after the physicist Isaac Newton.
Shows how much matter there is in a body, measured in kilograms.
A number that says how strongly a body in space pulls on each kilogram.
A measuring device with a spring, used to determine forces.

gewusst: Thanks to the small weight, a person on the Moon could jump about six times as high as on Earth.
At the equator weight is very slightly less than at the poles, because the Earth turns and is a little thicker there.
Astronauts in the space station float even though the Earth still pulls on them almost as strongly there, because they are constantly falling around the Earth together with the station.

teile.einleitung: The Global Positioning System, GPS for short, is a satellite navigation system of the USA with which you can determine your position anywhere on Earth. It only works because the satellites have extremely precise atomic clocks on board. And these clocks even have to be corrected according to Einstein's theory of relativity.
wichtigste: GPS is a satellite navigation system of the USA.
A GPS receiver works out its position from the travel times of the signals from at least four satellites.
The satellites circle the Earth at a height of about 20,200 kilometres.
Because of their high speed, the satellite clocks run about 7 microseconds slower per day.
Because of the weaker gravity at orbital height, they run about 45 microseconds faster per day.
The gravitational effect is greater, so overall the clocks run fast.
Without a relativistic correction, the position error would grow to over 10 kilometres after one day.

abschnitte.text: GPS was developed from the 1970s by the US Department of Defense and has been fully in operation since 1995. Today about 30 **satellites** circle the Earth at a height of about 20,200 kilometres. Each satellite goes round the Earth about twice a day. Besides GPS there are the European **Galileo**, the Russian GLONASS and the Chinese BeiDou.

Each satellite constantly sends a signal with its exact position and the time. The **receiver**, for example in a mobile phone, measures how long the signals have been travelling. Because they travel at the speed of light, it can work out the distance to each satellite from this. With at least four satellites it determines its position and at the same time the error of its own, less precise clock.

Light travels about 300 metres in a millionth of a second. That is why the clocks must be extremely precise, otherwise the position becomes inaccurate. The satellites therefore carry **atomic clocks** on board. Even an error of a few billionths of a second would give a position error of a few metres.

abschnitte.titel: The theory of relativity in everyday life
abschnitte.text: According to the **special theory of relativity**, fast-moving clocks run more slowly; for GPS by about 7 microseconds per day. According to the **general theory of relativity**, clocks run faster where gravity is weaker; at orbital height by about 45 microseconds per day. The gravitational effect is greater, so overall the clocks run about 38 microseconds per day fast. Without a correction, the position error would grow to over 10 kilometres after one day.

So that the clocks tick correctly as seen from the Earth, their **frequency** is set slightly lower even before launch. Because the orbits are slightly **elliptical**, the effect changes during one orbit; the receiver calculates this correction itself. The rotation of the Earth during the signal's travel time must also be taken into account; this is called the **Sagnac effect**. The European Galileo system has to be corrected for relativity in the same way.

begriffe.erklaerung: A spacecraft that circles the Earth in an orbit.
An extremely precise clock that uses the vibrations of atoms to measure time.
A millionth of a second.
Albert Einstein's theory of how space, time and gravity are connected.
A difference in travel time caused by the rotation of the Earth.

gewusst: Albert Einstein developed the special theory of relativity in 1905, while he was working at the patent office in Bern.
A GPS receiver does not send anything itself; it only listens, which is why any number of people can use GPS at the same time.
GPS also supplies a very precise time, which mobile phone networks and banks, for example, use for synchronisation.

teile.einleitung: In electrical engineering, earthing means connecting an appliance or a metal part to the ground so that electricity can flow. This lets dangerous current flow safely into the ground instead of through a person. Earthing protects us in every house without us noticing it.
wichtigste: Earthing is a conducting connection to the ground.
In electrical engineering the earth serves as a reference point with 0 volts.
The metal casings of many appliances are earthed so that fault current does not flow through people.
A lightning conductor leads the lightning current safely into the earth.
A foundation earth electrode is a metal strip in the concrete foundation of a building.
Equipotential bonding connects metal parts such as water and heating pipes.
Tanker lorries are earthed while being filled so that no dangerous charge builds up.

abschnitte.text: In **earthing**, an electrical appliance or a metal part is connected to the ground with a wire that conducts electricity. The Earth is so huge that it can take in or give off almost unlimited amounts of charge. That is why in electrical engineering it serves as a **reference point** with a voltage of 0 volts. All other voltages are measured against this point. Current always flows to where it can flow away most easily.

Many appliances such as washing machines or irons have a **metal casing**. If a cable inside is faulty, the casing could suddenly become live. That is why it is connected to the earth through the **earth wire**, a wire with yellow and green insulation. The fault current then flows away through this wire instead of through a person. Usually a fuse or a **residual current circuit breaker** also switches off the current immediately.

A **lightning conductor** consists of metal rods and wires on the roof that lead down into the ground. If lightning strikes, it leads the huge current safely past the wall of the house into the earth. This prevents the house from catching fire or people from being hurt. The lightning conductor was invented by the American **Benjamin Franklin** in the 18th century. In Switzerland, lightning protection systems are especially common on church towers, schools and tall buildings.

Modern buildings have a **foundation earth electrode**, a metal strip cast into the concrete foundation. Through it, all the earth wires of the house are connected to the ground. **Equipotential bonding** also connects metal parts such as water and heating pipes to each other. This means that no dangerous differences in voltage arise between them. This is especially important in bathrooms.

It is particularly dangerous to touch a faulty appliance barefoot on a wet floor. Then the body is well connected to the earth, and current can easily flow through it. **Static electricity** can also be dangerous, for example when petrol flows through hoses. That is why a tanker lorry is earthed while being filled, so that no charge builds up and no spark occurs. Workers who make computer chips also often wear earthing straps on their wrists.

begriffe.erklaerung: A conducting connection between an appliance or metal part and the ground.
A yellow and green wire that connects the casings of appliances to the earth.
Current that takes the wrong path because of a fault.
Connecting metal parts in the house so that no voltage arises between them.
A metal strip in the concrete foundation that connects the house to the earth.

gewusst: On the Swiss plug with three pins, the middle pin, which is slightly offset, is the earth connection.
A lightning bolt can reach currents of several tens of thousands of amperes.
The small shock you get when touching a door handle after walking across a carpet is a discharge of static electricity.

teile.einleitung: The load line mark is a marking on the side of a ship that shows how deep the loaded ship may lie in the water at most. It protects ships from being overloaded and sinking. After the man who campaigned for it, the Briton Samuel Plimsoll, it is also called the Plimsoll line.
wichtigste: The load line mark shows how deep a loaded ship may sink into the water at most.
The freeboard is the distance from the waterline up to the deck.
The mark is also named after the British politician Samuel Plimsoll.
The fresh water mark lies higher than the seawater mark, because a ship sinks deeper in fresh water.
The marking “W” stands for winter.
The tropical mark lies higher because the weather in tropical seas is usually calmer.
Since the International Convention on Load Lines of 1966, load line marks have applied worldwide.

abschnitte.titel: What the load line mark is
abschnitte.text: The **load line mark** consists of a circle with a horizontal line through the middle and several short lines next to it. It is painted or welded on both sides of a ship, in the middle. When loading, the **waterline** must not go above the matching mark. In this way there is always enough **freeboard**, that is distance between the water and the deck, so that waves do not slop in.

A ship floats because it displaces as much water as it weighs itself; this is **Archimedes' principle**. The more heavily it is loaded, the deeper it sinks. Because of the salt, seawater is slightly denser than fresh water and therefore carries better. In a river or a harbour with fresh water, the same ship therefore lies deeper. Cold water is also denser than warm water.

Next to the circle there are lines with letters for different conditions. **S** stands for summer, **W** for winter and **T** for tropical. F stands for fresh water and TF for tropical fresh water. In winter the permitted line lies lower, because there are more storms and the ship needs more reserve. In tropical seas the weather is usually calmer, so the ship may lie a little deeper there.

In the 19th century some shipowners sent overloaded and poorly maintained ships to sea to earn more money. Many of these **coffin ships** sank, and numerous sailors died. The British politician **Samuel Plimsoll** fought against this and demanded a compulsory load line. In 1876 a law was passed in Britain that required such markings.

Today the **International Convention on Load Lines** of 1966 governs load line marks for ships all over the world. Experts from classification societies calculate for each ship where the marks must be. The letters next to the circle often also show which society set the mark. Port authorities can check whether a ship is lying too low.

Although Switzerland has no sea, there is a **Swiss merchant fleet** whose ships have Basel as their home port. The international load line rules also apply to these ships. Rhine barges that travel as far as Basel have their own gauge marks, from which the load can be read. So Switzerland's supply of goods also depends on safely loaded ships.

begriffe.erklaerung: The distance between the waterline and the deck of a ship.
The line up to which a ship lies in the water.
A body in water becomes lighter by as much as the displaced water weighs.
How much mass there is in a particular space.

gewusst: A fully loaded cargo ship lies deeper in the fresh water of a harbour than out at sea.
Despite having no coast, Switzerland has its own ocean-going ships with Basel as their home port.
In English, gym shoes are sometimes called plimsolls, because their rubber strip is reminiscent of the load line.

teile.einleitung: The Cartesian diver is a simple physics toy that floats up and down in a bottle of water. If you squeeze the bottle, the little diver sinks; if you let go, it rises again. Behind this is a bubble of air that can be squeezed.
wichtigste: The Cartesian diver is a small body with an air bubble in a bottle completely filled with water.
Because of the air bubble, the diver floats at the top at first.
If you squeeze the bottle, the air bubble gets smaller and the diver sinks.
If you let go of the bottle, the air expands again and the diver rises.
You can make a simple Cartesian diver from a pipette.
It is named after the French scholar René Descartes.

abschnitte.text: A Cartesian diver is a small hollow figure or tube in which some air is trapped. It floats in a plastic bottle that is **completely filled with water** and tightly closed. At the top of the diver there is an **air bubble**; at the bottom it is open, so that water can get in and out. In German it is also called a bottle diver. It has been used for centuries to show physics to children and students.

When you squeeze the bottle, the pressure rises throughout the water. Water can hardly be compressed, but air can. That is why the **air bubble** in the diver gets smaller, and some water gets into it. This makes the diver heavier in relation to its size, and it sinks. When you let go, the pressure falls, the air expands again and pushes the water out, and the diver rises.

Whether something floats or sinks depends on **buoyancy**. The water pushes every body upwards with a force as great as the weight of the water it displaces. This rule goes back to the Greek scholar **Archimedes**. With a large air bubble the diver displaces a lot of water and floats. If the bubble gets smaller, the buoyancy is less than its weight, and it sinks.

You need an empty plastic bottle, water and a **pipette**, the kind you get from craft or laboratory suppliers. You fill the pipette partly with water until it only just floats upright at the surface. So that it does not tip over, you can attach a paper clip or some modelling clay to the bottom. Then you fill the bottle to the brim, put the diver in and screw the lid on. With a little practice you can also make the diver float halfway up.

Many fish have a **swim bladder** filled with gas, which helps them float in the water. A **submarine** dives on a similar principle: it floods tanks with water to sink and pushes the water out again with compressed air to surface. Divers also wear a vest into which they let air or from which they release air. The Cartesian diver shows all these ideas in a single toy.

begriffe.erklaerung: The force with which water pushes a body upwards.
How strongly a force presses on a surface.
A small tube with a rubber bulb with which you can suck up liquids drop by drop.
A gas-filled organ in many fish that helps them float in the water.

gewusst: The pressure your hand puts on the bottle spreads evenly through all the water to the diver.
In the past Cartesian divers were made of glass in the shape of little devils, which were also called bottle imps.
With a delicate touch you can make the diver float exactly in the middle of the bottle, like a real submarine.

teile.einleitung: A spring scale is a simple measuring device with a metal spring inside. If you hang something on it, the spring is stretched, and on a scale you can read how heavy the object is. In physics lessons it is also called a force meter, because it actually measures a force.
wichtigste: A spring scale contains a metal spring.
At the bottom it usually has a hook on which you hang the object.
A weight twice as heavy stretches the spring twice as far.
You read the result on a scale with marks.
If you take the weight off, the spring contracts again.
If you pull the spring far too hard, it stays worn out and overstretched.
In physics lessons the spring scale is also called a force meter.

abschnitte.text: A spring scale consists of a **coil spring** in a tube or casing, a hook at the bottom and a scale. If you hang an object on the hook, the Earth pulls it down and the spring gets longer. A pointer or the edge of a little tube shows on the scale how hard it is being pulled. The heavier the object, the longer the spring becomes.

A spring gets longer evenly as the force increases. If a weight pulls the spring 2 cm longer, a weight twice as heavy pulls it 4 cm longer. This rule is called **Hooke's law**, after the English researcher Robert Hooke. That is why the marks on the scale are equally spaced.

As long as you do not stretch a spring too much, it always returns to its old shape; it is **elastic**. But if you pull it far too hard, it is permanently deformed and worn out. After that the spring scale measures incorrectly. That is why every spring scale says up to what weight or force you may use it.

In physics lessons the spring scale is used to measure forces in the unit **newton**. An object of 100 grams is pulled by the Earth with about 1 newton. There are force meters with soft springs for small forces and with stiff springs for large ones. You can also use them to measure how hard you have to pull on a trolley.

Anglers often weigh their catch right by the water with a small spring scale. Travellers use **luggage scales** to check that their bags are not too heavy for the plane. In the past, fruit and vegetables at markets were weighed on hanging spring scales. On the Moon a spring scale would show only about a sixth, because the pull there is weaker.

begriffe.erklaerung: A coiled metal wire that can be stretched and springs back again.
A row of marks and numbers for reading a measurement.
Returning to its old shape after being stretched.
The unit of force, named after Isaac Newton.
Another name for the spring scale in physics lessons.

gewusst: A beam balance shows the same on the Moon as on Earth, but a spring scale does not.
In the past, bathroom scales also often worked with springs inside.
If you hang two identical spring scales one below the other, both show the same weight.

teile.einleitung: A bottle opener is a small tool with which you remove metal caps from glass bottles. It is also called a cap lifter. It works on a simple physical principle, the lever.
wichtigste: A bottle opener is a lever with which you achieve a lot with little force.
The hook grips under the edge of the cap.
A long handle needs less force than a short one.
The metal cap with points is called a crown cap and was invented in the 19th century.
A standard crown cap has 21 points.
The cap holds so firmly because its edge is pressed around the neck of the bottle.
Many Swiss Army knives have a bottle opener built in.

abschnitte.text: A **bottle opener** is usually a flat piece of metal with an opening and a hook. You place it on the cap so that the hook grips under the edge and the other side rests on top of the cap. Then you lift the handle, and the cap pops off. Other names are **cap lifter** or beer opener.

A bottle opener is a **lever**, one of the simplest machines of all. The pivot is where the opener rests on top of the cap. The force of your hand acts on the long handle, and the load is the edge of the cap at the short end. The longer the handle compared with the short end, the less force you need. This connection is called the **law of the lever**; it was already known to the Greek scholar Archimedes.

The metal cap is called a **crown cap** because with its points it looks like a little crown. It was invented by the American William Painter in 1892, that is in the 19th century. A standard crown cap today has 21 points. Inside it has a thin seal, once made of cork, today mostly of plastic. When the bottle is closed, the edge is pressed firmly around the neck, which is why it holds even under the pressure of carbon dioxide.

Many children in Switzerland know the bottle opener from the **Swiss Army knife**. There it often sits on a blade together with a small screwdriver. But there are also bottle openers on walls in restaurants, on key rings or on lighters. Some openers have a magnet that holds on to the cap.

Crown caps are made of sheet steel and in Switzerland can be collected with metal or can recycling. Glass bottles belong in the glass collection, sorted by colour. Without an opener you should not open bottles with your teeth, as this can damage them. The edge of a table is not a good idea either, because the glass can splinter.

begriffe.erklaerung: A rigid bar that moves around a pivot and increases force.
The point around which a lever turns.
A metal cap with points for glass bottles.
The rule that the longer the effort arm, the less force you need.

gewusst: The first crown caps had 24 points; today 21 is standard.
Because crown caps sit so firmly, matching openers had to be developed as soon as they were invented.
With a bottle opener you often multiply the force of your hand several times.

teile.einleitung: Direct current is electric current that always flows in the same direction. Batteries and solar cells supply direct current. Almost all electronic devices, from mobile phones to computers, work with it inside.
wichtigste: Direct current always flows in the same direction.
Batteries, rechargeable batteries and solar cells supply direct current.
A standard round AA battery has 1.5 volts.
A mobile phone charger converts alternating current from the socket into direct current.
An inverter converts direct current into alternating current.
In the 1880s Thomas Edison set up a direct current network in New York.
High-voltage direct current transmission is used to carry electricity over very long distances.

abschnitte.text: Electric current is the movement of charge carriers, usually **electrons**. In **direct current** they always flow in the same direction, from the negative terminal to the positive terminal. In the **alternating current** from the socket, on the other hand, the direction keeps changing. Direct current is often abbreviated to DC, from the English term direct current.

abschnitte.titel: Where does direct current come from?
abschnitte.text: **Batteries** and rechargeable batteries produce direct current through chemical processes. A round AA battery has 1.5 volts, a car battery 12 volts. **Solar cells** on house roofs also supply direct current. So that this electricity can be fed into the grid, an **inverter** converts it into alternating current.

A mobile phone charger converts the alternating current from the socket into direct current at a low voltage. For this it needs a **rectifier**, whose most important component is the **diode**. It lets current through in only one direction. Through a USB cable, usually 5 volts or a little more then flow to the phone.

In the 1880s the inventor **Thomas Edison** set up a direct current network in New York to supply light bulbs. His rival George Westinghouse, together with Nikola Tesla, backed alternating current. Alternating current could easily be raised to a high voltage with transformers and carried over long distances. That is why it won out in most power grids; this dispute is called the **war of the currents**.

Today direct current is making a comeback. With **high-voltage direct current transmission**, electricity is sent over hundreds of kilometres or through undersea cables, with fewer losses than with alternating current. Many trams in Swiss towns run on direct current from the overhead line. Electric cars also store their energy in batteries as direct current.

begriffe.erklaerung: Current that always flows in the same direction.
Current that keeps changing its direction, as in the socket.
A device that converts direct current into alternating current.
The unit of measurement of electrical voltage.

gewusst: The first battery was built by the Italian Alessandro Volta around 1800; the unit volt is named after him.
An electric eel produces electric shocks with direct current of several hundred volts.
In a laptop the chips work with direct voltages of only about one volt.

teile.einleitung: A gravity dam is a dam that holds back the water of a reservoir by its enormous weight alone. In cross-section it is triangular, very wide at the bottom and narrow at the top. The tallest gravity dam in the world is in Switzerland: the Grande Dixence in Valais.
wichtigste: A gravity dam withstands the water pressure with its own weight.
Its cross-section is triangular, wide at the bottom and narrow at the top.
Above all it must be secured against sliding and tipping over.
Water pressure increases with depth; at a depth of 100 metres it is about 9.8 bar.
It is especially suitable for wide valleys whose sides cannot take a large arch thrust.
During construction the concrete is cooled so that the heat of setting does not cause cracks.
At 285 metres, the Grande Dixence in Valais is the tallest gravity dam in the world.

abschnitte.text: Dams hold back rivers to form lakes, so that water can be stored and electricity produced. An **arch dam** is curved and passes the water pressure into the rock walls of the valley. A **gravity dam**, on the other hand, simply stands firm through its huge mass of concrete. It is especially suitable for wide valleys whose sides could not take a large arch thrust.

**Water pressure** increases evenly with depth. At a water depth of 100 metres it is about 9.8 bar at the foot of the dam, almost ten times the air pressure. That is why the dam is thickest at the bottom. The total force of the water on a strip 1 metre wide acts at a third of the water depth, measured from the bottom, and at a depth of 100 metres it is about 49 meganewtons.

The dam must neither **slide** on its foundation nor **tip** forwards. Its weight presses it firmly onto the rock and so creates friction. **Uplift pressure** is dangerous: water gets under the dam and pushes it upwards from below, which reduces its stability. That is why engineers build seals and drainage boreholes into the ground underneath.

Gravity dams need huge amounts of **concrete**. When concrete hardens, it produces heat, the so-called **heat of setting**. In such a thick dam this heat cannot escape quickly, and cracks could form as it cools. That is why the dam is built in blocks and the fresh concrete is cooled, for example with water in cooling pipes.

The **Grande Dixence** in the Val des Dix in the canton of Valais was completed in 1961. At 285 metres it is the tallest gravity dam in the world and almost as tall as the Eiffel Tower. About 6 million cubic metres of concrete were used to build it. It holds back the **Lac des Dix**, whose water produces electricity in several hydroelectric power stations.

begriffe.erklaerung: A wall that holds back a river to form a lake.
A curved dam that passes the water pressure into the sides of the valley.
The pressure of water that gets under the dam and pushes it upwards.
The heat produced when concrete hardens.

gewusst: With the concrete of the Grande Dixence you could build a wall 1.5 metres high and 10 centimetres thick once around the Earth; at least, that is how it is often described.
Many dams have inspection galleries running through them, which experts walk through regularly to monitor the dam.
Switzerland gets more than half of its electricity from hydropower.

teile.einleitung: Electromagnetic induction means that a changing magnetic field creates an electrical voltage in a wire. Michael Faraday discovered this effect in 1831. Almost all the electricity we use is produced in power stations with the help of induction.
wichtigste: A changing magnetic field creates an electrical voltage in a loop of wire.
Michael Faraday discovered electromagnetic induction in 1831.
A magnet at rest next to a coil at rest creates no voltage.
The faster the magnetic field changes, the greater the induced voltage.
According to Lenz's law, the induced current opposes its cause.
Generators, transformers and induction hobs are based on induction.
Wireless charging of a mobile phone also works by induction.

abschnitte.text: If you move a magnet into or out of a coil of wire, a connected meter shows a **voltage**. If the magnet stays still, the voltage disappears again. So what matters is not the magnetic field itself, but its **change**. This process is called **electromagnetic induction**, from the Latin word for leading in.

**Faraday's law of induction** says that the induced voltage is greater the faster the **magnetic flux** through the loop of wire changes. More turns in the coil also give more voltage. You can change the field by moving the magnet, turning the coil or switching a current on and off. If the circuit is closed, an **induced current** flows.

The Englishman Michael **Faraday** discovered induction in 1831 in London. He wound two coils around an iron ring and noticed that current briefly flowed in the second coil when he switched the first one on or off. Independently of him, the American Joseph Henry made similar observations. In 1834 Heinrich Lenz formulated **Lenz's law**, which is named after him.

In a **generator**, a magnet turns inside coils or a coil turns in a magnetic field. The constant change in the field produces alternating current. This is how the hydroelectric power stations in the Swiss Alps, wind turbines and the bicycle dynamo work. A **transformer** uses induction to step voltages up or down.

An **induction hob** creates a rapidly changing magnetic field under the glass ceramic. This induces currents in the base of an iron pan, which heat the pot directly while the hob itself stays cool. Wireless chargers for mobile phones and electric toothbrushes work in a similar way. Anti-theft devices in shops and bank cards for contactless payment also use induction.

begriffe.erklaerung: Creating a voltage through a changing magnetic field.
A measure of how much magnetic field passes through a surface.
The induced current always opposes its cause.
A device that converts alternating voltages using two coils.

gewusst: A magnet falling through a copper pipe is strongly slowed down by induced currents.
Faraday had hardly any schooling and started out as a bookbinder's apprentice.
On an induction hob, a pan made of glass or pure aluminium does not get warm.

teile.einleitung: A construction crane lifts heavy loads high up far away from its tower without tipping over. It manages this thanks to a heavy counterweight on the other side. It works like a seesaw, on which a heavy person near the middle balances a lighter one far out.
wichtigste: The counterweight of a tower crane hangs on the short counter-jib.
It usually consists of large concrete blocks.
The counterweight balances the turning moment of the load.
Turning moment means force times distance from the pivot.
Right at the end of the jib a crane may lift less than near the tower.
A load moment limiter stops the crane if a load far out becomes too heavy.
After work the crane is left free to turn, so that it lines itself up with the wind like a weathervane.

abschnitte.titel: How a tower crane is built
abschnitte.text: A **tower crane** consists of a tall tower, a long jib and a short **counter-jib**. At the top, the upper part with the jib and counter-jib turns around the tower. A trolley with the hook moves back and forth along the jib. The counterweights made of concrete blocks hang on the counter-jib.

A crane works according to the **law of the lever**. The turning moment is force times distance from the pivot, here the tower. If a crane lifts 20 kilonewtons at a distance of 25 metres and the counterweight sits 10 metres from the tower, it must weigh 50 kilonewtons. Then 20 times 25 equals 50 times 10, and the crane is in **balance**.

The further out a load hangs, the longer its lever arm and the greater its turning moment. That is why a crane may lift only a smaller load right at the end than near the tower. On many cranes there are signs with the permitted loads for different distances. The **load moment limiter** monitors this automatically and stops the crane if there is danger.

Without a load, the counterweight would pull the crane backwards. So that it still stands safely, a tower crane often has extra **ballast** at its base, also made of concrete blocks. Some cranes are also anchored in a concrete foundation. In this way the crane stays stable in every position.

Wind pushes on the long jib and can produce large forces. After work, therefore, the brake on the slewing gear is released, and the crane turns freely like a **weathervane**. In this way the jib always points with the wind and offers the smallest surface for it to push against. In a strong storm crane work is stopped completely.

begriffe.erklaerung: The short arm of the crane, on which the counterweights hang.
The turning effect of a force, calculated as force times distance from the pivot.
Extra weight that makes a device or vehicle stable.
A carriage that moves back and forth along the jib and carries the hook.

gewusst: The counterweights of a large construction crane can weigh several tonnes together, as much as several cars.
A crane is put up piece by piece with the help of another crane, usually a mobile one.
Crane operators often sit in a small cab high up on the tower or control the crane by radio from the ground.

teile.einleitung: Skydiving is a sport in which you jump out of an aeroplane, fall freely at first and then float down to Earth on a parachute. It is an experience somewhere between weightlessness and the thrill of speed. To make sure everything goes safely, you need good training and reliable equipment.
wichtigste: The phase between jumping out and opening the parachute is called freefall.
Normal sport jumps usually start at a height of about 4000 m.
Under an open parachute you sink at about 5 m/s.
When the parachute opens, the jumper feels a strong braking.
Every jumper carries a reserve parachute for emergencies.
In a tandem jump, a guest is strapped to an experienced jumper.
In 2012 the Austrian Felix Baumgartner jumped from a height of about 39 km.

abschnitte.text: A small aeroplane usually takes the jumpers up to a height of about 4000 metres. After jumping out, **freefall** begins, which lasts about a minute from this height. At a height of about 1000 to 1500 metres the jumper opens the parachute. After that they glide calmly to the landing area for a few minutes.

At first the jumper gets faster and faster because of gravity. But as the speed increases, air resistance grows strongly. Soon the two forces are equal, and the speed stays constant; this is called **terminal velocity**. Lying on the stomach this is about 200 km/h, head first much more. When the parachute opens, you are slowed down sharply and land at about 5 m/s.

The equipment includes a main parachute, a **reserve parachute**, a helmet and an altimeter. Many jumpers also have an **automatic activation device**, which opens the reserve parachute by itself if you are still in freefall too low down. The parachutes are packed and checked by trained experts. Anyone who wants to jump themselves first takes a course with theory and accompanied jumps.

In a **tandem jump**, a guest is strapped with a harness in front of an experienced tandem pilot. The pilot takes care of everything, from jumping out to landing. In this way you can experience a jump without long training. In Switzerland, tandem jumps with a view of the Alps are popular with guests from all over the world.

In 1797 the Frenchman **André-Jacques Garnerin** jumped from a balloon over Paris and is considered a pioneer of parachuting. On 14 October 2012 the Austrian **Felix Baumgartner** jumped from a balloon capsule at a height of about 39 km above the USA. In freefall he was the first person to break the sound barrier without a vehicle. In 2014 the American Alan Eustace jumped from an even slightly greater height.

begriffe.erklaerung: Falling while the parachute is still closed.
The highest falling speed, reached when air resistance and weight are equal.
A device that shows how high you are at the moment.
A jump for two, in which a guest is strapped to a professional.
Several jumpers form shapes together in freefall.

gewusst: In freefall you do not feel butterflies in your stomach as on a roller coaster, but rather a strong stream of air from below.
In formation skydiving, dozens of jumpers hold hands in freefall and form stars and patterns.
Felix Baumgartner fell from so high up that he had to wear a pressure suit like an astronaut.

teile.einleitung: Faraday's law of induction describes how a changing magnetic field creates an electrical voltage in a coil of wire. This electromagnetic induction was discovered by the Englishman Michael Faraday in 1831. Almost all the electricity from our sockets is produced in generators according to this principle.
wichtigste: A voltage is only induced when the magnetic flux through the coil changes.
The induced voltage equals the number of turns times the change in flux per unit of time.
If you double the number of turns, the induced voltage doubles.
In a constant magnetic field, a coil at rest supplies 0 volts.
If the conductor is at rest and only the magnetic field changes, this is called transformer induction.
A transformer does not work with direct current, because then the flux in the core does not change.
A loop of wire turning steadily in a magnetic field supplies a sinusoidal alternating voltage.

abschnitte.text: If you move a magnet into a coil of wire, a meter briefly shows a voltage. If you hold the magnet still, it disappears again. So what matters is the change in the **magnetic flux**, measured in webers (Wb). This phenomenon is called **electromagnetic induction**.

The law is: U = N · ΔΦ / Δt, where N is the number of turns and ΔΦ / Δt is the change in flux per second. If the flux through 100 turns changes by 0.02 Wb in 0.1 s, 20 V is produced. If it rises from 0 to 4 mWb in 500 turns in 0.2 s, that gives 10 V. The minus sign in the exact formula stands for **Lenz's law**: the induced current opposes its cause.

In **transformer induction** the conductor is at rest and only the magnetic field changes, for example in a transformer. In motional induction the conductor moves through a magnetic field. A rod 0.2 m long moving at 3 m/s at right angles through a field of 0.5 T produces 0.3 V. If a coil turns steadily in a magnetic field, a sinusoidal alternating voltage is produced; with 50 turns, 0.02 m², 0.1 T and 50 Hz, its peak is about 31 V.

**Michael Faraday** lived in England from 1791 to 1867 and was the son of a blacksmith. He first trained as a bookbinder and taught himself science largely on his own. In 1831 he discovered induction using coils around an iron ring. He became one of the most important experimental physicists, and the unit farad is named after him.

In hydroelectric power stations, for example at the reservoirs in the Alps, turbines turn huge **generators** and so produce electricity. **Transformers** convert voltages, for example from high-voltage lines to the 230 volts in the house. The bike dynamo, the induction hob and wireless charging of mobile phones are also based on induction. Electric toothbrushes are often charged in this way too.

begriffe.erklaerung: Producing a voltage through a changing magnetic field.
A measure of how much magnetic field passes through a surface, measured in webers.
The number of windings of wire in a coil.
A machine that converts movement into electric current.
A device that makes alternating voltages larger or smaller.

gewusst: When a politician asked Faraday what his discovery was good for, he is said to have replied that one day it would be possible to tax it.
An induction hob itself hardly gets hot; it heats the base of the pan directly.
Induction was also discovered independently by the American Joseph Henry, at about the same time as Faraday.

teile.einleitung: A fixed pulley is a wheel with a groove over which a rope runs, and whose axle hangs firmly from a beam or a ceiling. It does not save any force, but it changes the direction in which you have to pull. That is why it is much more comfortable to pull a load up with it.
wichtigste: The axle of a fixed pulley is attached to a fixed mounting.
A fixed pulley does not save any force; it only redirects the force.
You can pull downwards and use your own weight.
If you lift a load by 3 m, you also have to pull 3 m of rope.
In terms of physics, the fixed pulley is a lever with equal arms on both sides.
Because of friction you actually need a little more force than the weight of the load.
Combined with a movable pulley, it makes a block and tackle.

abschnitte.text: The **fixed pulley** is one of the simple machines, like the lever and the inclined plane. It consists of a wheel that can turn, with a groove in which a rope runs. The axle is attached to a fixed mounting, for example a beam, and does not move with the load. The load hangs on one end of the rope, and you pull on the other.

With a fixed pulley, without friction, you need exactly as much force as the load weighs. But it changes the **direction of the force**: instead of lifting upwards, you pull downwards. This is more comfortable, because you can use your own body weight. A person with a weight of 600 N can just hold a load of 600 N in balance in this way.

With a fixed pulley the length of rope pulled is equal to the height lifted: if you lift a load by 3 m, you have to pull 3 m of rope. This fits the **golden rule of mechanics**, according to which force saved is always paid for with a longer distance. Because the fixed pulley saves no force, it does not need a longer distance either. You can think of it as a **lever** with two arms of equal length, whose pivot is the axle.

In reality you need a little more force than the weight of the load. The reason is **friction** in the bearing of the axle and in the rope, which has to bend around the pulley. Well-greased ball bearings keep the friction small. For heavy loads a block and tackle is therefore often used, which combines fixed and movable pulleys and so saves force.

On a **flagpole** you pull the flag up with a rope over a fixed pulley at the top of the pole. Old draw wells and goods hoists on farmhouses work in a similar way. In top-rope climbing the rope runs through an anchor at the top of the rock to the person belaying; this anchor acts like a fixed pulley. Fixed pulleys are also found in cranes, lifts and fitness machines.

begriffe.erklaerung: A basic tool such as a lever, pulley or inclined plane that makes work easier.
A pulley that moves with the load and halves the force needed.
A combination of fixed and movable pulleys that saves force.
What you save in force, you must add in distance.

gewusst: Even in ancient Greece pulleys were used to lift heavy stones for temples.
A flagpole usually has exactly one fixed pulley at the top, so that the flag can be raised from the ground.
On sailing ships many ropes run over pulleys, which sailors call blocks.

teile.einleitung: A forced oscillation occurs when a system that can oscillate is pushed from outside again and again at the same rhythm. After a short time it then oscillates at the rhythm of the driving force, no longer at its own. If this rhythm exactly matches the natural frequency, the oscillation can become very large; this is called resonance.
wichtigste: After the transient phase, a driven system oscillates at the driving frequency.
At resonance the oscillator is 90° out of phase with the driver.
If the driving frequency is far below the natural frequency, the oscillator moves almost in phase with about the amplitude of the driver.
If the driving frequency is far above it, the oscillator moves in antiphase with a small amplitude.
Stronger damping makes the peak of the resonance curve lower and wider.
Pohl's wheel with an eddy current brake is a well-known school apparatus for forced oscillations.
A car's rear-view mirror often vibrates only at a particular engine speed, because there the engine frequency matches its natural frequency.

abschnitte.text: Every system that can oscillate, for example a swing or a spring with a weight, has a **natural frequency**. It oscillates at this frequency when you push it once and then let go. In a **forced oscillation**, on the other hand, the system is constantly driven at the same rhythm by a **driver**. This can be a motor, a hand or a sound wave. The oscillating system is also called an oscillator.

Right at the start, the natural oscillation and the forced oscillation overlap. This unsettled initial phase is called the **transient phase**. Because every real oscillation is damped a little, the natural oscillation disappears over time. After that the system oscillates steadily at the **driving frequency**. How strongly it oscillates depends on how close this frequency is to the natural frequency.

If the driving frequency is much lower than the natural frequency, the oscillator follows the driver almost **in phase** with about the same amplitude. If it is much higher, the oscillator can hardly keep up and moves in **antiphase** with a small amplitude. If the two frequencies almost match, **resonance** occurs and the amplitude becomes especially large. The oscillator is then 90° out of step with the driver. If you plot the amplitude against the frequency, you get the resonance curve.

**Damping** slows down an oscillation, for example through friction or air resistance. The stronger the damping, the lower and wider the peak of the resonance curve becomes. Without damping, the amplitude at resonance could keep growing and growing. In physics lessons this is often studied with **Pohl's wheel**. Here an **eddy current brake** with a magnet slows down the oscillating copper wheel to different degrees.

A swing goes high if you push it at exactly the right rhythm. A rear-view mirror in a car often vibrates only at a particular **engine speed**, because then the engine frequency matches its natural frequency. Bridges and buildings can also be made to oscillate by wind, footsteps or earthquakes. If the oscillation becomes so strong that something breaks, it is called a **resonance disaster**. That is why engineers build dampers into tall buildings and bridges.

begriffe.erklaerung: The frequency at which a system oscillates by itself when you push it.
The rhythm at which a system is driven from outside.
Especially strong oscillation when the driving and natural frequencies match.
A braking effect that makes an oscillation weaker.
The greatest displacement of an oscillation.

gewusst: Soldiers are told not to march in step when crossing some bridges, so that they do not set the bridge into resonance.
A trained singer can make a thin wine glass vibrate with the right note.
In some skyscrapers a huge pendulum ball hangs near the top and works as a damper against oscillations.

teile.einleitung: A fat fire is a fire in which hot oil or fat burns, usually in a pan or deep-fat fryer in the kitchen. It is especially dangerous because you must never put it out with water. But if you know how to react correctly, you can smother a small fat fire safely.
wichtigste: A fat fire starts when oil or fat gets so hot that it catches fire.
Never put out a fat fire with water, or there will be a dangerous burst of flame.
A lid helps because it takes the air away from the fire.
A fire blanket can also smother a fat fire.
Afterwards switch off the hob and do not carry the pan away.
In a larger fire, get everyone out of the room and in Switzerland call the fire brigade on 118.

abschnitte.text: If you heat oil in a pan for too long, it gets hotter and hotter and starts to smoke. At about 300 degrees the oil can catch fire all by itself, even without a flame. This often happens when someone forgets the pan on the hob. Old fat residues in deep-fat fryers or cooker hoods can also burn. That is why you should never leave hot oil unattended.

If you pour water onto burning fat, the water immediately sinks under the hot oil. There it evaporates explosively, because one litre of water produces about 1700 litres of **steam**. The steam carries the burning fat up into the air in fine droplets. A huge **burst of flame** results, which can shoot up to the ceiling and seriously injure people. This is also called a **fat explosion**.

Fire needs three things: fuel, heat and **oxygen** from the air. If you put a suitable lid on the pan, no more air reaches the fire, and it is smothered. A **fire blanket**, which you lay carefully over the pan, works just as well. Afterwards you switch off the hob and leave the lid or blanket in place until everything has cooled down. For fat fires there are also special fire extinguishers of fire class F.

If the fire has already spread, the rule is: getting yourself to safety is more important than putting it out. Everyone should leave the flat, and the doors are closed behind them. Then you call the **fire brigade** on the emergency number 118. You say where the fire is, what is burning and whether people are in danger. Never lift up a burning pan and carry it away, because the fat can slop over.

Children should only cook with hot oil together with adults. A suitable lid should always be within reach next to the hob when frying. Many families hang a fire blanket in the kitchen where it is easy to reach. Anyone who practises where the fire blanket hangs and how to pull it out will react faster in an emergency. A smoke alarm gives an early warning if something does catch fire.

begriffe.erklaerung: A fire of burning cooking oil or fat.
A sudden, very high flame.
To put out a fire by taking away its air.
The name for fires of cooking oils and fats.

gewusst: At demonstrations the fire brigade often shows how a cup of water on burning oil produces a flame several metres high.
Flour and salt are not safe ways to put out a fat fire either.

teile.einleitung: A standard weight is a body with an exactly known mass, usually made of metal. Standard weights are needed to weigh with a beam balance or to check scales. Each piece is marked with how heavy it is.
wichtigste: A standard weight has an exactly known mass.
Today standard weights are mostly made of metal, for example brass or stainless steel.
Each standard weight is marked with how heavy it is.
On a beam balance you put the weights on the opposite side from the goods.
When the balance is level, the goods are as heavy as all the weights together.
In the laboratory, small precise weights are handled with tweezers.
Standard weights are used to check whether scales measure correctly.

abschnitte.text: A **beam balance** has two pans on a beam that is supported in the middle. You put the goods on one pan and **standard weights** on the other. When the beam is level, both sides are equally heavy. If, for example, 100 grams, 50 grams and 20 grams balance an apple, the apple weighs 170 grams.

Standard weights come in a **set of weights** with cleverly chosen sizes, such as 1, 2, 2, 5, 10, 20, 20, 50 grams and so on. With them almost any weight can be put together. For example, 200 grams and 100 grams make 300 grams. If there are 200 grams of flour on the left and 100 and 50 grams on the right, a 50-gram piece is still missing.

In the past, stones, iron or bronze were also used as weights. Today precise standard weights are mostly made of **stainless steel** or brass, because these metals do not rust. Many have the shape of a small cylinder with a knob on top. Very small pieces under one gram are thin plates or wires.

Even a fingerprint of grease and dirt makes a very precise standard weight a little heavier. That is why small, precise weights are handled in the laboratory with **tweezers** or gloves. Standard weights are divided into **accuracy classes**. The most precise ones are used only in special laboratories.

Until 2019 the **kilogram** was defined by a cylinder of platinum and iridium near Paris, the international prototype kilogram. Since then it has been defined through a constant of nature, the **Planck constant**. In Switzerland the Federal Institute of Metrology METAS in Wabern near Bern makes sure that weights and scales measure correctly. Scales in shops are officially checked regularly, so that nobody gets too little.

begriffe.erklaerung: How much matter a body has, measured in grams or kilograms.
A balance with two pans on a beam that is supported in the middle.
A collection of standard weights in different sizes.
Officially checking whether a measuring device measures correctly.

gewusst: The former international prototype kilogram was established in 1889 and lay in a safe under three glass bell jars.
Even in ancient Egypt and Mesopotamia traders used weight stones to weigh goods.
A standard weight does not show weight as a force, but mass, and that is exactly the same on the Moon as on Earth.

teile.einleitung: The first law of thermodynamics is the law of conservation of energy for heat and work. It says that energy can neither come from nothing nor disappear; it can only be converted. That is why there can be no machine that does work for ever without a supply of energy.
wichtigste: The formula is ΔU = Q + W, where W is the work done on the system.
ΔU is the change in internal energy, Q the heat supplied.
According to the first law, a perpetual motion machine of the first kind is impossible.
If a gas takes in 500 J of heat and gives out 200 J of work, its internal energy rises by 300 J.
In a rigid container, heat supplied becomes internal energy completely.
If you compress a thermally insulated gas, it becomes warmer.
Julius Robert Mayer, James Prescott Joule and Hermann von Helmholtz discovered the law between about 1842 and 1847.

abschnitte.text: Every system, such as a gas in a cylinder, has an **internal energy** U. It lies in the movement and arrangement of its particles. It can be changed in two ways: by **heat** Q or by **work** W. That is why ΔU = Q + W, where W here is the work done on the system from outside. If the gas itself gives out work, W becomes negative.

For a long time people believed that heat was an invisible substance. In 1842 the German doctor **Julius Robert Mayer** realised that heat and work can be converted into each other. The Englishman **James Prescott Joule** showed with experiments how much work is needed for a certain amount of warming. In 1847 Hermann von Helmholtz formulated the general law of conservation of energy. Today the unit of energy is named after Joule.

A gas takes in 500 J of heat and does 200 J of work on its surroundings, so its internal energy rises by 300 J. In an **isothermal** expansion the internal energy of an ideal gas stays the same, so it gives out all 800 J of heat taken in as work. If a gas expands by 3 litres at 2 · 10⁵ Pa, it does 600 J of **pressure-volume work**. In a rigid container no pressure-volume work is possible, so 1200 J of heat increases the internal energy by 1200 J.

If you heat a gas at constant pressure, it expands and gives out part of the heat as work. That is why you need more heat than at constant volume. The **molar heat capacity** at constant pressure is therefore greater. To heat 1 mol of a monatomic ideal gas by 20 K at constant pressure, you need about 416 J.

For centuries tinkerers have tried to build a machine that runs for ever without being driven. Such a **perpetual motion machine** of the first kind would create energy out of nothing. The first law shows that this is impossible. Engines, power stations and our own bodies can only convert energy, for example chemical energy from food into movement and heat.

begriffe.erklaerung: All the energy contained in the particles of a body.
Energy that flows because of a difference in temperature.
Energy transferred by a force along a distance.
At a constant temperature.
An imaginary machine that is supposed to run for ever without a supply of energy.

gewusst: As early as 1775 the Paris Academy of Sciences decided to stop examining proposals for perpetual motion machines.
If you use a bicycle pump quickly, it gets warm at the bottom because the air is compressed.
Julius Robert Mayer got his idea as a ship's doctor, when he noticed that sailors' blood was a brighter red in the tropics.

teile.einleitung: An electromagnet is a magnet that you can switch on and off with electricity. It usually consists of a coil of wire wound around an iron core. Electromagnets are found in doorbells, loudspeakers, electric motors and huge cranes at the scrapyard.
wichtigste: An electromagnet works like this: current flows through a coil of wire and creates a magnetic field.
If you switch off the current, the magnetic field disappears almost completely.
An iron core in the coil strengthens the magnetic field greatly.
More turns and more current make the magnet stronger.
If you reverse the direction of the current, the north and south poles swap places.
The electromagnet was invented in the 1820s.
Electromagnets are found in motors, loudspeakers, relays and maglev trains.

abschnitte.text: Every electric current creates a **magnetic field** around it. If you wind a wire into a **coil** with many turns, the fields of the individual turns add up. This creates a magnetic field like that of a bar magnet, with a north pole and a south pole. Unlike a permanent magnet, the electromagnet only works while current is flowing.

If you put an **iron core** into the coil, the magnetic field often becomes a hundred times stronger or even more. This is because the tiny magnetic regions in the iron line up and help. More **turns** and a greater **current** also strengthen the magnet. You can build a simple electromagnet yourself: with a large iron nail, insulated wire and a battery.

In 1820 Hans Christian Ørsted discovered that current deflects a compass needle. In 1825 the Englishman William **Sturgeon** built one of the first electromagnets with an iron core. Shortly afterwards the American Joseph Henry improved it with many insulated turns. His magnets could lift loads of several hundred kilograms.

In a **doorbell** an electromagnet pulls a small hammer, which strikes a bell. **Loudspeakers** use an electromagnet to move a membrane and so produce sounds. A **relay** is a switch that uses a small current and an electromagnet to switch a large current. Every electric motor, for example in an electric bike, also uses electromagnets.

At scrapyards, **lifting magnets** pick up car parts weighing tonnes and drop them again when switched off. In hospitals, superconducting electromagnets in the **MRI scanner** create very strong fields for images of the inside of the body. At CERN near Geneva, more than a thousand huge magnets steer the particles in the LHC accelerator onto their circular path. In Japan and China, maglev trains float above the track thanks to electromagnets.

begriffe.erklaerung: Wire wound up in many turns.
A piece of iron in the coil that strengthens the magnetic field.
The area around a magnet in which it exerts forces.
An electrically controlled switch with an electromagnet.

gewusst: The magnets of an MRI scanner are tens of thousands of times stronger than the Earth's magnetic field.
You can build a small electromagnet yourself in a few minutes with a nail, wire and a battery.
As early as around 1830, Joseph Henry's electromagnets could lift almost a tonne of iron.
