teile.einleitung: The Earth's rotation is the turning of the Earth around its own axis. The Earth needs about 24 hours for one turn, and this creates day and night. Although we feel nothing of it, we are racing through space at high speed.
wichtigste: The Earth turns once around itself in about 24 hours.
The imaginary line around which it turns is called the Earth's axis.
The Earth turns from west to east, which is why the Sun rises in the east.
At the equator the ground moves at over 1600 km/h.
At the poles you move the slowest due to the Earth's rotation.
In one hour the Earth turns by 15 degrees.
Because of the Earth's rotation it is not midday everywhere at once, which is why there are time zones.

abschnitte.text: The Earth turns like a spinning top around the **Earth's axis**, an imaginary line from the North Pole to the South Pole. It turns from west to east. That is why it seems to us as if the Sun, Moon and stars rise in the east and set in the west. In reality, though, it is the Earth that moves and not the sky.

For one full turn compared with the stars, the Earth needs about 23 hours and 56 minutes; this is the **sidereal day**. It takes about 24 hours until the Sun is in the same place in the sky again, because in the meantime the Earth has moved a little further along its path around the Sun. In 24 hours the Earth turns 360 degrees, so in one hour it turns 15 degrees. Very slowly the rotation is braked by the tides, and over millions of years the days become a little longer.

At the **equator** a point travels the whole circumference of the Earth, about 40,000 km, in one day. That gives a speed of over 1600 km/h. In Switzerland the circle is smaller, and you move at about 1140 km/h. At the **poles** you only turn on the spot and move the slowest. We do not feel the movement because it is very even and the air moves along with us.

Because the Earth turns, one half is always lit by the Sun and the other is in the dark. Japan lies further east than Switzerland, so the Sun rises there many hours earlier. Because it is not midday everywhere at the same time, the Earth has been divided into **time zones**, each about 15 degrees wide. Switzerland belongs to Central European Time.

For a long time many people believed that the Earth stood still and the sky turned around it. In the 16th century Nicolaus Copernicus described a view of the world in which the Earth turns and circles the Sun. In 1851 the Frenchman Léon Foucault demonstrated the Earth's rotation with a long **pendulum** in Paris: the plane in which the pendulum swung slowly turned. The **Coriolis force**, which deflects large wind and ocean currents, is also caused by the Earth's rotation.

begriffe.erklaerung: An imaginary line through the North and South Poles around which the Earth turns.
An area on Earth where the same clock time applies.
The time for one full turn of the Earth compared with the stars, about 23 hours 56 minutes.
A long pendulum whose plane of swing slowly turns because of the Earth's rotation.
An apparent force that deflects moving air and water on the turning Earth.

gewusst: Because the Earth turns, it is slightly flattened at the poles and a little thicker at the equator.
Rockets like to launch towards the east and near the equator, because the Earth's rotation gives them extra speed.
Hundreds of millions of years ago a day on Earth was much shorter than today.

teile.einleitung: Electric potential shows how much energy an electric charge has at a particular place, relative to the size of the charge. You can imagine it like height in a landscape where charges roll downhill. The difference between two potentials is the well-known electrical voltage.
wichtigste: Electric potential is measured in volts.
Electrical voltage is the difference between two potentials.
You must choose a reference point with 0 V; in electrical engineering this is often the earth.
Surfaces with the same potential are called equipotential surfaces and are at right angles to the field lines.
Along an equipotential surface you can move a charge without doing any work.
Inside a charged metal body the potential is the same everywhere.
The potential of a point charge is proportional to 1/r.

abschnitte.text: The **electric potential** φ describes the potential energy of a charge at a place, divided by the charge. You can compare it with height in the terrain. A positive charge moves by itself from high to low potential, just as a ball rolls downhill. The unit is the **volt**, named after the Italian physicist Alessandro Volta.

The electrical **voltage** between two points is the difference between their potentials. A 1.5 V battery has exactly this difference in potential between its positive and negative terminals. Where the potential is zero can be chosen freely, similar to how heights are measured from sea level. In electrical engineering the earth or the **ground** of a device is often chosen as 0 V.

Points with the same potential form **equipotential surfaces**, similar to contour lines on a map. They are always at right angles to the electric field lines. If you move a charge along such a surface, you do not have to do any work. Around a point charge the equipotential surfaces are spherical shells, because the potential decreases with 1/r. In equilibrium, the surface and the inside of a metal body have the same potential everywhere.

When a charge q passes through a potential difference U, the field does the work W = q · U. A charge of 2 µC passing through 50 V thus gains 0.1 mJ of energy. An **electron** that passes through 100 V from rest is accelerated to about 5.9 million metres per second. In particle physics such energies are measured in **electronvolts** (eV).

The earth wire in sockets connects the casings of appliances to earth potential. If you touch such a casing, there is no dangerous voltage to the ground. Birds can sit on a high-voltage line because both feet have almost the same potential. It only becomes dangerous if you touch the line and the earth at the same time.

begriffe.erklaerung: Energy per charge at a particular place in the electric field.
The difference in electric potential between two points.
A surface on which the potential is the same everywhere.
The energy an electron gains when it passes through 1 volt.
A connection to the earth that serves as the 0 volt reference point.

gewusst: If you stand in a meadow with your legs apart during a thunderstorm, a nearby lightning strike can create a dangerous step voltage between your feet.
In the LHC particle accelerator at CERN, protons reach energies of several trillion electronvolts.
The word potential comes from the Latin potentia and means power or ability.

teile.einleitung: Coloured glasses have tinted lenses that let only part of the light through. This makes the world look yellowish, reddish or bluish, for example. Coloured glasses are used as sunglasses and ski goggles, for 3D films or simply for fun.
wichtigste: Through glasses with yellow lenses the world looks yellowish.
Simple cardboard 3D glasses often have red and cyan lenses.
With red-cyan 3D glasses each eye sees a slightly different picture, which is why it looks three-dimensional.
Through red lenses a blue sky looks dark.
If you take off red glasses after a long time, everything looks greenish for a moment.
Yellow or orange lenses help skiers to see bumps in the snow better in fog.
Special colour-filter glasses can help people with red-green colour deficiency to tell some colours apart more easily.

abschnitte.text: White light consists of many colours, from red through green to blue. The tinted lenses of coloured glasses act as **colour filters**: they let only some of these colours through and absorb the rest. That is why everything looks yellowish through yellow lenses. Through red lenses a **blue sky** looks dark, because hardly any blue light gets through. Objects in the colour of the lens, on the other hand, look bright.

Simple cardboard **3D glasses** have one red and one cyan lens. The picture for them consists of two slightly shifted part-images in red and cyan; this is called an **anaglyph**. Each lens lets only the matching part-image through, so each eye sees a slightly different picture. The brain puts the two pictures together into a three-dimensional impression. Because each eye gets only some of the colours, the colours of a film often look strange.

Skiers often wear goggles with yellow or orange lenses in fog. These filter out a lot of blue light and increase the **contrast**. This makes it easier to see bumps and hollows in the snow. In bright sunshine in the mountains, on the other hand, you use dark lenses with good **UV protection**. Cyclists and marksmen also use lenses of different colours depending on the light.

abschnitte.titel: The eye gets used to it
abschnitte.text: If you wear coloured glasses for a long time, your eyes get used to the colour. The **visual cells** for this colour become a little less sensitive, and the world soon looks almost normal. If you take off red glasses after a long time, for example, everything looks greenish for a moment. This is because green is the **opponent colour** of red. After a short time your eyes adjust again.

About eight per cent of men and far fewer women have a **red-green colour deficiency**. They find it hard to tell some shades of red and green apart. Special **colour-filter glasses** deliberately cut out certain parts of the light. This makes some colours easier to tell apart, even though the colour deficiency is not cured. For many of those affected this is a surprising experience.

begriffe.erklaerung: A transparent material that lets only certain colours of light through.
A picture made of two coloured, slightly shifted part-images for 3D glasses.
The difference between light and dark areas in a picture.
A visual weakness in which you find it hard to tell red and green apart.

gewusst: Many cinemas today no longer use red-cyan glasses, but glasses with polarising filters that do not distort the colours.
Red-cyan 3D pictures have existed since the 19th century.
Some people wear glasses with orange lenses in the evening to get less blue light from screens.

teile.einleitung: Fraunhofer lines are fine dark lines in the rainbow spectrum of sunlight. They reveal which chemical elements exist in the Sun and in distant stars. They are named after the Bavarian optician Joseph von Fraunhofer, who studied them closely in 1814.
wichtigste: In 1802 William Hyde Wollaston was the first to notice some dark lines in the solar spectrum.
In 1814 Joseph von Fraunhofer described more than 500 such lines.
Most of the lines are caused by absorption in the outer layers of gas of the Sun.
The double line D at about 589 nm comes from sodium.
The lines C and F come from hydrogen, H and K from ionised calcium.
The A and B lines are caused by oxygen in the Earth's atmosphere.
If the lines of a galaxy are shifted towards red, it is moving away from us.

abschnitte.text: If you send sunlight through a prism, it is split into the colours of the rainbow; this is the **spectrum**. If you look very closely, you can see many narrow dark lines in it. At these places light of a very particular **wavelength** is missing. These gaps are called Fraunhofer lines.

In 1802 the Englishman **William Hyde Wollaston** was the first to notice some dark lines, but he thought they were boundaries between the colours. **Joseph von Fraunhofer**, a glassmaker and optician in Bavaria, built particularly good prisms and measuring instruments. In 1814 he described more than 500 lines and labelled the most important ones with letters from A to K. These names are still used today.

In the hot interior of the Sun, light of all colours is produced. On its way out it passes through cooler layers of gas, whose atoms swallow up very particular colours; this is called **absorption**. Each element has its own fingerprint of lines. The Germans Gustav Kirchhoff and Robert Bunsen realised this in 1859 and so founded **spectral analysis**.

The bright yellow double line D at about 589 nanometres comes from sodium; the same yellow glows in old street lamps. The lines C and F belong to hydrogen, and the strong lines H and K in the violet to ionised calcium. The A and B lines do not form in the Sun at all, but through oxygen in the Earth's atmosphere. Opticians use refractive indices at certain Fraunhofer lines to define the **Abbe number**, which shows how strongly a glass spreads out the colours.

Thanks to the lines, we know what stars are made of, even though nobody has ever been there. In 1868 lines of an unknown element were found in the solar spectrum; it was named **helium** after the Greek word for sun. If the lines of a distant galaxy are shifted towards red, it is moving away from us. With this **redshift**, astronomers discovered that the universe is expanding.

begriffe.erklaerung: Splitting light into its individual colours.
The quantity that decides the colour of light, usually given in nanometres.
Atoms swallowing up light.
Identifying substances from their spectral lines.
The shifting of lines to longer waves when a light source moves away.

gewusst: Helium was first discovered on the Sun and only found on Earth decades later.
As a teenager Fraunhofer survived the collapse of the house where he was an apprentice, and afterwards he was given a gift by the Elector of Bavaria.
Today tens of thousands of dark lines are known in the solar spectrum.

teile.einleitung: Energy is the ability to make something happen: to move something, heat it, light it up or make it grow. Without energy no car would drive, no lamp would shine and your heart would not beat either. Energy cannot disappear; it only changes its form.
wichtigste: Energy is the ability to do work, to move or to heat.
Your body gets its energy from food.
Energy is measured in joules, electricity often in kilowatt-hours.
A hydroelectric power station uses the force of water.
A solar cell turns sunlight directly into electricity.
When a lamp shines, electricity becomes light and heat.
Wind and sun are energy sources that never run out.
Switching off the light when you leave a room saves energy.

abschnitte.text: **Energy** is found in everything that moves, is warm, shines or lies high up. There are many **forms of energy**, for example kinetic energy, heat, light, electrical and chemical energy. Energy is measured in **joules** (J), named after the Englishman James Prescott Joule. One joule is roughly the energy you need to lift a bar of chocolate one metre.

Your body gets its energy from **food**. Food stores chemical energy, which is released during digestion. On packaging the energy content is given in kilojoules (kJ) and kilocalories (kcal). Depending on age and activity, a child needs about 6000 to 10,000 kilojoules a day.

In a **hydroelectric power station**, flowing or falling water drives turbines that produce electricity. Switzerland gets over half its electricity in this way, for example at the Grande Dixence in Valais. In a **wind turbine** the rotor blades turn in the wind and drive a generator. A **solar cell** turns sunlight directly into electricity.

**Renewable energies** such as sun, wind, water and geothermal heat never run out. Oil, natural gas and coal, on the other hand, are **fossil fuels**, which formed over millions of years and will one day be used up. When burned, they release carbon dioxide, which drives climate change. That is why Switzerland wants to become climate-neutral by 2050.

Energy is never lost; it is only converted into other forms. When a lamp shines, **electrical energy** becomes light and heat. An old light bulb produced much more heat than light, whereas an LED is much more economical. When you ride a bike, the energy from food becomes kinetic energy.

Anyone who **switches off the light** when leaving a room saves energy. Switching appliances off completely instead of leaving them on standby, taking a short shower instead of a bath and airing rooms properly also help. The **energy label** on appliances uses letters and colours to show how economical an appliance is. Every kilowatt-hour saved protects the environment and your wallet.

begriffe.erklaerung: The unit of energy.
The energy a 1000-watt appliance uses in one hour.
Energy from sources that keep renewing themselves, such as sun and wind.
Coal, oil and natural gas, formed from plants and animals of prehistoric times.
A coloured label that shows how much energy an appliance needs.

gewusst: In about an hour and a half, the Sun sends as much energy to Earth as the whole of humanity uses in a year.
Your brain uses about a fifth of your body's energy.
At 285 metres, the Grande Dixence dam is the tallest gravity dam in the world.

teile.einleitung: The electronvolt, abbreviated eV, is a unit of energy used mainly in atomic and particle physics. It is the energy a single electron gains when it passes through a voltage of one volt. Because atoms and particles are so tiny, the joule would be far too large a unit for them.
wichtigste: One electronvolt is about 1.602 · 10⁻¹⁹ joules.
If an electron passes through 5000 volts, it gains 5000 eV, that is 5 keV.
A particle with double charge, such as an alpha particle, gains twice as much energy at the same voltage.
One megaelectronvolt (MeV) is about 1.6 · 10⁻¹³ joules.
The rest energy of an electron is about 511 keV, that of a proton about 938 MeV.
To ionise a hydrogen atom you need 13.6 eV.
In the LHC at CERN near Geneva, the protons have had an energy of 6.8 TeV per beam since 2022.

abschnitte.text: When a charged particle flies through an electrical **voltage**, it is accelerated and gains energy. An electron that passes through exactly 1 volt gains exactly 1 **electronvolt**. The energy is calculated as charge times voltage. For a particle with double charge, such as an alpha particle, the energy doubles: 1000 volts give 2 keV.

One electronvolt is about 1.602 · 10⁻¹⁹ joules, an unimaginably small amount of energy. For comparison: to lift a bar of chocolate one metre, you need roughly one joule. That is why prefixes are used, such as **keV** (kilo, a thousand), **MeV** (mega, a million), GeV (giga, a billion) and TeV (tera, a trillion). 1 MeV is about 1.6 · 10⁻¹³ joules.

In the world of atoms the electronvolt fits perfectly. To remove the electron from a hydrogen atom takes 13.6 eV; this is called the **ionisation energy**. A particle of visible light has roughly 2 to 3 eV. X-rays, on the other hand, have thousands of electronvolts. An electron passing through 100 volts already reaches a speed of almost 6 million metres per second.

According to Albert Einstein's famous formula E = mc², every mass contains energy, the so-called **rest energy**. That is why particle physicists often give masses in electronvolts. An electron has a rest energy of about 511 keV. A proton is almost 2000 times heavier and has about 938 MeV. The Higgs particle, discovered at CERN in 2012, comes to about 125 GeV.

At the **CERN** research centre near Geneva stands the **Large Hadron Collider** (LHC), the largest particle accelerator in the world. Its ring is about 27 kilometres long and lies deep underground on the border between Switzerland and France. Since 2022 the protons there have reached 6.8 TeV per beam. When two beams collide head-on, 13.6 TeV are available.

begriffe.erklaerung: The energy an electron gains when it passes through a voltage of 1 volt.
The smallest free electric charge, carried for example by an electron.
Removing an electron from an atom.
The energy contained in the mass of a particle at rest.
A large machine that uses electric fields to bring particles to almost the speed of light.

gewusst: One teraelectronvolt is roughly as much kinetic energy as a flying mosquito has, but for a tiny proton that is enormous.
The electronvolt is not one of the SI units, but it is officially accepted for use with them.
Old tube televisions accelerated electrons with many thousands of volts to draw the picture on the screen.

teile.einleitung: An electric field is the space around electric charges in which other charges feel a force. You cannot see it, but you can show it clearly with field lines. Electric fields make your hair stand on end and drive the current in every cable.
wichtigste: An electric field exerts a force on electric charges.
Field lines start at positive charges and end at negative charges.
Where the field lines are close together, the field is strong.
Two field lines can never cross, because the field has only one direction at each point.
The field of a single point charge is radial, that is star-shaped.
An electron is accelerated against the direction of the field.
Uncharged particles such as the neutron are not deflected in an electric field.

abschnitte.text: Every electric **charge** changes the space around it. In this space, the **electric field**, another charge feels a force. Like charges repel each other, unlike charges attract. The field strength E is the force divided by the charge and is given in volts per metre or newtons per coulomb.

To show the invisible field, you draw **field lines**. They start at positive charges and end at negative ones. Their direction shows where a positive test charge would be pushed, and the density of the lines shows the strength. Two field lines never cross, because the field has only one single direction at each point. The clear idea of field lines was introduced by the Englishman **Michael Faraday** in the 19th century.

Around a single **point charge** the field lines run radially, that is star-shaped in all directions. Between two parallel plates with opposite charges the field is almost equally strong and points the same way everywhere; it is called **uniform**. In equilibrium, field lines always meet a metal surface at right angles. Inside a metal body, on the other hand, the field is zero.

A positively charged particle is accelerated in the direction of the field, but an **electron** is accelerated against the direction of the field. This property is used to steer electron beams in tubes or electron microscopes. A **neutron** has no charge and therefore flies through the field without being deflected. In the particle accelerator at CERN near Geneva, too, particles are accelerated with electric fields.

A closed metal cage shields electric fields; inside it stays free of fields. This **Faraday cage** also exists in everyday life: a car or an aeroplane protects the people inside when struck by lightning. In a metal lift your mobile phone sometimes has poor reception. Cables are also shielded with metal mesh so that interference cannot get in.

begriffe.erklaerung: A property of particles such as electrons and protons that causes electrical forces.
An imaginary line that shows the direction and course of a field.
Shows how strong the force on a charge is at a particular place.
A field that is equally strong and points the same way everywhere.
A metal shell inside which there is no electric field.

gewusst: Sharks can sense the weak electric fields of their prey with special sense organs.
If you rub a balloon on your hair, an electric field forms that attracts small scraps of paper.
Huge electric fields also build up between the ground and thunderclouds until lightning discharges them.
